News.title: A level results day - live: Grade boundaries for AQA, OCR and Edexcel revealed
News.content:
A record number of students have gotten into university or college (stock)

UCAS figures show the most popular courses are engineering and technology, social sciences and law, with an increase in students getting accepted onto their firm choice

Students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland received their A-Level, BTEC and T-level results this morning - with a record high 262,820 18-year-old accepted onto courses at universities and colleges.

Figures show a significant gap between the proportion of A-level entries in London getting the top grades compared to the north-east or the East Midlands.

Some 32.7 per cent of entries in the capital were awarded A or A* this year, up from 32.1 per cent in 2025 and the highest for any region in England. The North East and the East Midlands had the joint lowest rate, at 23.1 per cent.

The proportion of A-level entries awarded top grades rose for the third year in a row, likely driven by the popularity of maths and students scoring highly in it.

More than a quarter (28.5%) of UK entries were awarded an A or A* grade, up by 0.2% percentage points on last year, when 28.3% achieved the top grades. Maths remained the most popular subject at A-level this year – the 13th year in a row it has topped the table.

News.title: Keely Hodgkinson shows true colours as she speaks out about what athletics has cost her
News.content:
Keely Hodgkinson shows true colours as she speaks out about what athletics has cost her

Keely Hodgkinson is going for gold at the European Athletics Championships after making numerous sacrifices to get where she is

View 3 Images Keely Hodgkinson has spoken about the downsides of her athletics career (Image: Time to ZOOM In/YouTube)

Keely Hodgkinson has opened up about the sacrifices she made to become one of world athletics' biggest stars. The Olympic 800m champion, 24, has the world at her feet as she looks to become European champion in Birmingham this week.

‌



But it hasn't all been plain sailing for the Manchester-born sensation, who has been forced to swerve some aspects of life most young women take for granted, most notably the time away from family and friends.

‌



Speaking ahead of the European Championships, she was asked what her success had cost her over the years. Hodgkinson told the Time to ZOOM In show with Jeremiah Azu: "I think it costs you a lot of sacrifice from family and friends.

‌



"I travel a lot, so I spend a lot of months of the year not at home. I'm quite fortunate that when I do go back home, my family's there."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

Hodgkinson admits her focus on her sport means she hasn't been able to explore other, undiscovered parts of her personality. She added: "Also, some parts of my personality. It [athletics] comes with a lot of discipline and time where you're thinking about how you can be better.

‌



Keely Hodgkinson's BBC interview gatecrashed moments after run as Brit caught by surprise READ MORE :

How to watch European Athletics Championships for free - TV channels and full schedule READ MORE :

"I'm big on self-improvement, both in personality and physically. You spend so much time on that, that you could have missed out on a whole other part of you that you haven't discovered."

Meanwhile, Hodgkinson insisted she has nothing to prove after kicking off her quest for a hat-trick of successive European titles with victory in her opening 800m heat in Birmingham. Hodgkinson crossed the line in one minute, 57.28 seconds, fastest of the heats.

View 3 Images Hodgkinson is one of the favourites for 800m gold in Birmingham (Image: Sona Maleterova/Getty Images)

‌



The Briton's showdown with Swiss rival Audrey Werro has been billed as the race of the championships, but Hodgkinson is taking it all in stride. She said: "I don't think I need to put out any kind of statement. I back myself, I don't need to go crazy trying to prove anything.

"That will come in the final, hopefully, when it really matters. Happy to do that, happy to be in shape and healthy, most importantly. I'm just ready."

View 3 Images Hodgkinson has spoken candidly about life as an athlete (Image: Steven Paston/PA Wire)

Article continues below

Hodgkinson is set for a scorching semi-final in Birmingham, where an amber warning for "extreme heat" has been issued for Thursday.

The 800m semis at the Alexander Stadium start at 12.10pm, when the Met Office expects the temperature to hit 32 degrees Celsius.

News.title: Criminal probe launched as pilot and student die in 'disturbing' Essex plane crash
News.content:
Criminal probe launched as pilot and student die in 'disturbing' Essex plane crash

Indian student Vamshi Mandala, 25, chartered the flight, piloted by Dylan Patel, 26, to celebrate finishing university - but it crashed into a field in Essex

View 3 Images Student Vamshi Mandala, 25, (Image: Essex Police)

A criminal investigation has been launched into the deaths of two people after an experience flight crashed into a field in Essex.

Indian student Vamshi Mandala, 25, chartered the flight to celebrate finishing university. It was piloted by Dylan Patel, 26.

The two-seat Cessna crashed over farm land in High Ongar on June 30. It was carrying out a 30-minute trip.

The plane came down near Mill Road just eight minutes after it had taken off from North Weald Airfield shortly before 12.30pm.

Essex Coroner's Court heard today that both men died at the scene from multiple injuries.

View 3 Images Pilot Dylan Patel, 26 (Image: Essex Police)

Lincoln Brookes, the senior coroner for Essex, said: "This is a real tragedy and the unexpected deaths of both of these young men in such traumatic circumstances can only be described as truly disturbing."

The coroner also revealed that Essex Police had asked for proceedings to be suspended "pending the outcome of a police investigation".

He warned their families that this process could take "considerable amount of time", thus a date for a full inquest could not be set. "I'm sure their passing has left a huge hole in your lives. I offer my deepest condolences to you all," Brookes said.

View 3 Images Police at the scene of the crash (Image: EssexLive)

Members of the public called police when they saw the plane coming down. Officer identified the pair using DNA and fingerprints.

"An ambulance was called and paramedics confirmed death at the scene," coroner's officer Debbie Wallace said at the inquest opening.

Article continues below

Flight tracking data showed the aircraft had been flown twice already that day. Mandala's friend was on one of the trips.

The flight experience cost at least £125 for a 30-minute journey. It also offered customers supervised access to the plane's dual controls.

News.title: Prince Edward and Sophie's son James receives A-Level results and reveals future plans
News.content:
Prince Edward and Sophie's son James receives A-level results and reveals future plans

James, the Earl of Wessex, who is the son of the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh and the youngest grandchild of the late Queen, has received his A-level results today

James Wessex on Palace balcony for Jubilee in 2022

The Earl of Wessex will start university in September after receiving his A-level results today, Buckingham Palace has announced.

‌



James Wessex like thousands of other teenagers across England, Wales and Northern Ireland, received his exam results this morning and it has been revealed the son of the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh will be attending the Royal Agricultural University in Gloucestershire to study Rural Land & Property Management.

‌



The 18-year-old, who is the King's nephew and the youngest grandchild of the late Queen, will not be taking a year out and will start there in a few weeks. Buckingham Palace did not share details of his A-level results or the subjects he studied at the private Radley College in Oxfordshire.

‌



Lady Louise Windsor joined by boyfriend as dad Edward presents Duke of Edinburgh award in Palace celebration READ MORE :

View 5 Images James with sister Lady Louise Windsor and mum Sophie, the Duchess of Edinburgh (Image: UK Press via Getty Images)

But to be accepted on the course, students need to achieve at least 104 UCAS points across three A-levels - or the equivalent of BCC. A statement from the Palace said: "Having achieved the grades he needed, The Earl of Wessex will be going to the Royal Agricultural University to study Rural Land & Property Management. He will head straight there without taking a year out."

The earl’s degree course is described on the university’s website as teaching "the fundamentals of rural professional practice as well as planning and development, law, valuation, building construction and management".

‌



It added: "You will develop an essential understanding of sustainability and wider business management to enable you to provide effective advice about farm, estate and other rural businesses while gaining an overall understanding of the multi-functionality of rural practice."

It comes just weeks after his older sister Lady Louise Windsor, 22, completed her degree in English and international relations and graduated from the University of St Andrews. She is planning a mix of working, volunteering, and travelling before looking at her future career options.

Like his sister, James has grown up away from the public spotlight, only joining his royal relatives at the most important royal occasions. He was at the state funeral of his grandmother Elizabeth II, joined the rest of his cousins for a special vigil over her coffin at Westminster Hall and also attended the Coronation of his uncle, the King.

‌



View 5 Images James has largely grown up away from the spotlight (Image: PA)

In recent years, he has also appeared publicly with his parents at events such as Trooping the Colour and the traditional Easter Sunday church service at Windsor Castle. In June he made his first appearance at Royal Ascot and was spotted in the royal box alongside mu, Sophie.

It recently emerged that, like his sister before him who took a job in a garden centre, James has been earning money helping out on the farm on the Sandringham estate. He reportedly has been spotted mucking in, getting his hands dirty as well as driving tractors.

‌



Royal expert Jennie Bond explained: “We know that James is an affable, popular young man who enjoys the outdoor life (especially at Balmoral). Fly fishing with his mum is a favoured activity and he is said to be pretty good at it. He enjoys the barbecues - he can flip a burger expertly! And, just like his sister, he has been brought up to mix with all sorts of people, and enjoys sleepovers and parties with friends.

"Sophie and Edward have been incredibly successful about keeping their children out of the limelight, James even more so than Louise. But by all accounts, he is an outgoing young man who will take his rightful place at official occasions, but will never be a full-time working royal."

He was born in December 2007 at Frimley Park Hospital in Surrey - close to his parents' home of Bagshot Park. His full name is James Alexander Philip Theo - with his middle name Philip clearly a nod to his late grandfather Prince Philip. When he was born, he was eighth in line to the throne, but has now dropped down to 17th.

‌



View 5 Images James with his parents and sister at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham (Image: Getty Images)

He previously had the courtesy title of Viscount Severn, but when his father Prince Edward became Duke of Edinburgh in March 2023, James was then styled by his father's previous title of Earl of Wessex.

It's unclear what he or his older sister Louise, who is about to embark on a gap year after graduating from St Andrews University, will choose to do in the future. However, in 2020, around the time that Lady Louise was finishing school, mum Sophie opened up about her two children's education.

‌



She previously told The Sunday Times: "We try to bring them up with the understanding they are very likely [going] to have to work for a living. Hence why we made the decision not to use HRH titles. They have them and can decide to use them from 18, but I think it's highly unlikely.”

Meanwhile, when it comes to royal A-Level results, some members of the Royal Family have fared better than others. Prince William studied for his A-levels at Eton College, and when he received his grades in 2000, he achieved an A in geography, a B in art and a C in biology.

5 View 5 Images Lady Louise Windsor with her parents the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh on her graduation day last month (Image: University of St Andrews/PA Wire) 5 View 5 Images Louise has completed her degree in English and international relations (Image: University of St Andrews/PA Wire)

‌



His younger brother Prince Harry also attended the same school and achieved a B in Art and D in Geography at A-level. The Princess of Wales went to Marlborough College in Wiltshire for her A-levels and her diligence resulted in As in Maths and Art, and a B in English.

Meanwhile, the King left his school of Gordonstoun in 1967 with two A-levels - a B in History and a C in French. He then proceeded to Cambridge University, where he earned a 2:2 degree in history.

Article continues below

Princess Eugenie earned two As in Art and English Literature and B in History of Art, surpassing her older sister Princess Beatrice, who received an A in Drama and Bs in History and Film Studies.

Lady Louise, the youngest granddaughter of the late Queen, received her A-level results in 2022. Buckingham Palace didn't disclose Louise's results, but given that she went to the University of St Andrews - one of the country's top universities - standard entry grades are set at AAA and minimum entry grades of ABB for English - the course she studied - so it's safe to assume she did very well.

News.title: Cast's John Power reveals 'special' insight into Oasis reunion ahead of Knebworth 2027 dates
News.content:
Cast's John Power reveals 'special' insight into Oasis reunion ahead of Knebworth 2027 dates

Cast frontman John Power has shared an insight into touring with Oasis last year and whether he will be at both the Etihad Stadium and Knebworth next year

View 2 Images Oasis will be hitting the road again next year (Image: Big Brother Recordings)

Cast's John Power has revealed whether the band will be at Knebworth with Oasis next year. Fans of the mega band are eagerly awaiting official confirmation that Liam and Noel Gallagher will once again be hitting the road next year.

‌



It's expected that the two brothers will be performing 12 nights at their beloved Manchester City ground, the Etihad Stadium, and will also return to Knebworth for six nights. Concert promoter SJM Concerts was recently granted a new events license for Knebworth House.

‌



But after supporting the band on their mammoth Oasis Live '25 tour last year, which he says was like a "communion," John Power has now revealed whether he'll be back on stage next year. Acting coy, John said: "Is that happening though?"

‌



View 2 Images John Power has given an update on whether he will be supporting Oasis next year (Image: Samir Hussein/WireImage)

Speaking to Chris Moyles on Radio X, John added: "There's a lot of rumours. I've been in this industry long enough to know that rumours are rumours, aren't they?" He went on to add that he's "hopeful" he'll be on the guest list for a show.

But when asked if he thought being a guest would be bittersweet, having supported Oasis last year, he responded: "We went out for 23 shows. I was like, right, okay, you're gotta have to let this go. Because I was - we were nearly in the band!

‌



"You know, you never get over your first love." John, who with his Cast bandmates and Richard Ashcroft got the crowd ready for the comeback of the century last year, said the tour was a huge experience for all involved.

He commented: "Every night we would go and watch the bands, right? And every night I would sing my heart out to all the songs. I knew them from when they first came out, but there was just something about the vibe.

"There was just something about it, a communion, a gathering. It became a happening more than a concert. And I think we needed it, you know?"

‌



John continued: "You know, the world is chaotic and it's quite a scary place out there. Sometimes you just need to gather the tribes and sing a song together. That's what happened that summer, and it was very special."

In recent days, Liam himself has been teasing fans on social media about the upcoming dates, with messages such as "Manifestation for the nation". And while he's not specifically confirmed anything, he did imply that confirmation is not too far away.

On Monday, one fan asked: "Do you not want us to be excited?" and Liam quipped back: "Yes, of course, be excited, smash things up. But these things take time to announce if they're getting announced. I'm all for announcing things if they need to be announced but just coz you got something to announce doesn’t mean you should announce."

‌



He later replied to another fan: "I don't know why everyone is rushing around, it's making me anxious, chill the f**k out." Sources close to the band have confirmed to the Mirror that the band plans to play the Etihad Stadium, most likely beginning in June. They will then return to Knebworth, the scene of their biggest-ever gigs, later in the year, with weekend slots, most likely in September.

Full confirmation of the tour and ticket prices is now just weeks away. The Mirror understands that any official announcement about tickets for the 2027 shows is being held back whilst the new documentary Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger is publicised and promoted.

The London Premiere takes place on September 7, and so tickets may well go on sale after this date or after the promotion has finished. Both Noel and Liam are expected at the London premiere and the World premiere at the Venice Film Festival.

News.title: The Friday's Girl star Sheila Mathews dies as tributes paid to 'longest serving performer'
News.content:
The Friday's Girl star Sheila Mathews dies as tributes paid to 'longest serving performer'

Sheila Mathews, dubbed Britain's longest serving performer' has died aged 99, after a glittering career that spanned almost a century

View Image Sheila Mathews and her husband Charles reading in 1957 (Image: PA)

Sheila Mathews has died, aged 99. Having first performed aged three, Sheila's 96 years in the spotlight meant she was dubbed 'Britain's longest serving performer'.

‌



The iconic actress and singer was best known for her appearances on nightly music show Friday's Girl, becoming a household name to more than 12 million viewers. She was also at the launch of ITV back in 1955 and landed her own show the evening after. Across her career, she went on to be in popular soaps including Crossroads and Emmerdale.

‌



Intermission Magazine announced her death earlier this week: "We received the sad news that the multi-talented Sheila Mathews, whose career in the golden days of British entertainment was vast and varied, has died aged 99.

‌



“Neil Clark met Britain’s longest serving performer for our Intermission magazine and we present this in tribute to her remarkable life and career. Thank you for the memories Sheila. RIP.”

Sheila first began performing on stage in 1930. By 1943, she was appearing on the West End alongside future comedy star Eric Morecambe, in Strike a New Note. Eric went on to be part of iconic comedy duo Morecambe and Wise, with Ernie Wise, but died in 1984.

Sheila was briefly engaged to a magician and entertainer called Peter Waring, but did not marry him. In 1957, Sheila married director Charles Reading, who was the only man to have directed the Duke of Edinburgh in a film. Charles died in 1999, aged 88. In the course of their 42 year marriage, Sheila and Charles had two children, Sally and Jane, who have survived her.

‌



When she took on Friday's Girl, a show built to showcase her singing, Sheila became one of the first popular singers to top the TV ratings. She later added presenting as a string in her bow, by taking on shows such as On View, from 1957 to 1962, and later In My View.

Tributes flooded in for Sheila, including from former colleagues, friends and family. One fellow actress, Marianne Welsh wrote on Facebook: "Sheila played my mother in the musical The History of Mr Polly at the Churchill Theatre Bromley in 1977 and I often gave her a lift home to where she was living at the time in a house on the slope to Muswell Hill as I lived in Tottenham.

"I always remember how welcoming it looked with a lamp left on in the lounge. She was excellent in the show and a lovely lady and we used to have great chats on the way home."

Article continues below

A friend added: "I knew Sheila, a wonderful and forever beautiful lady. Heard the sad news this morning. Rest in peace my dear."

News.title: Met Office issues 15-hour power cut alert as 47 areas face extreme heat – list

Met Office issues 15-hour power cut alert as 47 areas face extreme heat – list

The Met Office has warned people living in 47 areas that they should brace for 'adverse health effects' with power cuts also possible as temperatures reach 38C

UK weather: Amber warning in place for extreme heat

The Met Office has updated today's "extreme heat" amber alert to cover a swathe of new areas as parts of the UK face 38C.

‌



There are now 47 places covered by the weather alert, which warns "adverse health effects are likely to be experienced" in the coming hours.

‌



The alert came into force at 9am this morning and runs until midnight. It covers areas of the East Midlands, East of England, London and the South East, North West England, South West England, West Midlands, and Yorkshire and the Humber.

‌



The Met Office warning added: "The highest temperatures will be in parts of the the Midlands and western England, where 37 or even 38 Celsius could be reached."

View Image The amber weather warning is in place today (Image: Met Office)

Some changes in working practices and daily routines are also likely to be required in the affected areas and some heat sensitive systems and equipment may fail, with the potential for some power cuts and the loss of other services too, the forecaster warned today.

News.title: 'I'm a pharmacist and eating habits are making you feel hungrier'
News.content:
'I'm a pharmacist and eating habits are making you feel hungrier'

A pharmacist has explained how to get it right

View 3 Images Eating habits can be derailed during hot weather (Image: StockPlanets via Getty Images)

An expert has explained common summer eating habits that could be making you hungrier and sabotaging your body’s natural ‘fullness’ signals.

‌



Mike Wakeman, researcher, pharmacist and the brains behind Evera Nutrition, said: “Summer should make healthy eating easier as people prefer lighter foods at this time of year. But holidays, BBQs, alcohol, grazing and later meals can quietly disrupt the signals that normally tell us when we’ve eaten enough.

‌



“Hunger isn’t simply about willpower – appetite is controlled by a sophisticated conversation between the gut and brain. When we eat, the gut releases hormones including GLP-1 and GIP that help coordinate blood glucose and communicate fullness to the brain.

‌



“And disrupting our normal eating routine may affect these signals. In a controlled 14-day study, women following an irregular eating pattern had a substantially lower post-meal GLP-1 response than after regular eating, despite being given identical foods. Other research found late eating altered the release of two other appetite hormones - ghrelin and leptin - increasing hunger and driving the urge to eat.”

View 3 Images There's been plenty of barbecue weather in the UK this summer (Image: G-PETER-73 via Getty Images)

Five ways your summer diet could be working against your natural fullness signals

Grazing all day

Mike said: “Snacking and constant BBQ picking can replace proper meals. Instead, build meals around protein and fibre. One large study found higher-protein meals increased fullness and GLP-1, while reducing hunger and the hunger hormone ghrelin."

‌



Not eating enough filling fibre

Mike said: “One particularly interesting fibre is glucomannan from the konjac plant, which absorbs water and expands in the stomach. As a result, glucomannan contributes to weight loss in the context of an energy-restricted diet when consumed daily in three 1g doses before meals with water."

Don’t fall for ‘fat-burning’ quick fixes

Mike said: “Summer can bring the temptation to look for a single ‘fat-burning’ food or ingredient, but appetite and weight regulation are complex. Look at the bigger picture – regular meals, enough protein and fibre, plus for weight loss help and support try Evera Nutrition Go Lean Plus. Backed by research, it includes ingredients - glucomannan, resveratrol, hibiscus, green tea, berberine, curcumin, cinnamon and mulberry – which all help influence the fullness hormones - GLP/GiP – vital when it comes to weight management and weight loss. For instance, resveratrol has been shown to have a significant effect on BMI, waist circumference and bodyweight, while the catechins (EGCG) in green tea can help to reduce body weight, BMI and waist circumference.”

View 3 Images Treats can be more abundant in summer (Image: Fly View Productions via Getty Images)

Article continues below

Look beyond calories – plant compounds could play a role in fullness

Mike said: “Research shows that certain plant compounds can boost the body's natural fullness hormones, GLP-1 and GIP. Scientists are investigating how specific nutrients encourage hormone release, enhance signalling, or slow down their breakdown. For example, cinnamon, fenugreek, green tea and resveratrol (found in grapes) may positively impact these pathways. Polyphenols like quercetin- found in onions and apples - and curcumin from turmeric also show potential in stimulating the specialised intestinal cells that release GLP-1.”

Eating late into the evening

Mike said: “Long summer evenings can mean dinner gets eaten later. Researchers found eating later increased hunger even when calories, diet, activity and sleep were kept the same. Regular mealtimes may therefore help your body's natural appetite signals work more predictably.

“The simplest summer advice? Stop grazing, put protein and fibre back at the centre of meals, eat at reasonably consistent times – and think about how the nutrients and plant compounds in your diet may interact with your body's natural appetite and metabolic signalling.”

News.title: Met chief accepts mistakes made over Simon Levy but defends investigation into murders
News.content:
The head of the Metropolitan Police Sir Mark Rowley has defended the force's investigation into double murderer Simon Levy.

Levy was on bail and being monitored by police when he murdered Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo in March 2025 and Sheryl Wilkins five months later, as well as violently raping a third woman.

Sir Mark acknowledged mistakes over the force's handling of Levy, but said suggestions it had not tried to build a case over his first murder were "just not true", following criticism including from Labour MP Jess Phillips.

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that detectives had done "serious" work but "didn't have enough evidence" for a charge.

However, the Met did not seek a charging decision from the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) over Valencia-Trujillo's murder until after Wilkins had been killed.

The police and CPS has apologised over a series of decisions that left the convicted sex offender free to attack the women.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) is currently examining how Levy, 40, was managed over the four-year period from his first conviction in September 2021 for sexual assault up to his final arrest in September 2025.

At the Old Bailey on Wednesday, he was given a whole life prison sentence, meaning he will never be released.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Sir Mark - who on Wednesday called the case a "whole system failing" - said he had already apologised for what the Met had got wrong.

It emerged after Levy's conviction that the Met did not class Valencia-Trujillo's death in March 2025 as a murder, or pass the case to specialist homicide detectives, until after he had killed again.

But Sir Mark said "the public debate needs to be better informed" because "the facts on that are much more complex than people want to acknowledge".

He said that while Valencia-Trujillo's death was "clearly very suspicious and concerning", a pathologist was unable to determine a cause of death and the force "didn't have enough evidence to get to a charge".

Sir Mark added it was only after the murder of Wilkins that the Met had the "combined evidence" to move forward.

"So the inference that the Met didn't try on that case is just not true, the Met tried," he said.

However, the Met did not ask the CPS for advice about Valencia-Trujillo's death, let alone a charging decision, until after the murder of Wilkins, the BBC has previously reported.

The fact there was no formal cause of death would not have prevented the case being taken on by specialist homicide detectives, who are skilled at building murder cases even when there is not a formal cause of death.

Levy's semen was on Valencia-Trujillo and his blood was at the murder scene. CCTV that showed Levy in the area, walking in the same direction as Valencia-Trujillo shortly after she passed a camera, was not viewed by the local team despite being gathered.

Other possible relevant CCTV was never gathered, and had been deleted by the time the specialist murder team took over months later.

In that case, the local team investigating the death did not engage with the Met's specialist murder teams apart from the day her body was discovered in March 2025.

A specialist homicide team attended the crime scene that day and recommended the case stay with local officers pending further enquiries, but there was no further contact until after Wilkins was murdered in August.

News.title: Once-in-a-generation solar eclipse wows millions in UK and Europe
News.content:
The UK and Europe have enjoyed their most dramatic solar eclipse for nearly 30 years, with millions thought to have witnessed the once-in-a-generation event.

Those watching the astronomical phenomenon from the UK were treated to a partial eclipse, which peaked shortly after 19:00 BST, when most saw more than 90% of the Sun covered by the Moon.

But parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain experienced the complete darkness and spectacle of a total eclipse.

Large crowds at viewing sites across the UK and Europe reacted with gasps and cheers, with astronomy enthusiasts saying it served as a reminder of how "amazing" the Universe is.

News.title: Watch: Key moments from Karoline Leavitt's White House tenure as Trump says she will leave post
News.content:
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will step down from her role at the end of August to spend time with her young children and family, after welcoming her second child in May.

"Karoline will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party," President Donald Trump wrote in a social media post announcing her departure.

Leavitt became the youngest press secretary in the country's history when she took the job in January 2025 at age 27.

News.title: Scientists invent 'world's greenest party balloon'
News.content:
Scientists in London have invented what they claim is the world's first fully biodegradable party balloon.

Researchers at Imperial College London say standard balloons can take years to break down and can release harmful chemicals.

But their new balloon biodegrades within nine months.

The research was part-funded by a party planner, who wanted to reduce the impact of balloon litter on marine wildlife.

The new balloon, called Bioloon, is no more expensive than a standard balloon and is easier to blow up, according to the scientists.

"Regular balloons are treated with a process to make them strong and stretchy," said 29-year-old co-inventor Juliana Cumming, a PhD researcher at Imperial. "But that process also stops them fully degrading and causes toxic chemicals to leach into the environment."

News.title: UK economy grows but experts warn of challenging months ahead
News.content:
Summer sun and sports fixtures helped the UK economy grow between April and June, according to official data, but some economists warned the outlook for the rest of the year was weaker.

The economy expanded by 0.4%, in line with market expectations but below a 0.6% increase in the first three months of this year.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said growth had "remained relatively robust", with the UK ahead of other G7 countries for growth this year so far.

Experts questioned whether this resilience would be maintained, however, given growth was fuelled by some temporary factors and energy prices could remain volatile if the Middle East conflict continues.

The British economy is now 1.2% bigger than a year ago, the ONS said, despite fears that the Iran war, which started at the end of February, and politically uncertainty around Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister would hold back growth.

Between April and June, sectors including computer programming, advertising and the pharmaceutical industry lifted growth. That was offset by falls in power generation and sewerage.

The ONS said some businesses reported that "good weather and sporting events may have had a positive effect" in June, boosting month-on-month growth to 0.3%.

The men's football World Cup, which kicked off mid-June, increased customers at hospitality venues showing the matches.

June also saw several of summer's heatwaves. However, May's growth was revised down from 0.1% to zero growth.

News.title: Polls open in Clacton by-election
News.content:
The polls have opened in Clacton-on-Sea as a record number of candidates vie to become the town's next MP.

An electorate of 79,785 registered voters have the chance to vote for one of 34 candidates standing in the Essex resort - the most ever to stand in a British election.

Fifty-one polling stations have opened, covering Clacton and the surrounding towns of Jaywick, Frinton and Walton-on-the-Naze. The constituency also has rural villages including St Osyth, Weeley and Great Bentley.

Voters will need to show a form of acceptable ID - such as a driving licence or passport - to be able to cast their ballot.

They will receive the longest ballot paper in British electoral history at 90cm - about 3ft long - to choose their candidate and cast their vote.

There are 12 political parties and 20 independents standing.

Polling stations will remain open to anyone registered to vote until 22:00, with the count taking place overnight.

News.title: Leading doctor rebukes NHS chiefs over transplant failings
News.content:
While NHS Blood and Transplant manages organ donations and supports transplant centres, services are commissioned and paid for by NHS England.

But in a letter to NHS England and a small group of patient advocates, Manas said the central body had created a "fragmented" system "with poor accountability".

There is a "mismatch", he said, between each hospital's waiting lists, organ availability, capacity to carry out surgeries and the availability of operating theatres.

This is "leading to last-minute cancellations [and] unpredictable utilisation of donated organs," he warned.

The BBC reported in March that the UK, once a world leader, had fallen behind major Western nations in heart and lung transplantation, though it fares better in other areas such as kidney transplantation.

The NHS transplants one in 10 lungs and one in seven hearts that are donated - half the proportions seen in some other countries.

It has not invested in modern technology at the same rate as other countries, and suffers from a lack of theatre space, intensive care beds and staff.

Wales and Northern Ireland do not have a heart and lung transplant centre, so patients commonly travel to England for surgery. There is one heart transplant centre in Scotland.

News.title: Results, appeals and resits - what to do if things don't go to plan
News.content:
Hundreds of thousands of students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland have opened their A-level, T-level and BTec results.

They were released at 08:00 BST on Thursday 13 August.

Those who have applied to university should be able to see whether they have been successful too, as the Ucas Hub updates at the same time.

Here is everything you need to know about results, appeals and resits.

News.title: Man jailed over one-punch death after pub row
News.content:
A man who fatally punched a fellow regular at a pub in a row over a phone charger has been jailed for five years after being convicted of manslaughter.

Harry Mannion, 28, punched 62-year-old Tony Powles to the ground during a row at the Red Lion on Batley Road in Wakefield on 9 October.

Powles, a father-of-four who was due to marry his partner the following week, suffered a "catastrophic brain injury" when he hit his head on the floor and died 13 days later, Leeds Crown Court heard.

In a victim impact statement, his daughter Rebecca Powles described him as the "absolute pillar of our family", adding: "He had so many friends and was loved by absolutely everyone who knew him."

Rebecca Powles said the family had been "forced to suffer beyond the boundaries of normal grief", telling the court: "We will never, ever forget having to make the excruciating decision to turn off his life support."

Mannion, himself a father of a five-year-old daughter, had denied manslaughter - claiming to have acted in self-defence - but was found guilty following a trial in June.

The court heard how the pair were both regulars at the Red Lion and had been "pub friends".

At the time Mannion, from Barnsley, was in a relationship with the pub's manager, while Powles had gone there that evening with his family.

Tensions arose when the defendant "took a dim view" of one of Powles's daughters serving behind the bar as part of her training to work there, prosecutor Matthew Harding said.

Later, Mannion was said to have taken exception to Powles's sister, Linda Wilson, using a phone charger belonging to him which had been behind the bar.

An argument ensued and Wilson left the bar.

When Powles found out about the disagreement, CCTV footage showed him approach Mannion at the bar, "when words were exchanged", said Judge Simon Phillips KC.

Powles then threw the charger, catching Mannion on the side of his head, before headbutting him.

About a minute later, when Powles was being restrained with his hands by his side, Mannion "threw a forceful punch at [the victim's] head", Judge Phillips said.

"This was retaliation from you, done in drink, from what had gone on moments before," Judge Phillips told the defendant, who appeared in court via video link from HMP Leeds.

News.title: Man dies days after explosion at bungalow
News.content:
A man has died in hospital days after a suspected gas explosion at a bungalow.

The explosion, which happened at 09:45 BST on Sunday, destroyed the home in Cobb Hall Road in Newton Longville, a village near Milton Keynes.

Thames Valley Police said a man in his 60s was taken to hospital where he was receiving treatment for his injuries. His death was announced on Thursday.

Det Insp Philip Turner-Robson said: "This is a tragic development and our thoughts are with the man's family and friends at this extremely difficult time."

He added: "Thames Valley Police is managing a coronial investigation into the circumstances surrounding the explosion and collapse of the property, working jointly with the Health and Safety Executive.

"Our inquiries remain ongoing as we seek to establish the full circumstances of what happened."

News.title: Streets evacuated after massive fire destroys homes
News.content:
Homes have been destroyed and 20 people had to spend the night in a leisure centre after a massive fire in south Wales.

There are no reports of casualties, but six bungalows were evacuated near Hazelwood Road, Newbridge, in Caerphilly county, on Wednesday.

"The houses were absolutely gutted. Their cars were damaged too," said councillor Adrian Hussey.

He said residents had tried to put the fire out but could not because it had been so severe.

It is still not clear how the fire started, but First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said fire services in Wales had been "at full stretch" because of the heatwave and wildfires this summer.

News.title: Arrest in Thetford migrant address sharing investigation
News.content:
Police have arrested a man as part of an inquiry into how the addresses of asylum seekers were shared during disorder linked to anti-immigration protests in a town, the BBC can reveal.

Properties in St John's Way, Bracken Road, Clover Way, Elm Road and Chester Way in Thetford, Norfolk, were recently targeted by crowds over three nights.

The man, in his 60s, was arrested on Friday on suspicion of assisting an offender and inciting racial hatred and has been released on bail until 14 October.

The houses are believed to have been used by Serco, a firm contracted to accommodate migrants, which said it was investigating allegations "relating to how address information has been made public".

The firm added it was working with the Home Office and Norfolk Police "to ensure that appropriate safeguarding measures are in place".

After his arrest, the man in his 60s was taken to Wymondham Police Investigation Centre for questioning.

News.title: Scottish Labour leader hopefuls warn against party divisions
News.content:
Scottish Labour leadership contenders have warned about the dangers of internal feuds and briefings at their first party hustings in Glasgow.

Monica Lennon, Joe Fagan and Michael Marra made their cases to succeed Anas Sarwar as they pitched to rebuild Scottish Labour after May's crushing electoral defeat.

Those attending the hour-long event were met by a handful of pro-Palestine protesters, whose shouts were heard during the first part of the event.

All three candidates promised to change, rebuild and unite the party following its worst Holyrood election defeat since devolution.

News.title: 'Online trolls who target me are bored and jealous'
News.content:
A woman who posts food reviews on social media has spoken out against the level of online abuse she receives after some trolls have urged her to take her own life.

Gloucestershire's Becca Stock, who has millions of followers on TikTok, said while "bored" and "jealous" people do target her online, they are in the minority.

She has shared her experience of online bullying following the University of Gloucestershire publishing new research into what drives digital abuse.

Dr Amy Grubb, associate professor of forensic psychology at the University, said posting comments online creates the "perfect storm" for abuse as the "digital environments reduce normal social restraints".

The research comes as mental health charities are reporting that online harms are having a growing impact on young people's wellbeing.

News.title: GB's Hudson-Smith wins historic 400m gold on home track
News.content:
On his childhood track, in front of a stand named in his honour, hometown hero Matthew Hudson-Smith was not going to be denied.

A full-circle moment, completed by writing his name in history.

More than two decades after stepping foot inside Alexander Stadium for the first time aged nine, Hudson-Smith delivered Great Britain's latest gold in Birmingham to become the joint-most decorated man of all-time at European Championships.

The 31-year-old celebrated the third European 400m title of his illustrious career by making his way into the crowd and placing a hand on the banner bearing his name.

Moments before, Hudson-Smith had stormed down the home straight, just as he had countless times before as a member of local club Birchfield Harriers.

This time, though, the Olympic and world silver medallist did so to rapturous cheers inside the arena which fostered his love for the sport.

With his eighth podium at the championships, Hudson-Smith equalled French sprinter Christophe Lemaitre's men's record medal tally - with the relays still to come.

"Honestly, words can't describe how much that meant to me," he told BBC Sport.

"Nobody was going to beat me on this track. This is my home. I know this track like the back of my hand. I have my stand. Now I'm going to go for Mayor of Birmingham and Wolverhampton!

"I knew I was the best in the world. I knew that, on paper, I was a second faster than every single one of these guys. It was about me and the clock."

News.title: Why is Amanda Knox's upcoming Edinburgh Fringe comedy show causing controversy?
News.content:
Amanda Knox, a woman involved in one of the world's most famous murder cases, is set to perform a comedy show at The Edinburgh Festival Fringe.

Knox was convicted and later acquitted of murdering her British roommate, Meredith Kercher, in Italy in 2007.

Knox's show, Cartwheel, is about motherhood and how she will explain her experiences to her daughter, according to the festival's website.

"I don't joke about Meredith's death. I joke a lot about how I was vilified, but I don't joke about her murder," she had told the Telegraph newspaper, external.

Kercher's sister, Stephanie told BBC Breakfast her sibling "wouldn't find these topics of any comedy value".

A petition against the show, set up by a friend of Meredith, has been signed by just over 2,400 people, and says the show disrespects her memory and also risks normalising violence against women.

A spokesperson for Knox said the show, set to run over 11 days from Friday, honours Kercher's memory.

Find out more about what Stephanie Kercher told the BBC.

News.title: Europe wildfire tracker: France and Spain at extreme risk of new fires as temperatures soar to 42C
News.content:

Europe is in the grip of its fifth heatwave this summer, raising fears that extreme temperatures could trigger another set of wildfires across the continent.

Wildfires have scorched more than 505,000 hectares (ha) of land across Europe during an unusually active wildfire season. A relatively wet winter that fuelled growth in vegetation was followed by rolling heatwaves which dried it all out, making the land more prone to catching fire.

During the same period, the extreme heat has been linked to 25,000 deaths this year, according to Bloomberg research covering Spain, France, the UK, the Netherlands and Switzerland.

Western Europe is suffering its hottest ever summer, with temperatures well above average.

On Thursday, temperatures are set to reach highs of 42C in Spain, including in the popular tourist hotspot of Cordoba, and 39C in Bordeaux, where a huge blaze forced the evacuation of more than 200,000 people last month.

Here, The Independent looks at where the risk of wildfires will be in the coming days.

Fire danger forecast

open image in gallery Large swathes of the continent remain under 'very high' wildfire risk, with some patches (shown in dark red) at ‘extreme’ risk ( Copernicus EFFIS )

The EFFIS current situation viewer shows vast swathes of western, central, eastern and southeastern Europe are at “very high” risk of a wildfire on Thursday. Some areas, shown in dark red on the map, are at “extreme” risk.

The main wildfire threat will continue moving eastwards before abating in much of western Europe early next week, when southern Spain and and central European countries are at the highest risk.

Fires were ongoing in western Europe as of Thursday with around 1,200 people evacuated from a campsite on Wednesday after two wildfires spread near a beach in the country’s north.

The prefecture for the administrative department of Pas-de-Calais, in the country's north and bordering the Strait of Dover, said one of the wildfires was under control, but conditions were "unfavourable" for the other one. Access was difficult and the fire was spreading unimpeded toward the south.

Entire regions burnt

open image in gallery Record amounts of land have burnt in the EU in 2026 ( Copernicus EFFIS )

A record amount of land has burnt this summer, surpassing the total for 2025 at this time of the year and more than double the 20-year average between 2006 and 2025.

As of 5 August, some 505,583 hectares (ha) of land had burnt, compared to 379,392 at this point in 2025, and well above the 2006 to 2025 average of 197,347 ha.

The fires have already cost the continent up to £16.4 billion in economic costs, estimates published by forecaster AccuWeather showed last Thursday. This includes the cost of emergency response, damage to property, and health impacts.

In one of the largest fires around Bordeaux, a record-setting fire burned around 420 square kilometres of land.

Record-breaking temperatures

open image in gallery The continent is far warmer than average for this time of year ( Copernicus EFFIS )

Western Europe reported a record-breaking 24-hour average temperature of 21.62C for June and July, according to a report by the EU’s Copernicus climate change service released on Monday.

This is 2.79C above the average temperature during the 1991 to 2020 period, smashing the previous heat record set in 2022.

Spanish forecaster Aemet says that tourist hotspots in Spain including Cordoba (42C), Sevilla (40C), Granada (39C), and Madrid (39C) will all see temperatures in the region of 40C on Thursday, while other touristy areas including Barcelona, Malaga and Alicante are all forecast to be in the low-to-mid 30s in the coming days.

Large parts of Spain, barring the eastern, southern and northwestern coasts, will be placed under yellow and amber warnings for the next three days.

In France, temperatures will near 40C in the popular tourist spots of Bordeaux, Nantes, and Toulouse.

Average rainfall plummets

open image in gallery Europe's summer has also been unusually dry, with red areas on the map showing areas with below average rainfall ( Copernicus EFFIS )

Prolonged drought conditions have played a critical role in driving up the wildfire risk, with droughts that began in May deteriorating in July and August.

Data from the European Drought Observatory updated on 10 August shows that 50 per cent of the UK and EU is suffering some level of drought intensity, whether at ‘watch, ‘warning’ or ‘alert’ level. Nine per cent was at the alert level in July.

Almost the entire continent, barring parts of Scandinavia, is set to experience less rainfall than usual in the week between 10 and 16 August, according to estimations by Copernicus based on the ECMWY Monthly Forecast System.

Europe’s four major rivers, the Loire, Po, Rhune and Danube, have been pushed to record low levels this month, according to Copernicus.

“The drought has built up since early spring due to lower rainfall and higher than average temperatures, turning into fuel for the devastating wildfires in France and Spain in July,” the EU’s Joint Research Centre said.

A Reform councillor has been suspended after resurfaced social media posts appeared to show him calling for the Commons speaker to be hanged.

In response to a post about then Commons speaker John Bercow, an account linked to Kirklees councillor David Rowan wrote on social media in October 2019: “Hang the Dwarf”.

In another post, which has not yet been deleted, the account also made homophobic comments, having said he doesn’t believe “gays should have kids full stop”.

A Reform UK spokesperson said: “Cllr Rowan has been suspended from Reform UK pending investigation.”

open image in gallery ( X )

Another post from Mr Rowan’s account also called for Westminster to be turned into a Wetherspoons, writing: “Think we should get our pick forks and whippets and demolish London.”

Mr Rowan, who was elected in May, also appeared to show support for far-right campaigner Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, known as Tommy Robinson, writing: “Thommy Robinson I salute you for caring.”

The Independent has approached Mr Rowan for comment.

Mr Rowan’s suspension comes weeks after a Reform councillor was charged with posting a grossly offensive message on social media. Glenn Gibbins, of Sunderland City Council, allegedly made the post, which referenced the Nigerian community, in 2024.

open image in gallery Cllr Rowan, who was elected in May, also appeared to show support for far-right campaigner Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, known as Tommy Robinson, writing: ‘Thommy Robinson I salute you for caring.’ ( Kirklees Council )

Nigel Farage continues to raise concerns about his own safety in the wake of the killing of Reform UK’s Ann Widdecombe.

Mr Farage has previously raised concerns about MPs’ security, including his own, and said after her death: “And I do fear that for anybody in public life, or especially the political space, things have become even more dangerous to them.”

The Reform UK leader said his party “had been treated very differently to everybody else” before the death of the former MP.

Counterterror police investigating the death of Ms Widdecombe have now reopened a year-old probe into an alleged firebomb attack at Mr Farage’s home in south London, reports have said.

Officers said the incident, which The Telegraph described as a “lit incendiary device” being posted through Mr Farage’s letterbox, was reported in April 2025.

Asked about the probe, Mr Farage told reporters at a press conference earlier this week: “It’s a great, great tragedy that it took the death of Ann for the security services in Britain to finally take seriously the safety and security of Reform politicians and Reform prominent figures.

“Up until that moment, we had been treated very differently to everybody else.”

open image in gallery Nigel Farage continues to raise concerns about his own safety in the wake of the killing of Reform UK’s Ann Widdecombe ( Reuters )

According to The Telegraph, Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice pressed his panic button at his house last Christmas after being approached by an aggressive man outside parliament. Officers then made an arrest.

Reform UK MPs were given round-the-clock security protection, paid for by the party, after Widdecombe’s death over fears of similar attacks.

Reform UK spokesperson and former Tory minister Widdecombe died on 8 July after she was hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, a court heard.

Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged with her murder on 20 July. He has not yet entered a plea and has been remanded in custody until his next court appearance.

News.title: As Abdul El-Sayed breaks a barrier, anti-Muslim vitriol surges on multiple fronts
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. Abdul El-Sayed made history this month in Michigan by becoming the first Muslim nominated by the Democratic Party to run for the U.S. Senate. But elation among many of his fellow Muslim Americans was tempered by awareness of persisting and widespread anti-Muslim sentiment across much of the nation.

Some Republicans, including President Donald Trump, swiftly began referring to the nominee by his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, while depicting him as a danger to America. “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a Trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic,'' said U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., in a post on X.

El-Sayed says such attacks betray a weakness in those who launch them.

“We all pray for the same things. ... We want what’s good for our kids and our families,” he told MS NOW after his primary victory. “They're going to use Islamophobia, because their ideas are tired.”

The vitriol extends far beyond the political class. Tensions related to anti-Muslim sentiment have heightened in several communities around the country, where some residents have bitterly opposed proposals to build new mosques.

“American Muslims have made incredible political and societal progress in recent years,” said Edward Ahmed Mitchell, national deputy director of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, or CAIR. He cited increased visibility in entertainment and sports and the election of Democrat Zohran Mamdani as New York City's first Muslim mayor.

“But there also is a very concerted backlash to this progress,” Mitchell said. “You've seen this in the resurgence of anti-Muslim hate and rhetoric, the targeting of mosques.”

A Dallas suburb is a flashpoint

McKinney, Texas, a large suburb in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, is one of the flashpoints. Despite angry anti-Islam remarks at a heated city council meeting on Aug. 4, the council voted unanimously to approve a site plan for the McKinney Islamic Association’s proposed new mosque, classroom building and gym.

Among those urging the council to give the plan fair treatment was George Fuller, a former mayor of McKinney, a nonpartisan position. Opponents of the mosque project booed him, and some shouted “traitor” as he left the council chamber. One woman could be seen on video physically accosting him.

“I have never witnessed so much hate, anger and lack of humanity in our beautiful community gathered in one place as I did today at City Hall,” Fuller later wrote on Facebook.

During the hearing, which lasted more than four hours, the speakers included U.S. Rep. Keith Self, a Republican whose district includes McKinney. To loud applause, he urged the council to reject the mosque proposal.

“I know you’re in the accommodation phase, but the intimidation phase follows quickly,” Self said. “Child marriage. Honor killings. Don’t tell me it can’t happen here.”

Fuller also went to the microphone, evoking the broader phenomenon of divisive political rhetoric.

“Sadly, we live in a time when some have discovered that the easiest way to gain attention or win elections is not by offering solutions but by manufacturing fear, dividing communities, demonizing neighbors and turning misinformation into a political strategy,” he said.

In North Carolina, anger flares over approval for a new mosque

The scenario was similar in Mooresville, North Carolina, when town commissioners held a public comment session on Aug. 3 about a proposed mosque that had already been approved, with early phases of construction underway.

Angry residents at the meeting voiced hostility to Islam and assailed the commissioners for not being more forthcoming about the project as it took shape over previous months. One speaker cited violence in Nigeria by Islamist extremists as a reason for concern in Mooresville. Another depicted Islam as “a political regime with the ultimate goal of takeover in regions and nations.”

CAIR’s regional manager, Al Rieder, issued a statement denouncing “the hateful and conspiratorial anti-Muslim rhetoric” that surfaced at the meeting and expressed concern about the safety of Muslims in the area about 25 miles (40 kilometers) north of Charlotte.

“Muslims are your neighbors, your doctors, your teachers, your local politicians, your police,” he said.

A few hours after the public meeting, the town commissioners released a summary of the mosque project, which calls for a two-building Islamic center on a parcel acquired in 2019 by a local Muslim organization.

The commissioners said that the parcel is in an area zoned to allow religious assembly and that the mosque proposal was handled the same way as a proposal for a new church.

“All decisions must be based on adopted ordinances, objective standards and legal requirements, which do not allow for different rules for different religious groups,” the commissioners said. “We encourage all members of our community to remain respectful in their discussions and interactions as this project moves through the appropriate processes.”

In Oklahoma, Muslim leaders fight against the rebuff of a new mosque

A mosque controversy has been raging for many months in Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, Tulsa's largest suburb.

Back in January, at a stormy meeting attended by hundreds of people, the city council voted 4-1 to reject a rezoning proposal by the region's Islamic Society to build Broken Arrow's first mosque. Before the vote, dozens of residents voiced anti-Muslim views while opposing the project.

Council members who rejected the mosque had raised concerns about its potential impact on infrastructure such as roads, sewers and flood plain management.

But the Islamic Society is persisting with its quest. On Aug. 3, it filed a lawsuit against the mayor and four councilors, alleging that the vote reflected “a wave of bigoted opposition from members of the community and local politicians.” The lawsuit contends that the council violated state and federal laws governing religious land use, treating the mosque proposal differently from other comparable rezoning requests.

“They did not want a mosque in their city. They did not want Muslims here,” said Meghan Murphy, an attorney with CAIR’s Legal Defense Fund, at a news conference announcing the lawsuit. ”So they made up a reason, and in doing so they violated the law.”

Some see a terrorism threat while others see baseless scaremongering

Opposition to mosque construction isn't a new phenomenon: In Murfreesboro, Tennessee, an effort launched in 2010 to block a mosque project dragged on for more than three years. The mosque was built anyway as the case moved through the courts, but members of the Muslim community faced public protests, vandalism, arson and a bomb threat during that span.

The latest anti-mosque campaigns coincide with a broad wave of anti-Muslim rhetoric from Republican officeholders over the past year. In Congress, several bills were introduced targeting sharia, the moral and spiritual framework that guides Muslims in prayer and ethical conduct. Some Republicans say they’re concerned about growing Muslim populations in major cities and potential ties to terrorism — fears that CAIR and other civil rights groups say are unfounded and being exploited for political purposes.

Republican governors in Texas and Florida have endorsed efforts to shut down CAIR, saying it has ties to terrorism. CAIR has denied the allegations and filed lawsuits calling the governors' efforts unconstitutional.

Muslim American leaders view the vitriol as political scaremongering.

“Every election year, we expect a rise in anti-Muslim hate,” said CAIR's Mitchell. “It's been worse this year than it has been in years.”

Fulham’s pre-season friendly with Malaga descended into chaos on Wednesday night, ending with Alvaro Arbeloa’s men walking off the pitch as the Spanish side took a penalty into an open net.

Malaga snatched a last-gasp equaliser against the Cottagers at the Estadio La Rosadela, with Eneko Jauregi converting from the spot in stoppage time to make it 2-2 after Calvin Bassey was penalised for a handball.

Cancelling put Alex Iwobi’s 57th-minute effort, it was the second time Fulham had surrendered a lead in the friendly, with Ryan Sessegnon trading a goal with Malaga’s Chupe in the first half.

However, the game did not end in friendly fashion, with new Fulham manager Alvaro Arbeloa seeing red for remonstrating with the referee at full-time.

open image in gallery Alvaro Arbeloa was sent off after the friendly ( Getty )

He then headed straight down the tunnel with the rest of his players, believing the match was over, while LaLiga outfit Malaga were expecting a penalty shootout to decide the winner of the Costa del Sol Trophy.

Malaga’s players remained on the pitch but Fulham did not reappear.

Spanish striker Eneko Jauregi appeased the crowd’s desire for penalties by placing the ball on the spot and converting into an open net, before celebrating with the home fans.

open image in gallery Eneko Jauregi fired into an empty net after Fulham walked off ( Getty )

Fulham has since asserted that both sides agreed the match would end without a penalty shootout if a draw was played out.

"We can confirm that prior to the match, both teams agreed that there would not be a penalty shootout in the event of a draw," the club wrote on X.

However, Malaga contest this and insisted that a shootout had indeed been scheduled.

"Although a penalty shootout had been scheduled, Fulham left the pitch, claiming that a shootout had not been included in the contract,” Malaga said on their club website.

Fulham, who have won just one of their five pre-season outings this summer, end their 2026/27 preparations against Stuttgart on Saturday at Craven Cottage.

They begin their Premier League campaign against Chelsea on Monday 24 August.

Olivier Award-winning actor Sharon D Clarke has been diagnosed with cancer, the Royal Shakespeare Company has announced, while revealing their production of Othello has been postponed.

Best known for her theatrical performances in Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom and Caroline, or Change, Clarke, 60, had been due to take on the titular role in a radical new production of Othello at the Swan Theatre next year.

But on Thursday (13 August), the RSC announced that the production had been delayed as Clarke “takes time to undergo treatment for cancer”.

In a statement, the Holby City star, who received an MBE in 2017, said: “I would like to thank all the beautiful people at the RSC for their understanding, love, support and healing energy. Othello will be my north star as I undergo treatment.”

open image in gallery Actor said that Othello would be her ‘north star’ during treatment ( Getty )

Clarke said that she, her family and wife, writer and director Susie McKenna, had been “overwhelmed, humbled and buoyed by the tidal wave of love that we have received and are so blessed to have an army of strength and support to hold us up”.

“Love and thanks to my beautiful people,” she said.

Those with tickets to see Clarke in Othello would be automatically refunded, the RSC said, adding that a replacement production for the 13 February to 3 April 2027 period would be announced in time.

Director Monique Touko, whose recent work has included Marie & Rosetta at @sohoplace and Jaja’s African Hair Braiding at the Lyric Hammersmith, said: “On behalf of the entire creative team, we send Sharon all the love for her ongoing treatment and recovery.”

She continued: “As a director, I have been incredibly blessed to collaborate with Sharon on this major reframing of Shakespeare’s tragedy, which reimagines Shakespeare’s Othello through the lens of misogynoir.

“Sharon is the ultimate collaborator. Her generosity and passion for this project continues to astound me and I look forward to us coming back together when the time is right to share this production with the world.”

open image in gallery With Queen Camilla in February 2025 ( Getty )

Announced in July, the original description for the RSC’s new Othello read: ”Set in a climate-threatened future in which a Black lesbian holds a seat of power, this movement and music-infused Othello by Monique Touko re-imagines Shakespeare’s 400-year-old story through the lens of misogynoir, as an unsanctioned marriage perilously crosses boundaries of race, sex and status, allowing jealousy, suspicion and malign intent to close in.”

A three-time Olivier winner, Clarke landed her first TV role in 1986’s The Singing Detective, and has worked consistently on stage and screen ever since.

To many audiences, she is best known as Lola Griffin from BBC medical drama Holby City. Clarke, who praised the show for its positive portrayal of a Black woman on TV, originally played the role from 2005 to 2008, before reprising the part in 2019.

In recent years, Clarke has also appeared in Rocketman, Red, White and Royal Blue, and Wicked and its sequel on the big screen, and Doctor Who, Showtrial and Mr Loverman on the small.

Most recently, Clarke starred as Lady Bracknell opposite Ncuti Gatwa in the National Theatre’s production of The Importance of Being Earnest.

News.title: 12 clever Tesco Clubcard tricks every shopper should know
News.content:
Tesco’s Clubcard has become a familiar part of supermarket shopping, with millions of households using it to access member-only prices and collect rewards. But if you’re only using your card to get a few pounds off your weekly shop, you could be missing out on some of its other perks.

Clubcard members earn points as they spend, which are then turned into vouchers that can be used on future Tesco purchases or with a range of partner brands. The value of those vouchers can vary depending on how you choose to use them, while there are also ways to boost your points balance without simply spending more money.

There’s another reason to check your Clubcard account, too. If you’ve accumulated points or vouchers and forgotten about them, you could be leaving money on the table, particularly if they’re approaching their expiry date.

From getting more value from your rewards to making sure nothing goes unused, these are the Clubcard tips worth knowing.



How to find out how many Clubcard points you have

To find out how many Clubcard points you have, simply sign in to your account online or on the Tesco app. Your balance will also be shown at the bottom of your most recent Tesco receipt, provided you scanned your Clubcard at the checkout.

You can turn your points into vouchers once you have at least 150 points (worth £1.50), either through the Tesco app or online. These vouchers can be used in-store at Tesco but you can also double their value by spending them with Tesco’s reward partners.

It’s also worth checking your account for any vouchers you’ve forgotten about. According to MoneySavingExpert, more than £11m worth of Clubcard vouchers are reportedly due to expire on 31 August. Clubcard vouchers are usually valid for two years from the date they’re issued, so any that are approaching their expiry date need to be used by the deadline.

open image in gallery ( iStock )

Where to spend your Tesco Clubcard vouchers

Save on Disney+

You can use Clubcard vouchers towards a Disney+ subscription, whether you're a new or existing subscriber. £9 in vouchers (900 points) gets you three months of the standard with ads plan, while £15 (1,500 points) gets you three months of standard without ads.

Get a free fractional share worth up to £100.

Capital at risk. Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

Get a free fractional share worth up to £100.

Capital at risk. Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

To redeem, choose your preferred Disney+ option through Tesco’s reward partner, exchange your vouchers and look out for a confirmation email containing your redemption code.

New subscribers can follow the link in the email to activate their subscription. Existing subscribers need to cancel their current subscription and reactivate it using the instructions provided by Tesco. You can continue using your existing subscription until it expires.

Triple your points with certain restaurants

Clubcard vouchers are usually worth up to twice their face value with Tesco’s reward oartners, but selected restaurants are currently offering triple the value. These include PizzaExpress, Las Iguanas, Bella Italia and more.

To use them, sign in to Tesco, choose your restaurant and enter the amount of vouchers you want to exchange. Tesco will email you a code to use when paying.

Check the individual restaurant’s terms before you go, as restrictions can apply to when and how Clubcard vouchers can be used.

open image in gallery ( iStock )

Before you book, it’s worth checking if you can get a better restaurant deal elsewhere and save your Clubcard points for something else. There are tons of restaurants offering kids eat free offers during the summer holidays, including all of the restaurants listed above, which could potentially be more worthwhile than using your Clubcard voucher.

In most cases, you won’t be able to claim an offer and use your Clubcard points, so it’s worth weighing up which will help you save more.

Days out

There are tons of days out available via Tesco’s reward partners, from Chessington World of Adventures to Cineworld. By spending your points this way, you’ll be able to double their value compared with what you would get if you spent them on groceries.

For example, £5 in Clubcard vouchers can be worth up to £10 when exchanged with Tesco’s reward partners, including attractions such as Legoland, so it’s worth checking what you have to spend if you’re planning a family day out.

Choose the day out you want through Tesco’s reward partners, exchange your Clubcard vouchers for a reward partner code, and Tesco will send it to the email address linked to your Clubcard account. You can then use the code with your chosen partner, subject to its individual terms and conditions.

open image in gallery ( iStock )

Hotels

Planning a holiday? You can use your Tesco Clubcard vouchers towards hotel stays with reward partners including Hotels.com, Mercure and Best Western, with vouchers worth up to twice their face value with some partners.

But remember, before exchanging your vouchers, make sure you shop around. Once converted, they can only be used with your chosen reward partner, and you may find a better price elsewhere.

Railcards

If you regularly travel by train, a railcard can be a useful way to cut the cost of your journeys, offering one-third off most fares. You can also put your Clubcard vouchers towards the cost, potentially making the saving even bigger.

For every £2.50 in Clubcard vouchers (250 points), you can get £5 to spend on selected Railcards, including the 16-25, Senior, Disabled Persons, Family & Friends and Two Together Railcards.

To redeem your vouchers, find your chosen Railcard on Tesco’s reward partners page and exchange your vouchers for a Railcard code. It’s also worth taking a look at our TrainPal discount code page , you may be able to get up to 20 per cent off the price of a railcard, which could be a better deal than using your Clubcard vouchers.

Swap Clubcard points for Virgin Atlantic points

If you fly with Virgin Atlantic, it could be worth converting your Tesco Clubcard vouchers into Virgin Atlantic Flying Club loyalty scheme points. You can exchange £1.50 worth of vouchers for 300 Virgin Points.

For full information on how to swap your points, see the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club page on Tesco’s website.

open image in gallery ( iStock )

Donate to charity

You can also put your Clubcard vouchers towards a charitable donation, although they’re redeemed at their face value rather than increased in value.

Tesco supports a range of charities, including FareShare, the Trussell Trust, British Heart Foundation, WWF and Cancer Research UK. To donate, choose your preferred charity through Tesco’s Clubcard charity page and follow the steps to make your donation online.

Magazine subscriptions

You can save on the cost of a magazine subscription by using your Tesco Clubcard vouchers at double their value. Exchange your vouchers for money to spend towards Hearst magazine subscriptions and you’ll be able to redeem your discount when you subscribe to the likes of Good Housekeeping, HouseBeautiful, and Country Living.

The Bauer Media Group is also partnered with Tesco, meaning that you can use your Clubcard points towards the cost of a subscription to Empire, Grazia, Country Walking and more.

More Tesco Clubcard tricks

Extend the life of Clubcard vouchers

Clubcard vouchers are usually valid for two years from the date they’re issued. If yours are approaching their expiry date and you’re not ready to spend them, there’s a way to potentially extend their validity.

The trick involves making a small purchase through one of Tesco’s reward partners, such as a charity donation. The amount you don’t spend is then returned to your Clubcard account as points. For example, if you use 50p from a £3 voucher, the remaining £2.50 would be credited back as 250 points.

You can then convert those points into new vouchers, which will have a fresh expiry date two years from the date they’re issued.

However, is a caveat: Tesco’s terms and conditions allow it to refuse a reward partner order if it believes the service is being used to extend the validity of vouchers. So, while the method has been reported to work, it isn’t something Tesco officially guarantees.

Get points for filling in surveys

You can collect additional Clubcard points by completing surveys through Shopper Thoughts. Each survey awards between 25 and 150 points, depending on its length. Once you’ve collected 500 points, you can redeem them for £5 in Clubcard vouchers, which could be worth up to £15 when used with selected Tesco reward partners.

To get started, complete your first survey, then link your Tesco account by heading to your profile and linked accounts on Shopper Thoughts. Once linked, you’ll be able to start earning Clubcard points from eligible surveys.

Earn points when sending parcels

If you regularly send parcels, you can earn Clubcard points on eligible postage bought directly through Evri’s website. Simply use Tesco’s ‘Send a parcel’ button to head to Evri.com, follow the usual booking process and enter your Clubcard number when you reach the basket. Tesco says you’ll collect one Clubcard point for every £1 spent.

The points will be added to the Clubcard account linked to the number you entered, usually within 14 days of placing your order. Just make sure you enter your Clubcard number correctly, as Tesco says points can’t be moved to another account if you enter the wrong number.

Charge your car and collect points

If you drive an electric car, you can earn Clubcard points while charging at Tesco. Just download the Pod Point app, find a Pod Point charger at a Tesco store and link your Tesco Clubcard. You’ll then collect one Clubcard point for every £1 spent on charging at eligible Pod Point chargers at Tesco stores.

The points should be added to your Clubcard account within seven days of your billed charging session, according to Tesco. So, if you're already stopping at Tesco and charging your car while you shop, you may as well pick up a few extra points at the same time.
