World.title: ‘That wasn’t my son’: Mother of Berlin Pride attacker confronts his turn to terror
World.content:
In the wake of the devastating events of July 25, Abdul Ballout's mother tries to reconcile the son she knew with what authorities have established about his radicalization.

The woman whose son brought terror to Berlin is sitting on a worn red leather couch in a three-room apartment in Berlin’s Tiergarten district. It is Thursday afternoon, and she is pointing to the several missed calls on her phone screen.

They are all from the evening of July 25. They are all from the same person: Abdul Ballout, her son.

“He was terribly afraid for me,” she says quietly, her voice trembling. “I didn’t know why.”

She scrolls through the call log — the last traces of her child from the day of the attack, the day the unknown 21-year-old became the most wanted man in Germany.





She wants the public to get to know him — the son, the brother, the young man that she knew. “I find the way people talk about him incredibly painful, to be honest,” she says. “He was a good person.”

These are the subjective recollections of a mother who cannot and will not accept what her son did — and whose account is difficult to reconcile with what authorities established about him both before and after the attack.

She asks that her name not be published, nor any photograph or recording of her voice.

“I have two other children I have to think about,” she says.

* * *

On the evening of July 25, Ballout drove a rented van into a crowd on the fringes of Berlin’s Christopher Street Day parade.

After coming to a stop, he got out of the car and, according to authorities, began attacking people with a machete before fleeing on foot. One person was killed, and at least 29 were injured.

Around 20 hours later, special forces tracked Ballout to a garden in suburban Spandau, where he allegedly attempted to attack officers with a knife when they tried to arrest him. Police opened fire, and Ballout was shot dead. Nine days later, he was buried at Gatow Cemetery in Berlin.

A digital display on a bus stop in Berlin shows the photo of Abdul Ballout on July 26, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images

The person killed in Ballout’s attack was a 65-year-old woman from Poland who had traveled to Berlin with her daughter specifically for Christopher Street Day.

Not far away, a gay refugee from Iraq was celebrating at an electronic music event when panic spread through the streets. He had fled a country where being openly gay could put his life at risk. Germany was supposed to be different.

Granted anonymity to speak openly, he said: “For many people, freedom is something they never have to think about. For me, it means being able to love someone, to leave the house in the morning without wondering whether I could be attacked or killed for who I am.”

After the attack, he said, that feeling of safety cracked. “That old fear was suddenly back.”

Sitting across from me just weeks later, Ballout’s mother is dressed in all black, her headscarf framing a face that looks exhausted. There are deep shadows beneath her eyes. She speaks so quietly that at times I have to lean in to hear. The only other sound in the room is the monotonous hum of a fan.





On the coffee table lay empty coffee cups, an open packet of TUC crackers and a box of iron tablets. Propped between them is a framed photograph of Ballout, a faint grin on his face.

She doesn’t want to begin our conversation with the attack; she wants to start with her son. She reaches for her phone and starts showing me videos. In one, he is a little boy in swim trunks, running along a beach and laughing. In another, he is an adult, dancing exuberantly through the living room with his family. He jumps onto the couch and pulls his sisters along, making everyone laugh.

His mother talks of evenings spent together watching television or playing Monopoly, how he would sometimes cheat if he were about to lose. As she speaks, her smiles give way to tears, and her tears give way to smiles.

The contrast with the image of the terrorist could hardly be greater.

* * *

Four days before our interview, I visited the neighborhood where Ballout grew up. Children were crisscrossing a courtyard, neighbors leaning out of windows or standing outside doorways. I asked them about him.

All their answers were strikingly similar: “He always said hello;” “he was polite;” “he was helpful.”

No one disputed what Ballout did. No one tried to excuse it. And yet, no one could explain how the young man they knew was capable of such an act.

German police stand near a white van used in the attack. | Omer Messinger/Getty Images

Sitting in his mother’s living room a few days later, her phone rings, and for a brief moment, Arabic singing fills the room. “That’s his voice,” she says. Her ringtone is a recording of her son reciting an Islamic prayer.

But is it just an innocuous recording?

Court records show Ballout repeatedly posted videos containing Islamic State propaganda dating back to 2024, before starting to circulate recordings of his own. In some of the audio files obtained by WELT, which is — like POLITICO — part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters network, he recited the Quran; in others, he appeared to preach. He had hundreds of followers on TikTok and Telegram, with comments praising his voice.

But Ballout’s online messages were radical, speaking of “unbelievers,” God’s “agonizing punishment,” and his rejection of democracy and the German legal system.





Online, he went by the name Abu Muawiyah — a reference to the first caliph of the Umayyad dynasty who emerged victorious over the Prophet Muhammad’s son-in-law Ali and his followers, from which Shiite Islam later emerged. It is also a signal of his shifting faith, as Ballout converted from Shiite to Sunni Islam in 2021.

Was this also a break with his family? His mother gives no indication it was.

She speaks calmly about religion, and without hesitation. She says she was born in Beirut and grew up in Germany. She can neither read nor write Arabic and has therefore never read the Quran in its original language.

German policemen scan the ground of Tiergarten park, near the scene of the attack. | Omer Messinger/Getty Images

“I’m not particularly strict about religion,” she says. But her son was different.

For the last several years, he had increasingly been trying to push her toward stricter observance, urging her to pray regularly, to take her religious obligations more seriously and to engage more deeply with Islam.

“He told me every single day how important it was to pray and that it was my duty.”

* * *

Speaking about the days leading up to the attack, one word keeps coming up in our conversation: fear.

Her son had changed, she says. He seemed more nervous, more tense, more restless. He had started changing his phone number constantly — at least five times in 10 days.

“Why are you changing your number again?” she had asked him. But his answer was always roughly the same. Some people kept calling him; he felt followed, harassed and no longer safe.





To this day, it makes no sense to his mother. But to investigators, this is the behavior of someone who had realized he was on their radar — and was planning something big.

In late May 2026, Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office classified Ballout as a high-risk individual capable of committing a serious act of politically motivated violence. And the reasons for this are documented across dozens of pages of case files.

In 2021, Ballout took part in street dawah events organized by a Salafist group in Berlin, where Islamists seek new followers and often distribute copies of the Quran. This is where Berlin’s State Criminal Police Office first took an interest in him.

From 2023 onward, he increasingly frequented mosques influenced by Salafist ideology — which espouses an ultraconservative, fundamentalist view of Sunni Islam — while investigators noted he began openly expressing his rejection of Germany’s free democratic order.

Flowers and candles lie at a makeshift memorial in Tiergarten park on July 27, 2026, two days after the attack. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images

In the summer of 2024, he repeatedly posted propaganda from the Islamic State organization, and in May 2025, attempted to join the terrorist group in Africa but was refused entry into Mauritania. Shortly after, he tried to travel to Syria via Lebanon to receive weapons training, communicating with IS members through Telegram.

Lebanese authorities arrested Ballout in July 2025, and a military court sentenced him to three months in prison for incitement to religious conflict. In court, he spoke of two cousins on his father’s side who had died fighting in Syria.

Returning to Germany in November 2025, Ballout was then arrested at Berlin airport and taken into custody on suspicion of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state. According to the case files, he presented himself as a preacher in prison. His religious fervor intensified, and his appearance changed. Ballout’s father later told Der Spiegel that he had argued with his son over his long hair and beard, which he regarded as a sign of religious extremism.





Finally, in May of this year, Ballout was sentenced to one year and 10 months in prison but was initially released under the supervision of a probation officer while the court deferred its verdict on whether to suspend the sentence. This judicial decision is now at the center of a heated debate in Germany over how the country handles high-risk Islamist offenders.

From then on, police kept him under surveillance.

Did his mother know any of this? She shakes her head.

* * *

There is only one incident Ballout’s mother is willing to discuss: July 2 this year, his birthday. That day, she says, showed just how closely her son was being monitored.

Ballout had been playing outside with his sister, spraying her with a water gun, she says. Shortly afterward, officers from the State Criminal Police Office appeared. They had assessed the situation as a possible threat.

But investigators describe the scene differently.

It was already dark, and Ballout had stepped outside for just a few seconds, holding what appeared to be a handgun but was difficult to identify, they said. He tucked it into his waistband and went back inside. When officers eventually searched the apartment, they found only a toy gun.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks at the Marienkirche church in Berlin on July 26, 2026. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images

Investigators believe the 21-year-old was testing whether he was under surveillance — and how much time he had before police would intervene.

And while his mother insists she noticed nothing that would suggest Ballout was preparing an attack, she does not rule out the possibility that others knew of her son’s plans. However, she gives no names.

He spent most of his time with family, she says. He had few friends, at least no one she knew particularly well.

* * *

The day of the attack began, in her memory, just like any other. Both mother and son slept in late, then ran errands. Ballout was unemployed and had no particular obligations, she says. In the late afternoon, he left the apartment before a family gathering that evening.

Then, suddenly, the calls started piling up.

At 5:10 p.m., Ballout called his mother. An hour later, he called again. Then again. Each time, she says, the conversation revolved around the same question: “Are you okay?” He had never done that before.





Then, after one of the calls, she received a short message: “Take care of yourself.”

The words still haunt her today.

At 7:05 p.m., Ballout called again. He asked that his mother inform her partner of over two years that he had a new phone number again. Ballout’s parents have been divorced for three years, but Ballout continued to see and speak with his father regularly, she says. And as the family prepared for the evening, the phone kept ringing.

They were supposed to have dinner at his sister’s place. Schnitzel, his favorite meal, was on the menu. Ballout loved these family gatherings, his mother says. “They always made him happy.” That is precisely why so much of what happened next is incomprehensible to her.

Police investigation marks on the ground near the scene of the attack. | Filip Singer/EPA

“He wanted to live,” she says, her voice rough.

He had spoken of the future, about having a family of his own, about all the things that still lay ahead of him. Nothing had suggested this might be a farewell.

Shortly before 10 p.m., her partner received one more call. They were the last words Ballout deliberately addressed to his family: “Get my mother to safety.”

Minutes later, the van drove into the crowd.

* * *

By the time Ballout’s mother was driven home by her partner that night, the first reports of the attack had started to circulate. At that point, she still didn’t know exactly what had taken place. But when she entered the apartment, she says, something immediately caught her attention.

A key was still in the door.

And right beside it, on the hallway shoe cabinet, were documents that seemed to be deliberately placed where they could not be overlooked. It was the rental agreement for a small van. It listed Ballout as the renter.





“That was when I knew immediately that it couldn’t mean anything good,” she says.

That same night, she took the documents to the police. And as she was questioned, a picture slowly started to emerge — one she initially refused to accept.

At the same time, she kept trying to reach her son, sending message after message. But there was no reply. She only learned the truth the next day, when her daughters called and told her about the reports on the news.

Her son was dead.

Since then, she has spent hour after hour in her Berlin apartment searching for explanations, her thoughts circling endlessly around her son’s last words, his fear and whether there may have been something in those calls that she failed to recognize. She cannot let go of the distorted image she has of her son, of the good boy who wanted to start a family.





Asked what she would say to the victims of the terrorist attack, she thinks for a long time. She is sorry, she eventually says.

“I would also tell them that wasn’t my son.”

Additional reporting by Lennart Pfahler.

Julia Zabert is a trainee journalist with the Global Reporters Network at the Axel Springer Academy. The Academy trains the next generation of leading journalists through hands-on, innovative work with a clear focus on the future of journalism. More information at axelspringeracademy.com.

World.title: The one French politician who’s not on vacation this summer
World.content:
Gabriel Attal, center, shakes hands with a police officer during a campaign visit to Vannes, France on July 25, 2026. | Sebastien Salom-Gomis/AFP via Getty Images

Presidential candidate Gabriel Attal is forgoing the traditional August holiday in a desperate attempt to catch up with his rivals.

PARIS — Former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal is trying to jump-start his presidential prospects by taking advantage of his rivals enjoying France’s cherished August break.

Attal, a former prime minister who now leads President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist political party Renaissance, is betting that by keeping a busy schedule during the holiday and meeting with people across the country — including those at vineyards, markets and ports as well as vacationers in picturesque seaside towns — he can show voters what sets him apart from the field.

“It’s a rather bourgeois assumption to think that all French people take time off or go on vacation,” said a representative for Attal’s team who, like others in this story, was granted anonymity to speak candidly about campaign dynamics. “There’s no way he’s going to suspend his campaign over the summer.”



But political reality is also forcing Attal to campaign in August for the vote in April of next year. If he wants a real shot at catching up in the polls, there’s little time to waste.

Surveys have consistently shown the 37-year-old trailing Edouard Philippe, his main ideological rival for centrist and center-right votes. Given the contest goes to a two-candidate runoff if nobody wins a majority in the first round, the two men have tentatively agreed that only one of them should be on the ballot so they don’t split their shared voter base — which could cost both of them a spot in the second round.

Philippe, far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen, far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon and conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau are all among the presidential hopefuls taking long summer breaks, only interrupting their time off for the occasional op-ed or statement on major events like the wildfires that ravaged southwest France.

Edouard Philippe speaks at a rally in northern Paris on July 5, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images

Their reasoning for slowing down during the peak holiday season is straightforward: Voters want to rest and recharge, so candidates shouldn’t harass them with politics and should instead enjoy one last bit of respite before the race enters its decisive stretch.

“We shouldn’t bother the French people while they’re on vacation,” said a Retailleau adviser.

Attal is betting otherwise that a summer spent campaigning can help close the gap in the polls.

“A campaign is about winning over the French one by one … [Attal] wants to show that he’s more determined than the others,” added his adviser.

The right track

It’s unclear for now to what extent Attal’s summer work will reap dividends with voters, as most pollsters who would investigate that question have themselves set out-of-office messages.

But the absence of other candidates on the campaign trail has given Attal an opportunity to dominate headlines, and he’s used it to make a play for right-wing voters.



At the start of the month, Attal, a member of parliament who represents a Paris suburb, gave an interview to the right-wing weekly Le Journal du Dimanche in which he called for lower immigration, a sweeping streamlining of France’s administrative procedures and more effective enforcement of criminal sentences.

He then traveled to western France, where, in front of cameras, he confronted a group of French gens du voyage — a legal classification for traditionally itinerant communities, including Roma and Manouche, and long a target of the French right — who had occupied land without authorization.

The encounter can be seen below in a report from CNEWS, in French.

French municipalities are required to provide designated stopping sites for traveling communities, but those obligations are not always met — or the sites provided are insufficient — sometimes resulting in unauthorized occupations of public or private land.

For both Attal and Philippe, making inroads on the right will be crucial. Macron’s 2022 reelection was buoyed by older, more affluent voters who had traditionally backed conservatives.

But Philippe begins that contest with a built-in advantage.



He is a former member of the conservative party Les Républicains and has always identified as a man of the right. Attal, who started his political career in the youth wing of the center-left Socialists, has resisted the label.

One conservative minister in the current French government, who has not endorsed a candidate for 2027, readily described Philippe as belonging to his political camp. Attal, the minister said, has a “very flexible” ideological spine.

Sarah Paillou and Anthony Lattier contributed to this report.

World.title: Nigel Farage paints himself as local hero in fight to win Clacton
World.content:
One Meta ad suggests he is the only candidate to have visited forgotten areas of the constituency. A further clip shows a local resident giving Farage a positive review of his work — and is presented as proof that opposition complaints he has neglected the patch since his 2024 general election victory in the seat are “cobblers.”

With over 7 million followers across the leading social media platforms — making him by far the most-followed U.K. party leader — Farage has also been churning out election content across TikTok, Instagram and X.

Even with that reach, the Reform UK leader appears to be the only candidate running in Clacton who has used paid Meta features to bolster his online campaign.

Almost £1,000 has been spent on videos of Farage urging local supporters to request the party deliver and install an “I’m with Nigel” garden sign. Meanwhile, around £500 went to ads asking voters to return their postal votes and “send a message to the establishment.”

The largest single sum — between £4,000-£4,500 — was spent on an almost five-minute campaign video in which Farage waxes lyrical about the connection he’s made with local constituents, while claiming his party’s surging success has resulted in the powers-that-be using “foul means” to hamper him.

“Rather than being judged by the political class and the mainstream media, I am going to let you, the voters in the Clacton constituency, make a decision,” he said. “I want you to be my judge, not the political elite.”

World.title: How Russian attacks, European protectionism and drought are trapping Ukraine’s vital grain
World.content:
With missile strikes keeping cargo ships away from its ports, Kyiv is scrambling, yet again, for a way out via Europe. But its fallback routes run overland through EU countries, including Poland, Hungary and Slovakia, where previous waves of Ukrainian grain left governments facing a fierce domestic backlash.

The last surge of Ukrainian agricultural exports through Eastern Europe unleashed mass protests from farmers, particularly in Poland, who complained that cheap Ukrainian produce that was meant to merely pass through the region was instead ending up on their domestic markets. Poland imposed a ban on Ukrainian grain in 2023, alongside similar measures in Hungary and Slovakia, defying EU trade rules and souring relations with Ukraine.

Kyiv's fresh pleas — and insistence that the grain would only transit through its EU neighbors — have prompted Warsaw to reassure its own farmers that none of it will end up in Poland.

“We are doing everything to keep the embargo,” Polish Agriculture Minister Stefan Krajewski told Radio ZET on Monday, referring to Poland’s ban on Ukrainian grain imports.

Blocked bounty

One of the world’s largest grain producers, Ukraine typically sends more than 90 percent of its agricultural exports by sea. The disruption of that trade after Russia’s 2022 invasion helped drive global food prices to record highs. This summer, Russia and Ukraine have intensified attacks on each other’s ports and shipping across the Black Sea.

Ukraine exported just 463,000 metric tons of grain in the first nine days of August — about one-third of the usual pace, said Vysotskyi. By November, when the new harvest comes in, the country risks running out of storage for grain it cannot export.

World.title: Eurovision 2027: A guide to Burgas, Bulgaria’s sunny seaside host city
World.content:
Many of us thought that Bulgaria winning the Eurovision Song Contest would mean the capital, Sofia, would be hosting in 2027.

 

However, it’s now been revealed that Burgas will play host.

Far less known internationally, it’s already one of the country’s best-loved seaside escapes and Eurovision’s arrival next May will put its beaches, buzzing waterfront and relaxed summer atmosphere firmly on the international map.

While the contest will bring the crowds, there’s plenty here beyond the Eurovision bubble, from long sandy beaches and leafy parks to seafood restaurants, cultural sights and a lively arts scene.

Whether you’re heading over for the show or simply want to see what all the fuss is about, here’s how to make the most of Burgas.

How to get there

Burgas, the fourth-largest city in Bulgaria, is located on the Black Sea, known for its sandy beaches and clear blue seas.

It’s about 400 kilometres from Sofia and just under 150 kilometres south of Dara’s – 2026’s Eurovision winner – hometown of Varna.

Burgas airport is actually better served than you might think.

It’s located just 10 kilometres from the city centre, and welcomes direct flights from many European hubs including London, Rome and Berlin. Getting to the city centre from the hub is simple, as there’s a frequently-running bus route between the two.

If you’re combining a trip to Burgas with a visit to Sofia, trains run about eight times a day, with the fastest journey taking just five hours and 43 minutes.

Buses are even faster, taking a minimum of five hours from Sofia to Burgas. They run on average six times per day.

When you arrive in Burgas, e-bike rental is everywhere and the city has a decent public transport network, with Burgasbus the easiest to navigate.

Where to stay

Eurovision’s arrival in a city is notorious for driving up accommodation prices, but Burgas is actually usually very affordable when it comes to hotels.

A spot check by the Euronews Travel team found private rooms from €32per night in August, and four-star hotels from €67 a night.

It’s also possible to secure a one-night stay at the five-star beachfront Hotel Residence Promenade for €130.

What to see in Burgas

No trip to the city is complete without a visit to one of its beaches – and there are spots for every vibe.

Central Beach and Northern Beach are buzzy and packed with restaurants and bars, while Sarafovo Beach and Kraymorie Beach are more laidback and known for their natural beauty.

The Pier of Burgas is a must see after a day at the beach, offering great views of the city and an ideal place to watch the sunset.

The city's pier is a must visit when in Burgas Anton Nikolov/Unsplash

Nearby, you’ll find the Sea Garden, a 5km-long route of paved walking trails through a vast public park.

It’s also suitable for bicycling and visitors can catch a glimpse of exotic plant species, cultural monuments and see some of the most impressive Balkan architecture in the region.

Burgas’ Old Town is pedestrianised and boasts endless restaurants, bars and shops as well as the Orthodox Church of Saints Cyril and Methodius.

Culture is a big deal here, too. The Sand Sculptures Festival runs from the beginning of July to the end of September, and showcases the best of international pop culture.

Spice music festival is another highlight, with ‘Despacito’ singer Luis Fonsi having headlined earlier in August.

What to eat and drink

Bulgarian cuisine might not be as famous as eats from other parts of Europe, but there’s still plenty to try, and Burgas has its own local specialities to sample.

Being coastal, fish is obviously a favourite and midi po burgaski, local mussels cooked in their shells with onions, tomatoes, peppers, and savoury herbs, is particularly popular, as is Black Sea turbot, which is served grilled.

Bulgarian food is famously underrated - and Burgas is a great place to try it Stefan Vladimirov/Unsplash

Burgas is also a great place to try foods from wider Bulgaria, including strandzhanski dyado, a traditional cured, spiced meat, and the national dish of Shopska salata, made with diced tomatoes, cucumbers, onions, and peppers and topped with grated sirene, a white brine cheese.

When it comes to beverages, don’t miss Burgas 63, a rakia made with local grapes, Bulgarian wines including the well-bodied red Mavrud, and local lagers Burgasko, established in Burgas in 1971.

Food and drinks here are remarkably inexpensive. According to cost-of-living data platform Numbeo, a meal at an inexpensive restaurant will set you back an average of €12.39, while half a litre of local draft beer €1.79, and a meal for two at a mid-range restaurant – that’s three courses, without drinks – is €40.90.

World.title: Putin watches Russian navy drills off Russia's Sakhalin Island
World.content:
Footage released by Russian state television showed President Vladimir Putin aboard the missile cruiser Varyag, the flagship of the Pacific Fleet, watching live‑fire naval exercises and an underwater explosion off Russia’s Far East. He later travelled to one of the archipelago's four main islands, marking the first visit to the Kurils by a Russian president since Dmitry Medvedev went there in 2010.

 

Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described the visit as "absolutely unacceptable", saying the islands were an inherent part of Japan. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi also summoned Russia's ambassador in Tokyo to lodge a formal protest, warning that the visit could further damage already strained relations.

The Kuril Islands have been disputed by Russia and Japan since 1945, when the Soviet Union seized the archipelago. Home to around 20,000 Russians, the islands are strategically important to Moscow for their military position and access to the Pacific, while the surrounding waters and nearby Sakhalin are rich in fishing, oil and gas. Putin’s visit and the naval drills reinforce Russia’s territorial claims and military presence in the region, sending a clear message to Japan and its Western allies.

World.title: China's lead in orbital data centres risks leaving Europe behind
World.content:
China's push into orbital data centres risks leaving Europe behind, according to a new policy brief from the European Space Policy Institute (ESPI).

 

Orbital data centres are increasingly seen as key strategic assets for processing the vast amounts of data generated by AI and satellite systems.

The brief, titled "Constellating Compute: China's Domestic Policy Towards Orbital Data Centre Leadership," warns that if the technological gap widens significantly, Europe risks having to compute its own space data through third-party actors and losing access to orbital information.

European efforts are under way but remain limited in scale.

The EU-funded research project ASCEND, backed under Horizon Europe since 2023, found that orbital data centres could strengthen European digital sovereignty.

The European Space Agency (ESA) has also worked with UK firm Open Cosmos on the Φ-sat-2 satellite, which carries AI capabilities for Earth observation.

French start-up ALATYR has also announced plans to manufacture robotically assembled orbital data centres. Even so, compared with developments in China and the US, the gap in Europe is starting to widen.

Why is China ahead in the orbital data centre race?

China has treated space-based computing as a national strategic priority, giving rise to a wave of state-backed initiatives and policies to support the goal.

Central to this effort is the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), which first formalised orbital data centres in a new strategy, alongside the Beijing Municipal Government and the Zhongguancun Science Park.

China has combined top-down policy drafting, private and state-owned industry adaptation, municipal and provincial government incentives, and support for non-state actors and working groups, according to the brief.

High-profile prototype constellations have driven early implementation. The Three-Body Constellation, launched by start-up ADAspace in May 2025, marked the first operational example of space-based computing.

In a joint laboratory with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, ADAspace has since used the constellation's in-orbit computing power to control a robot on the ground, one of several technical trials the company has run since the satellites reached orbit.

Other companies have followed. Beijing Orbital Twilight Technology Co., Ltd. (Orbital Chenguang) announced an undisclosed equity round alongside €7.4bn worth of debt financing in April 2026.

Nayuta Space unveiled its ALAYA supercompute constellation, planned to deploy 12,500 computing satellites. Shanghai Xingshu Tiansuan Space Technology Co. unveiled its Xingshu Plan at the World AI Conference in July 2026, envisioned to grow to 1,000 satellites.

China Mobile, Zhejiang Lab, Bailing Aerospace, Zhongke Tiansuan Technology and Interstellar Glory Space-Based Computing Technology (iSpace) have also announced their own constellations.

Beijing's municipal government has moved to incubate the sector further, issuing a call for orbital data centre project proposals in June 2026 alongside the Zhongguancun Science Park, and launching a space computing innovation centre bringing together rival companies including GalaxySpace and Landspace under a company-plus-alliance model.

According to state broadcaster CGTN, the centre's priority areas include space-based computing chip design, high-performance computing payloads and integrated space-ground cloud computing technologies.

CASC has also outlined a five-year plan for the sector, agreed with the Chinese Society of Astronautics in January 2026 under the guidance of state bodies including the China National Space Administration.

According to CGTN's reporting on the plan, it includes building gigawatt-level space digital infrastructure combining cloud, edge and terminal technologies, though the underlying policy documents do not appear to have been formally published, and Euronews could not independently verify the claims.

The brief recommends that the EU establish coordinated political guidance, investment support and a regulatory framework for orbital data centre development, that a flagship initiative be included in the Horizon Europe Moonshot Projects under the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework, and that European space actors convene working groups with international counterparts on standards and data sovereignty.

World.title: Russian drone strikes passenger train in Odesa region, killing driver
World.content:
Footage filmed in Ukraine’s Odesa region on Thursday 13 August 2026 by the national emergency services shows a severely damaged passenger train locomotive, as firefighters extinguish the flames. A nearby carriage has shattered windows, while passengers board evacuation buses with their luggage.

 

A Russian jet-powered Shahed drone struck the locomotive of the Odesa-Dnipro passenger train in the Berezivka district on Thursday morning, killing the driver and his assistant, Ukrzaliznytsia chairman Oleksandr Pertsovskyi said. A monitoring team had detected the drone and ordered the train to stop near a station, but the drone's sudden manoeuvre left the crew too little time to evacuate after stopping the train. All 340 passengers were evacuated safely and taken to Odesa by 21 buses.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the operator could not have been unaware the train carried civilians and renewed calls for stronger air defences. Russia launched 133 drones at Ukraine overnight, with 111 intercepted, the air force said, as strikes also wounded six people elsewhere in the country.

World.title: This boutique hotel in Lisbon has an in-house library, rooftop sunset sessions and a pillow menu
World.content:
For travellers to Lisbon, a new boutique hotel has opened offering a different kind of hospitality from most city centre accommodation.

 

Villa Dorothéa lies in the Portuguese capital’s Lapa district, occupying a carefully restored 19th-century hamlet. It is spread across five interconnected houses set between cobbled pathways, quiet courtyards, and terraces scented with jasmine and bougainvillaea.

The hotel has no formal lobby. Instead, guests follow footpaths paved with traditional Portuguese stonework, passing ceramic tributes to the area’s fishing heritage and historic tiled plaques that connect the house, hotel, and surrounding city.

A micro-neighbourhood in busy Lisbon

Villa Dorothéa is designed as a private micro-neighbourhood within Lapa, threaded through with passageways that give it the feel of a village.

The houses date back to 1878 and were originally home to the families of the city’s fishermen.

The interiors, by LACASTA Interior Design Studio and Carla Kottmann, combine architectural details with contemporary furnishings that sit alongside collected objects, books and decorative pieces to create the familiarity and character of a private residence.

Villa Dorothéa encourages guests to take life slowly. Villa Dorothéa

At the heart of the property is The Secret, a 25-seat gastrobar extending between a secluded courtyard and a rooftop overlooking the city. It is open to both guests and external diners and draws inspiration from the city’s culture of long evenings, shared plates and conversation.

It also serves signature cocktails inspired by Luís de Camões’ Os Lusíadas, a 16th-century epic poem about maritime exploration.

As for breakfast, there’s specialty coffee from nearby award-winning roastery Filtrô and bread delivered fresh each morning by local artisan bakery Pão do Pastor.

Enjoy Lisbon’s slower side

Villa Dorothéa encourages guests to take life slowly. The hotel is home to a library curated in partnership with the Lisbon bookshop Salted Books.

Launching later this summer, Villa Suppers will bring guests and Lisbon locals together around long communal tables, drawing inspiration from the tradition of Portuguese family lunches.

The houses date back to 1878 and were originally home to the families of the city’s fishermen. Villa Dorothéa

Its ongoing social calendar will also include a series of events throughout the year such as sunset DJ sessions on the roof terrace, Champagne rituals and wine tastings with local producers.

As for wellness, each room has its own yoga mat and accessories, while group classes are available in partnership with LX Portal Yoga Studio across the street. In-room Swedish massages by wellness pioneer Cristina Lobo can also be arranged on request.

The property has introduced a dedicated pillow menu, with a choice of a cooling gel pillow, an ergonomic memory foam pillow, and an aromatherapy memory foam pillow infused with CBD, lavender, essential oils and chamomile.

Why you should stay in the Lapa neighbourhood

Lapa is one of Lisbon’s most distinguished residential neighbourhoods, known for its graceful architecture and colourful streets.

From the 16th century onwards, the area became known for the palaces and estates of noble families and prosperous merchants, later attracting the Portuguese aristocracy and bourgeoisie.

The arrival of embassies and diplomatic residences in the early 20th century further shaped the discreet, cosmopolitan character that Lapa retains today.

The neighbourhood houses some of the city’s most talked-about restaurants – including Skizzo, Da Noi and Familjen – alongside a host of independent design shops, artists’ studios and artisanal coffee spots.

World.title: Missed the eclipse? Here’s where to travel to see 2027’s ‘eclipse of the century’
World.content:
Missed this year’s eclipse and have serious FOMO? Don’t worry, because there’s another one coming up in 2027 – and it’s being described as the ‘eclipse of the century’.

 

Taking place on 2 August 2027, this eclipse will be the longest on easily accessible land until 2114, with totality lasting six minutes and 23 seconds at the point of the greatest eclipse in Egypt.

For context, yesterday’s eclipse lasted for two minutes and 18 seconds at its maximum point.

You don’t have to travel all the way to Egypt to see it either, as the path of totality will pass through the Strait of Gibraltar before continuing through parts of North Africa and the Middle East.

Where in Europe and beyond to see the 2027 eclipse

It’s another big one for Spain, although the cities in the path of totality are different to this year’s eclipse.

In Marbella, totality will last for three minutes and 21 seconds, while in Cádiz, it will be dark for two minutes and 56 seconds.

Ceuta and Melilla, Spain’s exclaves on the coast of North Africa, will also see the totality for four minutes and 49 seconds, and four minutes and 34 seconds, respectively.

The British Overseas Territory of Gibraltar is another European option, with totality lasting four minutes and 28 seconds.

Lampedusa, one of Italy’s Pelagian Islands, will see totality for two minutes and 56 seconds.

In Morocco, Tangier will see totality for four minutes and 51 seconds. Several cities in Tunisia lie in the path of totality, with the southeastern port city of Sfax descending into darkness for two minutes and 56 seconds.

Given the fact that the greatest eclipse is in Egypt, it’s unsurprising that many umbraphiles (aka eclipse chasers) are headed there for the big day.

In the Siwa Oasis, it will last five minutes and 33 seconds; in Asyut, six minutes and seven seconds; and in Luxor, six minutes and 22 seconds.

In Saudi Arabia, totality will last five minutes and 53 seconds in Jeddah, and five minutes and 10 seconds in Mecca.

If you are planning a trip, I suggest booking a hotel ASAP as many properties are already fully booked, and those that aren’t are seriously pricey.

Worried about the heat in some of these cities? I chatted to Dr. Kelly Korreck, a programme scientist for eclipses at NASA Headquarters, earlier this year, who told Euronews Travel that the temperature could drop as much as 10°C.

Other eclipses to make a note of

An annular solar eclipse – where the moon doesn’t completely cover the sun, leading to a “ring of fire” effect – is coming up on 26 January, 2028.

It will start in South America before passing through Portugal, including Madeira, and cities in Spain including Barcelona, Córdoba, Cádizm and Seville. The maximum coverage is around 84%.

Australia and New Zealand will next see a total solar eclipse on 22 July, 2028. Cities in the path of totality include Sydney, Queenstown and Dunedin.

World.title: Snow cannons and reservoirs: How Swiss resorts' winter equipment could help put out wildfires
World.content:
There's barely any snow in sight above Adelboden in the intense August sunshine, never mind skiers. But the Swiss resort may have a new way to put its snowmaking equipment to work as Europe bakes through hot summers: helping douse forest fires.

 

Glaciers in Switzerland and around the Alps have been retreating rapidly in recent years, among other changes attributed to the impact of climate change caused by human activity. Snowfall has become less frequent and reliable over recent decades.

That's a big issue for a mid-altitude ski resort like the Adelboden-Lenk area, whose roughly 200 kilometres of slopes span an altitude between 1,000 and 2,300 metres. These days, an estimated 70 per cent of the snow on its slopes is made artificially.

Snow cannons and lances are the visible part of the snowmaking network. But much of it is out of sight: dozens of kilometres of underground water pipes that could prove useful beyond the winter months as the risk of wildfires grows even in places such as Switzerland’s Adelboden-Lenk ski area.

Snow cannons are stored during the summer months at the Adelboden-Lenk ski resort facility in the Lenk valley, Switzerland, Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. AP Photo/Hernan Munoz

How reservoirs of melted snow could be used to douse wildfires

“We can help firefighters with our infrastructure," says Jürg Klopfenstein, who is responsible for the resort's snowmaking operations. "Not primarily with our snow cannons, which can mainly be used to water the fields or aim them at surrounding infrastructure. But firefighters can use our infrastructure, and helicopters can refill their tanks using our water reservoirs.”

Those reservoirs collect rainfall and melting snow in the warmer months, and the water is used to produce snow during the ski season. The pipes and pumps connect 210 snow cannons and 50 snow lances in the Adelboden-Lenk area. In case of fire, the system could be used to create wet buffer areas, slowing the advance of flames and buying time until emergency services and air support arrive.

So far this year, Switzerland hasn’t experienced large-scale fires, unlike some of its neighbours. But the country is suffering from drought and the authorities assess the risk of wildfires as high across almost the entire nation, including the Bern region where Adelboden is located.

A water reservoirs for snowmaking photographed at the Lenk valley near Adelboden, Switzerland, Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. AP Photo/Hernan Munoz

Lack of humidity is 'a real problem' – even in spring

Like many other mountain areas, the Bernese Oberland isn't just a winter destination but attracts many mountain bikers, hikers, runners and paragliders in summer.

Stefan Buchs, the operations manager at the Adelboden-Lenk resort, says that different types of vegetation and different levels of soil humidity mean the large and frequent forest fires seen in southern Europe can't be extrapolated directly into a similar risk in the Alps.

But even so, “widespread wildfires are a likely scenario," he says. “We discussed this with the firefighters, and they recognised it already. They see that humidity is a real problem. It gets really dry even in the spring. Not just in the summer.”

Adelboden Mayor Willy Schranz says that “we must be prepared, because I am sure it won’t be the last summer like this one.”

A climate change expert with environmental group Greenpeace, Nathan Solothurnmann, cautions against overestimating what putting a snowmaking system to work against wildfires can achieve in the long run and in a wider context.

“This watering system that they’re planning in Adelboden might for sure help for a while," he says. “But of course the changes we're facing [are] much worse. All those types of adaptations, they just help for a while.”

"In most parts of Switzerland, there are no pipes buried underground that we can use when a forest is burning,” he adds.

World.title: What is Truth API? The $100,000 feed that has landed Trump a lawsuit
World.content:
The Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation went to court in New York on Wednesday to shut down Truth API, a subscription launched this month by Trump Media and Technology Group, the Nasdaq-listed company behind Truth Social.

 

The subscription provides privileged access to US President Donald Trump's social media posts straight to trading firms, sending them fractions of a second before they appear on the public timeline, which is enough time for high-frequency algorithms to execute thousands of orders before others process the information.

Contracts run from about $60,000 (€52,000) to $100,000 (€86,600) a month and cover the platform's 10 most-followed accounts, among them US President Donald Trump, the White House itself, US Vice President JD Vance, FBI Director Kash Patel and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

More than 10 customers have signed up, mostly high-frequency trading firms, according to company executives.

Interim CEO Kevin McGurn told an earnings call on Monday that subscribers receive news "fractionally faster" than everyone else, having earlier pitched it as a real-time channel for the platform's most market-moving posts.

FILE. The price chart for the Trump Media and Technology Group on the NASDAQ website is seen on a computer screen in New York, Apr. 2024 AP Photo/Patrick Sison

US President Donald Trump holds roughly 41% of the company through a revocable trust overseen by his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., with the stake currently worth close to $1 billion (€866mn).

Official announcements, The Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation argue, belong to the public rather than to whoever pays most for them.

Two constitutional claims

The complaint, which names US President Donald Trump alongside deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino, executive assistant Natalie Harp and the Executive Office of the President, calls the arrangement "profoundly corrupt".

It argues the service breaches the First Amendment by denying equal access to presidential announcements and the Fifth by conditioning that access on unreasonable sums, noting that many of the 9,000 to 11,000 posts Trump has published since January 2025 came with no White House statement.

"Trump is trying to enrich himself by privatizing government information," said Ben Muessig, editor-in-chief of The Intercept.

A Trump Media spokesperson countered that critics show "a failure to grasp the distinction between public and nonpublic information", adding that left-wing activists were weaponising the courts.

The White House has not commented on the lawsuit which follows a request last month from US Senators Elizabeth Warren and Adam Schiff for the Securities and Exchange Commission to examine whether the service undermines market integrity.

A pattern that predates the paywall

The service formalises an advantage that has drawn questions for months.

On several occasions this year, futures markets have registered unusual bursts of activity minutes before major Iran war announcements appeared on US President Donald Trump's account.

No investigation has reached a conclusion.

The clearest case came on 23 March, when the S&P 500 and oil futures recorded isolated volume spikes at about 6:50am in New York. Fifteen minutes later Trump posted that talks with Iran had taken place and strikes on its energy infrastructure were paused.

Equity futures jumped more than 2.5% and West Texas Intermediate fell almost 6%.

According to one analysis of 1,341 posts between late January and early April, conducted by the Queensland University of Technology, there were 15 episodes that raised suspicions of insider trading.

World.title: What would North Korean surge mean for Ukraine war?
World.content:
Ukraine is claiming that North Korea is preparing to send tens of thousands more troops to Russia, where they'll gain valuable battlefield experience. President Zelenskyy urged South Korea to work closer with Kyiv.

North Korea is preparing a massive troop surge to help its ally Moscow in its war on Ukraine, with up to 50,000 North Koreans to be deployed in Russia, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Late last month, the Ukrainian leader said Russia wanted to bring in another 30,000 North Korean troops, before adding this weekend that Pyongyang decided to have between 30,000 and 50,000 North Koreans deployed on Russian territory. He did not specify if this number included the North Korean troops already taking part in the conflict.

In the comments published this weekend, Zelenskyy also warned North Korea was gaining valuable experience in modern warfare and urged South Korea to boost cooperation with Ukraine on air defense and drones. Two days later, Zelenskyy said Russia had received more North Korean ballistic missiles, which were allegedly used in an attack on Zaporizhzhia.

North Korea suffered thousands of causalities in Ukraine war

Russia and North Korea signed a defense pact in the summer of 2024, with North Korea starting to send combat troops to Russia several months later. Analyst believe some 14,000 to 15,000 personnel were deployed, mainly in the Kursk region. Pyongyang later agreed to send another 6,000 sappers and military construction workers. North Korea has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery rounds and ballistic missiles, according to South Korean and Ukrainian authorities. South Korean intelligence estimates that around 6,000 North Korean soldiers have been killed or wounded.

This image, published by Ukrainian officials, shows North Korean soldiers being fitted for Russian uniforms Image: Ukraine Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

On Thursday, Japan's Kyodo News cited Ukrainian military intelligence as confirming the upcoming North Korean surge. Ukrainian sources say up to 50,000 North Korean troops could be deployed to Russia by the end of November; The troops would reportedly take over duties in Russia's Kursk, Bryansk and Belgorod, freeing Russian forces for the Ukrainian front.

Pyongyang's surge 'seems to be becoming a reality'

South Korean lawmaker Yu Yong-won told DW the military cooperation between Russia and Korea was growing ever closer.

Yu is a former military journalist who visited Ukraine in 2025 and again in February this year. He said he heard claims of the North Korean surge during his most recent visit to the war-torn country.

"I am concerned that this seems to be becoming a reality," he told DW.

North Korea expands its role in Russia's war against Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At the same time, Yu noted that 30,000 to 50,000 troops would be significantly more than the roughly 20,000 troops and support forces involved in the initial deployment.

"Whether such a large-scale additional troop deployment will actually take place," Yu said, "the continued expansion of military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow called closer attention from the South Korean government and military."

Will North Koreans watch Russians' back?

Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service (NIS), also seemed to signal caution.

"Ukraine initially spoke of 30,000 additional personnel before raising the estimate to 50,000 without releasing detailed evidence about the planned deployment," he told DW.

"North Korea has sufficient military manpower to make such a deployment possible without seriously weakening its defenses," according to Han.

"Even though the war is largely deadlocked, a country fighting a prolonged war will always perceive that it lacks manpower," Han said. "North Korean infantry could therefore guard Russian rear areas, allowing more Russian soldiers to be deployed to frontline combat in Ukraine."

Russian officials praise North Koreans

"North Korea also benefits from the arrangement; its troops are gaining experience in 21st-century warfare while testing weapons under actual battlefield conditions; deeper cooperation could increase North Korea's access to Russian expertise in missile, naval and air-defense technology," Han said.

North Korea gains critical intel by aiding Russia in Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The security expert also estimates that, out of 6,000 North Korean causalities, some 2,000 may have been killed.

"Some 1,000 to 2,000 combat troops and engineers are believed to have returned home, where veterans and families of the dead have reportedly received housing and other preferential treatment," Han said.

"North Korean troops suffered heavy initial losses but became more effective as they adapted to the battlefield," Han said. "Their aggressive fighting style may explain why Putin and other Russian officials have praised their bravery."

North Korean women also moving to Russia

Ahn Chan-il, head of the World Institute for North Korea Studies and a former North Korean soldier, believes that "a deployment of 50,000 is militarily feasible" and that Pyongyang would send "elite special operations troops."

"North Korea's special operations forces are particularly skilled in reconnaissance, surprise attacks and ambushes, and have demonstrated their combat capabilities on the Kursk front, making them attractive to the Russian military," said Ahn, who defected in 1979.

"If 30,000 troops are deployed, however, the contingent would likely include not only special operations forces but also infantry, engineers, construction workers and female medical personnel," he added.

Why North Korea is now Europe's problem To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"North Korean women have recently been observed heading to Russia, but it remains unclear whether they are being sent for reconstruction work or as medical personnel."

Ukraine war as training grounds for North Korean military

According to Ahn, "surviving soldiers could bring valuable combat knowledge back to North Korea. Some could become junior officers or instructors, spreading lessons learned from drone warfare, reconnaissance and other aspects of the Ukraine conflict throughout the military."

"However, young soldiers are being exposed to life outside one of the world's most isolated societies. More importantly, a sharp rise in casualties could make the war harder to portray as a success," added Ahn.

"A limited number of fallen soldiers can be celebrated as heroes," Ahn said. "But tens of thousands of dead and wounded could leave behind grieving families and disabled veterans, potentially turning North Korea's battlefield experience into a domestic burden."

World.title: Germany: Buildings evacuated over suspected explosive
World.content:
Authorities have begun evacuating buildings around a Bavarian train station as specialists examine a suspicious object on the tracks. Rail traffic is currently suspended in the area.

Buildings near a train station in the southern state of Bavaria are being evacuated as a precaution after police said that an object found on the tracks could contain explosives.

Emergency crews were clearing directly affected buildings while Federal Police specialists continued examining the object, Middle Franconia police said.

A technician discovered the suspicious item in the track bed at the entrance to the station in the town of Treuchtlingen.

Specialists have already X-rayed the object, but police said further examinations were needed because the possibility of an explosive hazard could not yet be ruled out.

Police said the object was being lifted using a robot to allow further investigations.

A federal police bomb disposal team is examining the object Image: Felix Kirberg/dpa/picture alliance

Road and rail closures remain in place while the investigation continues. Regional services are affected, with trains terminating early at suitable stations. Replacement buses and large-capacity taxis have been arranged.

Long-distance services are being diverted via the city of Ingolstadt. Police have urged people to avoid the area and take alternative routes.

World.title: Germany news: Far-right leader backs left-wing populist
World.content:
08/13/2026 August 13, 2026 Merz calls for defense of democracy on Berlin Wall anniversary

The Berlin Wall started as a barbed-wire barrier but became a massive cement barrier in many places Image: Kindermann/United Archives/IMAGO

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has called on people to keep up the fight to retain freedom and democracy as Germany marks the 65th anniversary of the construction of the Berlin Wall.

"Sixty-five years ago, the leadership of former East Germany had the Wall built. Today, our country has been united longer than it was divided and we live in freedom and peace," Merz wrote on the platform X.

"The lesson of the Wall remains: Freedom and democracy are not a given. We must always fight for them," he wrote.

Merz's remarks come amid a surge in popularity of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), a party seen by many as anti-democratic in its ideology.

On August 13, 1961, on what would become known as Barbed Wire Sunday, communist East Germany sealed the border between Berlin’s eastern and western sectors before building a wall that was to divide the city for the next 28 years.

People trying to cross the Wall to leave the authoritarian state were often shot dead, and the barrier came to symbolize the repressive political system behind it.

In remarks to the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, he commissioner for culture, Wolfram Weimer, warned against "positive distortions of former East Germany" by the far-right AfD and the Left Party.

Weimer criticized such "collective forgetting, repression and downplaying of former East Germany" as the biggest challenge to properly commemorating the crimes of the regime there.

World.title: India news: Parliament ends turbulent monsoon session
World.content:
08/13/2026 August 13, 2026 Protests mark monsoon session of parliament

On the very first day of the monsoon session on July 20, parliament was rocked by a massive youth-led march trying to get to its gates as part of the Cockroach Janta Party movement demanding the resignation of the now former education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over exam irregularities.

The protesters were met with baton-charges and tear gas firing, and since then the opposition has railed against the violent crackdown, demanding an answer in the parliament from Union Home Minister Amit Shah over alleged police brutality.

On Wednesday, Shah said that the Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government was ready for a discussion on the student protests which were triggered by a slew of medical entrance exam paper leaks. The leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha, Congress's Rahul Gandhi, turned down the debate offer saying that the youth wanted answers on who ordered the use of force on protesters and "not a lecture" from Shah.

Addressing a press conference on Thursday, Union Minister of Parliamentarty Affairs Kiren Rijiju accused the opposition of "running away from discussions" and alleged that opposition disruptions affected parliament's productivity.

During the 19-day monsoon session several demonstrations were held by the Congress-led alliance of opposition parties called the INDIA bloc on the parliament premises against the police action and a donation embezzlement controversy linked to the Ram Temple, a shrine central to Modi's Hindu-first politics.

Lawmakers from Modi's ruling coalition also began staging their own demonstrations, including on the last day over another student protest in Jharkhand — where the Congress party is an ally of the ruling coalition. Tear gas, batons and water cannons were also used to disperse the protesters marching towards the state assembly in Ranchi.

World.title: Colombia earthquake: Rescue operation enters 'final phase'
World.content:
Rescuers are racing against a critical 72-hour window to find survivors after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake that has killed 265 people, left hundreds missing, and displaced tens of thousands across western Colombia.

Rescuers worked through a third straight night with time ticking towards the 72-hour mark since a powerful earthquake hit Colombia. That's the period aid agencies consider most critical for finding survivors alive, though it can stretch longer if trapped people have access to food and water.

"We're entering the final phase," Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said, adding that survivors could still be found afterward but that the odds grow steadily worse. He said crews were still detecting signs of life beneath the rubble and urged speed: "Every minute is vital."

Rescue workers ask for silence as they search for survivors at the site of collapsed buildings Image: Raul Arboleda/AFP

The latest on the Colombia earthquake

The death toll from the quake has climbed to 265, President Abelardo de la Espriella said Wednesday.

De la Espriella said roughly 3,500 people have been injured and nearly 500 remain unaccounted for, though a crowdsourced tracking site used by families put the number of missing far higher, at more than 4,100. More than 25,800 families have been affected in total, he said.

The magnitude 7.4 quake — the strongest to hit Colombia in decades — struck on Monday morning near San Jose del Palmar in the northwestern Choco region. It tore through cities across western Colombia, with Cali and Pereira among the hardest hit, along with Manizales and Quibdo.

In Cali, volunteer rescuer Johana Sanchez described teams pausing every 30 minutes to listen for survivors. "So far, three people have been pulled out alive and three dead," she told AFP.

Officials say 140 buildings collapsed entirely and thousands of homes were damaged or destroyed.

Families grapple with human toll

In Palmira, Santiago Lloreda told Reuters the quake killed his mother and his 13-month-old daughter, Salma, who was too young to have fingerprints on file and would need to be identified through DNA testing. He described his mother as the family's caretaker, saying she "gave everything up to look after the baby."

A man who only gave the news agency his first name, Ricardo, traveled from Miami to recover his sister's body and said his niece was awaiting surgery for a fractured skull, jaw and leg, and a collapsed lung: "She's alive. We know she's going to get better."

Colombia races against time after worst quake in a decade To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Thousands have been left homeless, with many sleeping outdoors in parks or emergency shelters set up in schools and sports arenas, either because their homes were destroyed or out of fear of aftershocks.

Colombia's geological service has recorded 130 aftershocks since Monday's quake.

International aid set to pour in

Response efforts have been especially difficult in Choco, the quake's epicenter, a remote and impoverished region already strained by decades of conflict and displacement. Additionally, lost cell service has made it hard to assess damage in communities reachable only by river.

"This earthquake compounds an already severe humanitarian situation, and there is a need for increased support for the humanitarian response," said Giovanni Rizzo, Colombia director for the Norwegian Refugee Council.

And UN resident coordinator María Jose Torres said in a statement Tuesday that aid groups already working in the region on an earlier peace effort were able to pivot quickly to disaster relief.

The United States has pledged more than $15 million and sent response teams. Mexico has sent military aircraft carrying nearly 20 tons of food along with security personnel, with more aid and rescue specialists on standby. El Salvador's president offered two planes carrying 100 tons of supplies, and a search-and-rescue team from Mexico said it arrived directly from Venezuela, which faced its own major earthquakes in June.

Quake response provides test for new Colombian president

De la Espriella, inaugurated just three days before the earthquake struck, declared an economic emergency and three days of national mourning, and pledged to establish a fund to rebuild hospitals, schools, homes and infrastructure.

"This is undoubtedly a tragedy of immense proportions," he said. "Our efforts are focused on those who remain missing." He has not yet detailed what the economic emergency measures will involve.

Notably, de la Espriella won office on a platform of reduced public spending and a tougher security approach. Analyst Tiziano Breda, of the conflict-monitoring group ACLED, told Reuters that de la Espriella had campaigned in part on cutting funding to the country's disaster-response agency — the same unit now leading the emergency effort.

Experts have cautioned that more seismic activity is possible, if not imminent. "Let's remember that Colombia is full of active fault lines," Rodrigo Leon Loya, a seismologist at the University of the Andes, told AP. "The question isn't whether it can happen again. The question is rather when an earthquake of similar magnitude will occur at another of Colombia’s seismic sources," he warned.

World.title: US: Karoline Leavitt to step down as Trump's spokesperson
World.content:
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt is to leave her job at the end of the month, President Donald Trump says. Leavitt, 28, is the youngest-ever person to have held the position.

Karoline Leavitt, will leave her role as White House press secretary at the end of the month, US President Donald Trump said Tuesday.

Leavitt is one of the best-known faces and most ardent defenders of the MAGA movement.

Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that Leavitt was stepping down to "spend more time with her beautiful young children and family," adding that it was "a decision I totally understand and respect!"

Leavitt clung close to Trump as his press secretary Image: Brian Snyder/REUTERS

Who is Karoline Leavitt?

Leavitt, now 28, who took on the job in January 2025 aged 27 at the start of Trump's second term in office, has been the youngest-ever White House press secretary.

She recently returned from parental leave after giving birth to her second child, a daughter, in May. She also has a 2-year-old son.

After initially wanting to be a journalist, Leavitt soon entered politics. She joined the White House press office during Trump's first term, working under then-spokeswoman Kayleigh McEnany.

After Trump lost the 2020 presidential election to Joe Biden, Leavitt worked for the office of Congresswoman Elise Stefanik, a highly loyal Republican supporter of Trump.

Leavitt later unsuccessfully ran for a seat in the House of Representatives in 2022.

She also worked as a spokesperson for MAGA Inc., a super PAC supporting Trump, before joining his successful 2024 campaign.

'The honor and adventure of a lifetime' — Leavitt

In a post on X, Leavitt waxed lyrical about her period in the job.

"Serving as the White House Press Secretary over the past year and a half has been the honor and adventure of a lifetime," Leavitt wrote.

"I am incredibly grateful to President Trump for granting me so many extraordinary opportunities, such as working in the West Wing and spending countless hours in the Oval Office, flying around the world and meeting foreign leaders, and traveling across our beautiful country and meeting Americans from all walks of life."

She said her "bittersweet decision to depart the White House" was due to the difficulties of combining motherhood with the demands of the White House position.

Leavitt: A devoted defender of Trump

Leavitt, who Trump says will remain "one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party," has been a key figure in promoting the president's ideology and views, sometimes stretching the truth to do so.

Her very first press conference, on January 28, 2025, was notable for her false claim that $50 million (€43.4 million) in US taxpayers' money had been earmarked to buy condoms in the Gaza Strip.

Since then, she has staunchly defended Trump's hard-line policies while deflecting questions such as those concerning the president's ties with the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

She was also known for denigrating mainstream media outlets in line with Trump's hostile attitude to reporters who gainsay him.

Her devotion has brought her consistent praise from the president, who has now called her "one ‌of the best White House Press Secretaries in the History of the Office."
