World.title: The danger is not over: Budapest water supply under pressure again
World.content:
Hungary’s main water utility for the capital has once again urged consumers to reduce unnecessary water use as persistently low levels on the Danube put growing pressure on the Budapest water supply. The situation is particularly serious in Dunabogdány, north of the capital, where the remaining capacity of the local system has fallen to a critical level.

According to 24.hu, Budapest Waterworks (Fővárosi Vízművek) warned that although the Danube could temporarily rise by a few centimetres, a lack of rainfall across its catchment area means water levels may soon begin falling again.

The company said the latest forecast required both close attention and responsible water use. While the utility is working to maintain a secure drinking-water supply, prolonged low water levels on the Danube are creating increasingly difficult conditions for water production.

Budapest water supply: residents asked to avoid unnecessary use

Budapest Waterworks has asked all consumers to moderate their use of mains drinking water and prioritise essential everyday needs.

Large-scale uses that can be postponed should be avoided, the company said. Such activities typically include filling swimming pools, washing cars and extensive garden watering.

The issue is particularly important for foreign residents and visitors to understand because much of Budapest’s drinking water is closely linked to the Danube. The capital relies heavily on bank-filtered water: wells located along the river draw naturally filtered groundwater from gravel layers connected to the Danube.

Low river levels therefore do not automatically mean that Budapest is running out of drinking water, but prolonged drought can make extraction more difficult and increase the technical and energy demands on the system.

This is not the first water-saving warning of 2026

The latest appeal is not an isolated event this year.

During the extreme heat at the end of June, water consumption across the area served by Budapest Waterworks rose sharply. On 29 June, around 640 million litres of drinking water were consumed in a single day, according to an earlier report by the Budapest municipal news portal Énbudapestem. In some parts of the capital and surrounding settlements, consumption was several times higher than the 2025 daily average.

At the time, Budapest Waterworks was already asking consumers to use water carefully and, where possible, to avoid carrying out water-intensive activities during peak evening hours.

The warnings became even more urgent in Dunabogdány in July. On 30 July, Sokszínű Vidék reported that the utility had already appealed to local residents several times to reduce consumption, asking them to avoid watering gardens, filling pools and washing cars. Despite those requests, demand continued to rise.

As we wrote yesterday, PM Magyar announces moves to raise the Danube near Paks nuclear power plant

Dunabogdány faces the most critical situation

Conditions are currently most severe in Dunabogdány, a popular settlement on the Danube Bend roughly north of Budapest.

Local wells are producing around 1,000–1,050 cubic metres of water per day, while daily consumption stands at approximately 1,100–1,150 cubic metres, according to 24.hu. Production capacity could fall further if the Danube continues to recede.

Budapest Waterworks warned that reserves in the local system have been reduced to a minimum, meaning that any further increase in consumption or an unexpected technical problem could threaten the continuity of drinking-water supplies.

Dunabogdány Mayor András Liebhardt has pushed back against criticism of local residents. In an earlier statement reported by Sokszínű Vidék, he argued that higher summer consumption also reflects the seasonal increase in the village’s population due to tourism and people temporarily living there.

Low Danube levels causing wider problems in Hungary

The exceptionally low Danube has implications well beyond the Budapest water supply.

During the extreme heat around the end of July and beginning of August, the river fell to exceptionally low levels. The conditions also affected operations at Hungary’s Paks Nuclear Power Plant, illustrating how prolonged heat, drought and low river flows can place simultaneous pressure on the country’s water and energy infrastructure.

For Budapest Waterworks, the immediate message remains precautionary rather than a declaration of a capital-wide water shortage. Consumers are nevertheless being asked to avoid unnecessary high-volume water use as long as the Danube remains unusually low and rainfall across its catchment area remains limited.

World.title: Horror crash on Hungarian motorway: Child thrown from British-registered car
World.content:
Four people, including two children, were injured in a serious crash on Hungary’s M7 motorway near Zalakomár on Wednesday afternoon, after a British-registered car collided with a road maintenance truck.

One of the children was thrown from the car in the impact and was airlifted to hospital. According to the National Ambulance Service, the child suffered serious injuries but was in a stable condition. Two adults and the other child sustained minor injuries.

British-registered car crashed into maintenance truck

According to 24.hu, the accident happened on the Budapest-bound carriageway of the M7 motorway, between kilometres 189 and 190 near Zalakomár in Zala County. As per the police, the British-registered passenger car crashed into a road maintenance vehicle for reasons that are not yet known. All four occupants of the car were injured.

The force of the collision caused one of the children to be thrown out of the vehicle. Several ambulance units, including an air ambulance, were dispatched to the scene. The seriously injured child was transported to hospital by helicopter, while the two adults and the other child were taken to hospital with less serious injuries.

M7 motorway temporarily closed

The Budapest-bound side of the M7 was completely closed while police investigated the crash and emergency crews carried out the necessary rescue and recovery work. Drivers were diverted towards Route 7 at the Zalakomár junction, causing disruption to traffic in the area.

The closure was later lifted on Wednesday afternoon, and the M7 motorway at Zalakomár was reopened to traffic. The circumstances of the crash are under investigation.

World.title: Was there really any difference between András Baka’s removal in 2011 and Tamás Sulyok’s in 2026?
World.content:
Many see András Baka becoming Hungary’s next president as a form of historical justice after his controversial removal. But does that make the removal of Sulyok any more democratic?

The similarities between the removal of András Baka in 2011 and that of Tamás Sulyok in 2026 are difficult to ignore. In both cases, a constitutional change was used to bring the mandate of an incumbent constitutional office-holder to an early end.

That makes Baka’s election as Hungary’s next president all the more intriguing. Many see it as historical justice after his controversial removal under the Orbán government. But it also raises a difficult question for Tisza: if Baka’s removal was an abuse of constitutional power, what makes Sulyok’s removal any different?

What happened to András Baka?

András Baka became President of Hungary’s Supreme Court in 2009. He publicly criticised several government reforms affecting the judiciary and warned that they threatened judicial independence.

His mandate was then terminated years before it was due to expire, as the constitutional framework of Hungary’s judiciary was fundamentally reorganised.

The case eventually reached the European Court of Human Rights. In 2016, the Court ruled that Hungary had violated Baka’s rights, finding that the premature termination of his mandate was linked to his public criticism of constitutional and legislative reforms concerning the judiciary.

The story therefore seems almost tailor-made for historical justice. The former chief justice who became one of the symbols of the Orbán era’s rule-of-law problems has now been elected president in the middle of a political transition whose central promise is to restore the rule of law. But this is exactly where the comparison becomes uncomfortable.

The resemblance is striking

Let us put the two cases next to each other and look at the constitutional mechanism itself. Baka’s mandate was brought to an early end by a constitutional provision stating:

The mandates of the President of the Supreme Court and the President and members of

the National Council of Justice shall be terminated when the Fundamental Law comes into force.

Sulyok’s mandate, meanwhile, is being terminated by another constitutional provision:

On the day following the entry into force of the Seventeenth Amendment to the

Fundamental Law, the mandate of the President of the Republic in office shall terminate.

The circumstances are certainly not identical. András Baka was the President of the Supreme Court, and his removal took place amid a fundamental restructuring of the judiciary. The European Court of Human Rights subsequently found a violation of his Convention rights.

Sulyok, by contrast, is being removed by a newly elected parliamentary majority that has the constitutional majority required to amend the Fundamental Law.

But the central question remains. Should a parliamentary majority be able to change the constitution specifically so that the mandate of an incumbent constitutional office-holder ends? If the answer was no when Orbán’s government did it, why should the answer automatically become yes when Tisza does it?

Was electing Baka a mistake?

Politically, probably not. Baka is an exceptionally powerful symbol for Tisza. His career allows the new government to present the presidency as part of a restoration of judicial independence and democratic institutions.

Fidesz, meanwhile, can hardly attack András Baka without reopening the uncomfortable question of why he was removed in the first place. In the short term, therefore, his election is a clever political move. In the longer term, however, Baka could become one of Tisza’s biggest constitutional headaches.

From now on, whenever the legality or legitimacy of Sulyok’s removal is debated, Baka’s name will inevitably be brought into the discussion. Critics can draw the parallel in a single sentence: In 2011, one government used constitutional change to remove an inconvenient constitutional figure. In 2026, another government did something remarkably similar.

Of course, Tisza can argue that it is dismantling a political and constitutional system built by Orbán and that it has received a democratic mandate to do so. But that is precisely where the rule-of-law test begins. Constitutional safeguards are not supposed to protect only the politicians we support. They are supposed to protect institutions even when the people in power are the ones we strongly disagree with.

And that is why Baka’s election is such a powerful — and potentially awkward — symbol. The former chief justice removed through constitutional engineering has returned as president. The question is whether Hungary has truly learned the lesson of his case. Or whether it has simply changed who gets to use the same constitutional tools.

But why did Tisza ultimately choose András Baka over Judit Polgár for the presidency? We explored the reasons in more detail in this article.

World.title: Hungary could get a new public holiday: Christmas Eve could become a day off this year!
World.content:
Christmas Eve could become a genuine public holiday in Hungary as early as this year, meaning employees may no longer have to make up the day by working a Saturday. A new proposal says the change could be introduced with a simple parliamentary majority.

24 December could become a statutory day off

Hungary could make 24 December a public holiday as early as 2026, with no referendum or two-thirds parliamentary majority required under the current legal framework.

According to Világgazdaság, the National Federation of Workers’ Councils (Munkástanácsok Országos Szövetsége) and trade union organisation Egyenlő.hu submitted a concrete proposal to the Ministry of Social and Family Affairs in July. If the proposal reaches Parliament in the autumn and is approved, Christmas Eve could become a public holiday without requiring employees to make up the day by working a Saturday.

The proposed solution is legally simpler than the issue might suggest. Rather than creating a new national holiday, 24 December would simply be added to the list of statutory public holidays in Hungary’s Labour Code.

At present, the list includes 1 January, 15 March, Good Friday, Easter Monday, 1 May, Whit Monday, 20 August, 23 October, 1 November, and 25 and 26 December.

Under the current system, 24 December is not a public holiday. Instead, the government can designate it as a rest day in the annual working-time schedule, with employees then required to work on a nearby Saturday.

This is exactly what is planned for 2026: Christmas Eve falls on a Thursday, making 24 December a designated rest day, but employees are currently scheduled to work on Saturday, 12 December in exchange. The proposed amendment would change this arrangement permanently.

No more Saturday make-up day

If 24 December were added to the Labour Code’s list of public holidays, it would no longer need to be designated as a day off through a separate ministerial decree every year. Most importantly, the Saturday make-up working day would disappear as well.

According to the organisations behind the proposal, amending the Labour Code would only require a simple parliamentary majority. There would be no need to amend the Fundamental Law’s provisions concerning public holidays, meaning a two-thirds majority would not be necessary.

It would be more than just another day off

There is an important legal distinction between a holiday and a statutory public holiday. Simply declaring a date a holiday does not automatically mean employees cannot be required to work. A statutory public holiday, however, comes with specific employment-law protections.

Csaba Bubenkó, deputy president of Munkástanácsok, said the proposed amendment would guarantee exemption from work and introduce stricter conditions for those who could still legally be scheduled to work. The rules on holiday pay supplements and compensation for absence would also apply.

The change would have a direct impact on retailers, too. Under the proposal, no separate shop-opening regulations would be necessary: designating 24 December as a public holiday would itself mean that shops could not open, while essential food supplies and public services would continue to be taken into account.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

A referendum may no longer be necessary

Other trade unions have also been working towards making Christmas Eve a public holiday. The Trade Union of Commercial Employees (Kereskedelmi Alkalmazottak Szakszervezete) has been working to collect the 200,000 signatures required for a referendum initiative certified by Hungary’s National Election Office.

The new legal proposal could make that process unnecessary. If Parliament simply adds 24 December to the Labour Code’s list of public holidays, there would be no need for the longer and more costly referendum process.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar previously promised that Christmas Eve would become a public holiday that would not have to be made up by working another day. In July, he also said he hoped the change could take effect as early as this year. However, the exact timing will depend on the legislative process and Parliament’s decision, so it is not yet certain that the new rules will apply this Christmas.

If Parliament approves the amendment in the autumn, 2026 could nevertheless become the first year in which 24 December is a fully fledged statutory public holiday rather than a transferred day off. And that would mean one thing many Hungarian workers will certainly welcome: no Saturday at work just to get Christmas Eve off.

World.title: Hungarian Wizz Air opens new base in another European city!
World.content:
Wizz Air is expanding its presence in Romania once again, announcing a new operational base at Brașov-Ghimbav International Airport from December 2026. The move will bring four new routes to the Transylvanian city and expand Wizz Air’s Brașov network to 15 destinations across seven countries.

The airline’s expansion comes despite a challenging financial period, with Wizz Air recently reporting a significant loss for the first quarter of its current financial year.

Wizz Air to base an aircraft in Brașov

From December, Brașov-Ghimbav International Airport will become home to one Airbus A321neo operated by Wizz Air, making Brașov (Brassó) the airline’s 10th operational base in Romania, Maszol.ro writes based on the report of economica.net. The new base will support four new routes connecting Brașov with:

Chișinău, Moldova

Barcelona, Spain

Madrid, Spain

Karlsruhe/Baden-Baden, Germany

Once the expansion is complete, passengers flying from Brașov will be able to reach 15 cities in seven countries with Wizz Air. The new routes are expected to significantly strengthen the airport’s international connectivity, particularly for travellers in southern Transylvania.

800,000 passengers have already flown with Wizz Air from Brașov

Wizz Air has operated from Brașov since August 2023. According to data from the local county council, its services have carried around 800,000 passengers from the airport so far. The airline says its continued presence demonstrates its long-term commitment to the region.

“Over the past three years, through our uninterrupted operations at Brașov Airport, we have demonstrated our long-term commitment to the region,” said András Radó, Wizz Air’s communications director.

He also described Romania as a key market for the airline. The new Brașov base comes just nine months after Wizz Air opened another base in Transylvania, at Târgu Mureș.

Romania a key market for Wizz Air

Wizz Air has been operating in Romania since 2006 and has established itself as the country’s leading low-cost airline. The carrier currently employs around 1,900 people in Romania and connects 14 Romanian cities with 83 destinations across 26 countries, operating a total of around 230 routes.

The expansion in Brașov therefore represents another significant step in the airline’s Romanian network, particularly as demand for international travel from regional airports continues to grow.

Photo: Wizz Air

If you missed it: Wizz Air Budapest-Tallinn flight returns to Budapest shortly after take-off

Wizz Air reports nearly EUR 200 million quarterly loss

The expansion comes at an interesting time for the airline financially. Wizz Air recently reported a EUR 198 million loss for the three months ending in June. This compares with a EUR 38.4 million profit recorded during the same period a year earlier.

Despite the substantial loss, the airline’s revenue increased by 5.5% year-on-year to EUR 1.51 billion, although this was slightly below analysts’ expectations of EUR 1.54 billion. The Brașov expansion nevertheless signals that Wizz Air continues to see considerable growth potential in Romania.

With a new aircraft based locally and four additional international destinations on the way, Brașov is set to become an increasingly important part of Wizz Air’s Romanian network from the end of this year.

World.title: Romania moves to restart strategic graphite extraction at Baia de Fier
World.content:
Romanian defense minister Radu Miruţă announced on Wednesday, August 12, that the graphite exploitation facility located at Baia de Fier, in Gorj County, will be reopened, with the state as the sole beneficiary of the exploitation license.

The exploitation obtained the necessary approvals from the Ministries of Economy, Environment, Finance, and Justice, according to the official.

“I am confident that next week at the latest, we will pass this government decision in the government meeting. The government decision is an important one because it represents the unlocking of the padlock so that the development at Baia de Fier and the exploitation of graphite can take place,” Miruţă explained.

Subsequently, an international tender will be organized to prepare the pre-feasibility and feasibility studies and other necessary documentation, with the first activities estimated to begin in 2028.

The European Commission approved the financing of the graphite exploitation in the sub-mountain area and extended EUR 200 million in financing for the implementation of this project.

Radu Miruță emphasized that the graphite exploitation activity will bring jobs and economic development. The president of the Gorj County Council stated that he discussed with the management of the state company that will handle the extraction of graphite and received assurances that more than 100 jobs will be created, according to Profit.ro.

Graphite is an increasingly sought-after mineral in modern technologies, being used, among other things, in the manufacture of conductors, as well as some essential components in mobile phones, and in the nuclear industry. Moreover, graphene, essential in green energy, is extracted from graphite, and one ton is sold for as much as EUR 200,000. Before it was shut down, the Baia de Fier factory produced 40,000 tons of graphite per year.

World.title: Romanian president again challenges law allowing hydropower projects in protected areas
World.content:
Romanian president Nicușor Dan has asked Parliament to reconsider legislation allowing the construction and completion of hydropower projects in protected areas, reopening a dispute over the balance between energy security and environmental protection.

Dan submitted the request to Parliament on August 12, according to Economedia, after the Constitutional Court rejected his objections to the legislation in June.

"Beyond the limits of constitutional control, we consider that the current assessment of the necessity, opportunity and efficiency of the adopted legislative solutions is required, including from the perspective of developments that have occurred since the initiation of the legislative proposal," Dan said in the note accompanying his request.

The president had previously argued that the legislation could allow protected-area boundaries to be reduced and environmental assessments to be waived for entire categories of energy projects, including projects declared by the Supreme Council for National Defence to be of national security interest.

The legislation, initiated by Social Democratic Party (PSD) senator Daniel Zamfir, is designed to facilitate the completion of unfinished hydropower projects.

State-controlled Hidroelectrica plans to resume and complete several projects originally started during the communist period. The Energy Ministry has proposed completing around 10 unfinished hydropower plants with a combined capacity of about 700 MW, arguing that substantial investments have already been made in the projects.

The projects have remained unfinished for years, with some facing environmental and legal obstacles. Their completion has gained renewed attention amid pressure to increase domestic electricity generation and strengthen Romania’s energy security.

Environmental organisations, including Declic and other civic groups, oppose the resumption of some of the projects because of their potential impact on river ecosystems. They argue that upgrading existing hydropower capacity could deliver energy gains with lower environmental costs than completing older projects in protected areas.

The dispute comes as Romania faces pressure on its electricity system following the shutdown of both reactors at the Cernavoda nuclear power plant because of exceptionally low Danube water levels. The government has also sought to maintain additional coal-fired generation capacity beyond existing decarbonisation deadlines.

Parliament will now have to reconsider the legislation following the president’s request, despite the Constitutional Court having already ruled on its constitutionality.

World.title: Assets of Romania-focused ETFs spike EUR 276 mln in first seven months of 2026
World.content:
Romania-focused ETFs listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange added EUR 276 million in assets in the first seven months of 2026, almost tripling in size from EUR 174 million at the end of 2025 to approximately EUR 450 million at the end of July 2026, according to an analysis by Divo Pulitika, Board Member at InterCapital ETF.

Of this increase, an estimated EUR 155 million came from fresh investor inflows, while approximately EUR 122 million was generated by the appreciation of Romanian equities.

The six locally listed Romania-focused ETFs now hold assets equivalent to approximately 1.3% of the Bucharest Stock Exchange's entire free float.

At the end of June, 28 foreign-listed ETFs with almost EUR 500 billion in combined assets had exposure to Romanian equities, holding approximately EUR 264 million in Romanian companies. While Romania represents only around 0.05% of the total assets of these funds, their Romanian holdings are already approaching 1% of the entire free float of the Bucharest Stock Exchange. The funds are managed by 12 international providers, including some of the world’s largest asset managers, such as Vanguard, Invesco, JPMorgan and Xtrackers.

According to Divo Pulitika, the increase in the value of Romanian ETFs is part of a much larger structural shift taking place across financial markets.

“ETFs continue to be one of the fastest-growing and most dynamic segments of the financial industry. Technology has made buying and selling ETFs increasingly simple and cost-efficient, while the range of products available to investors has expanded far beyond the world’s largest equity indices into individual countries, regions, sectors and increasingly specialized investment themes,” the analysis stated.

According to Bloomberg data, ETFs listed on European exchanges currently hold approximately EUR 3.3 trillion in assets, around three quarters of which are invested in equities. To put this into perspective, this is approximately 40 times the combined market capitalization of all Romanian listed companies.

The expansion of the global ETF industry is increasingly relevant for Romania because these products have become an important channel through which international capital reaches individual markets. Since the beginning of 2026, the value of Romanian equities held by foreign ETFs has increased by approximately EUR 31 million. Interestingly, however, this increase was driven by the appreciation of Romanian shares rather than by fresh investment. On a net basis, foreign ETFs recorded an estimated EUR 34 million of outflows from Romanian equities during the period.

A large part of these outflows can be explained by index mechanics rather than by a broader withdrawal of international ETF capital from Romania.

At the same time, one of the most important developments of 2026 is that the strongest ETF-driven inflows into Romanian equities are increasingly coming from the domestic market itself. The estimated EUR 155 million of net inflows into Romania-focused ETFs listed on BVB represents fresh investor capital, with the majority of these inflows coming from Romanian retail investors.

The timing has also been supportive. The Romanian equity market delivered the highest 10-year total return among the global markets analysed by InterCapital ETF, while 2026 has brought another approximately 50% increase so far. At the same time, the entry of major Romanian banking groups into the ETF segment has substantially increased the visibility, accessibility and distribution of these products among local investors.

Since the beginning of 2026, approximately EUR 165 million worth of ETF units have been traded on BVB, representing around 6.2% of total equity turnover. The figure is also notable when compared internationally, being broadly in line with the Netherlands, one of Europe’s established ETF hubs, and ahead of markets such as Spain at 0.3%, Hungary at 0.9%, Poland at 1.1%, Japan at 4.8% and France at 5.7%. ETF penetration remains higher in markets such as Croatia at around 10%, Italy at 13%, the UK at 20%, Germany at 22% and the US at approximately 30%.

InterCapital ETF is the first ETF manager in both Croatia and Slovenia and the first international ETF provider in Romania. The company currently manages 6 ETFs with over EUR 200 million in assets under management.

World.title: Northern Romania: resort of Sângeorz-Băi aims to build modern spa center
World.content:
Sângeorz-Băi, once a well-known balneoclimateric resort town in northern Romania, aims to resurrect its large hotels, which have been either closed or operating at minimum capacity, through the development of a modern spa center, according to G4Media.

The mayor of the town, Cătălin Bota, said that the only asset remaining in the ownership of the town is Mineral Water Spring 6. Based on this, the town hall submitted a project for a treatment facility and a spa complex in the resort park, but political changes and changes at the ministerial level have delayed the financing.

Some of the largest hotels in the town have already closed. The famous Someșul Hotel, owned by the trade unions, has been closed and abandoned for four years, having been emptied of furniture. Hotel Hebe, privatized, operates only during the summer, with minimal investments and a degraded treatment facility, moved to the ground floor.

Nevertheless, the local administration has modernized the utility networks and streets and is carrying out a project financed from European funds for the rehabilitation of the resort park. It will include an open-air museum created in collaboration with the Museum of Comparative Art, where 25 statues have already been restored.

“In the absence of funds from the government, the town hall intends to access European funds under the 2028-2034 financial framework, even if the co-financing rate is 50%,” said Cătălin Bota.

Representatives of the town hall claimed that public investment is the only chance to attract tourists again and to prompt private owners to invest, given that spa tourism has been neglected at the national level in recent years.

World.title: Transylvania Tapes: Found footage horror movie filmed in Romania has local premiere at Biertan festival
World.content:
Transylvania Tapes, a mix of the found footage and Eurohorror genres directed by filmmaker Brad Sykes, will have its Romanian premiere at the Lună Plină/ Full Moon Horror and Fantasy Film Festival in Biertan on August 16.

The film, shot entirely in Bucharest and Sighisoara, follows Mara Enescu, a young woman in her 30s who travels from Los Angeles to her home country of Romania to discover the truth about her mother’s disappearance in Transylvania years ago. Together with a cameraman friend, she journeys from Bucharest “to the birthplace of Dracula himself.”

The movie, produced by Josephina Sykes, stars newcomer Valeria Badiuc (in opening photo) as well as Gabriel Spahiu, who recently had roles in Radu Jude’s Kontinental '25 and Dracula, and Ion Haiduc, recently seen in Trancers: The Whole Dethly Affair.

Transylvania Tapes had its world premiere this June at the Horror-on-Sea Film Festival in the UK. It also screened at GrossFest Film Festival in Pittsburgh.

“Transylvania Tapes is a unique mix of found footage and Eurohorror genres that my wife and producer, Josephina, and I have been wanting to make for twenty years. After writing several different scripts, creating multiple budgets and taking far too many meetings, we finally decided last year that if we wanted to make our dream project, we needed to make it completely independently with the resources we had available. This meant calling in favors from friends going back to the late 1990s, when Josephina and I first met on a Romanian movie set, as well as working with some brand-new talent. Making Transylvania Tapes was an exciting journey for all of us and one of the most intimate, personal movies I have ever directed,” director Brad Sykes explains.

Filmmaker and author Brad Sykes graduated cum laude from Boston University’s film program. After moving to Los Angeles and working in production and development for companies including Paramount Pictures, Scott Free, and Full Moon Entertainment, Sykes made his professional writing/directing debut with the horror comedy Scream Queen, starring genre icon Linnea Quigley. Since then, he has written and directed over twenty-five feature films, including the digital 3D horror movie Camp Blood.

Sykes’ film Death Factory was its distributor's all-time top-grossing title. His other writing-directing credits include Goth, Mad Jack, Demon's Kiss, Plaguers (winner of Best Screenplay at the 2008 Estepona Film Festival and Best Actor Steve Railsback at 2008 Shockerfest), Hi-8: Horror Independent Eight and its sequels Hi-Death and Hi-Fear. He lives in Los Angeles with his wife, producer Josephina Sykes, where they operate Nightfall Pictures, a full-service development and production company.

Josephina Sykes, who was born in Bucharest, graduated in 1999 from the National University of Theatre and Film UNATC with a major in screenwriting. She also spent a semester at La FEMIS film school in Paris in 1998, on a scholarship from the French Foreign Ministry. After graduation, she worked for film studios Castel Film and Media Pro Pictures. Since relocating to Los Angeles in 2001, she has continued to work in film, both as a screenwriter and in production on various indie features. In 2004, she founded Nightfall Pictures, a full-service development and production company, with her husband.

She has produced several feature films, including the thriller Within the Woods, the drama Dead Letters, starring C. Thomas Howell, actioner Mutation, the debut of Katie Featherston, and the award-winning sci-fi/horror film Plaguers, starring Steve Railsback. She is one of the co-creators and executive producers of the horror anthology Hi-8: Horror Independent Eight, which was selected in the official competition of over twenty film festivals.

World.title: NATO firmly condemns Russia for violating Romanian, Polish airspace
World.content:
Ambassadors of NATO member countries met on Wednesday, August 12, in a session in Brussels to discuss the recent violations of the airspace in Poland and Romania, as well as the recent drone incidents.

The representatives “reiterated that Russia bears full responsibility for the airspace violations, which are dangerous and unacceptable, and demonstrate Russia’s increasing tolerance for risk.”

They also highlighted efforts to shore up NATO defenses in response to these new threats. “NATO continues to strengthen its integrated air and missile defenses across the Alliance, and Allies underlined the actions they have taken to bolster defenses on the eastern flank, from the Baltic to the Black Sea. NATO stands ready to deter and defend against any aggression,” the statement also mentioned.

At the same meeting, NATO members reaffirmed their full support for Ukraine in defending its freedom, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, as well as in achieving peace, while also specifying that “Russia’s irresponsible acts” will not deter them from their enduring commitment to Ukraine, especially as this commitment contributes to their own security.

In recent weeks, intelligence services from several member states have warned that Moscow could launch strikes against eastern states to test NATO’s reaction.

So far, Russian drones have infringed on Romanian airspace numerous times since the start of the war in Ukraine. Most recently, five drones were tracked nearing Romanian territory on the night of Wednesday, August 12, to Thursday, August 13, around 1 AM. One drone briefly entered Romanian airspace in Tulcea County but then exited and headed to Ukraine. Shortly after, explosions were reported. Another drone was detected in Romanian airspace around 9 AM. Two F-16 aircraft of the Romanian Air Force were scrambled to monitor the situation on both occasions, according to official sources.

At the end of July, a Russian ballistic missile fell approximately 60 km from Lublin (eastern Poland), which prompted the government in Warsaw to send a letter of protest to the Russian ambassador.

Also at the end of July, Romania summoned the Russian ambassador to Bucharest and expelled a Russian diplomat to protest against the violation of its airspace by Russian drones. Three Russian drones were shot down on Romanian territory on July 24-26, of which the first came within 80 km of Bucharest – after another Russian drone hit a block of apartments in Galati last month. Following the Galati incident, Romania closed Russia’s consulate in Constanta.

World.title: Romania’s Transgaz takes EUR 300 mln investment loan from Banca Transilvania
World.content:
Banca Transilvania is supporting one of the most significant investments in Romania’s energy infrastructure by providing EUR 300 million in financing to Transgaz.

This marks the largest bilateral financing provided by Banca Transilvania to the energy sector, Transgaz said in a note to investors.

The financing is intended for the development and modernization of the national natural gas transport infrastructure, in a context in which energy security, regional interconnection and infrastructure resilience have become strategic priorities for Romania and Europe, according to a joint statement from the two entities

“Transgaz’s 2026–2035 National Natural Gas Transmission System Development Plan includes strategic investment projects, supported by the Romanian Government, aimed at developing, modernizing, and interconnecting the National Transmission System as well as integrating the natural gas extracted from the Black Sea into the national energy system,” Ion Sterian, CEO of Transgaz, said.

World.title: Romania Shuts Nuclear Reactor on Danube as Power Crisis Deepens
World.content:
Romania shut down its last operating nuclear unit on Thursday as record-low Danube water levels threatened the cooling system at the Cernavoda nuclear power plant, adding to concerns over electricity supplies during a prolonged heatwave.

The shutdown leaves both reactors at the country’s sole nuclear plan offline. Cernavoda normally accounts for about 20 per cent of Romania’s electricity production.

Officials say the closure will not significantly affect Romania’s energy situation.

“Shutting down the last reactor is a controlled process that will only last about 10 days … during this time, Romania will have the resources to cover the energy deficit in the grid,” Romeo Urjan, director of the Cernavoda plant, said.

The Energy Ministry in a statement said higher wind power production is expected, while a coal-fired power unit is also due to restart.

Authorities are also preparing to increase electricity imports, mainly from neighbouring Bulgaria and Ukraine, to maintain supplies and avoid disruption, as demand remains high in the extreme temperatures.

The government has already urged households and businesses to reduce electricity consumption during peak evening hours until the end of the month, to ease the pressure on the power system during the ongoing heatwave.

More than 80 large industrial consumers have either reduced production or scheduled maintenance to cut electricity use, while restrictions have also been imposed on water use for agricultural irrigation.

The exceptionally low Danube levels have affected river transport, tourism and the energy sector. The government declared a nationwide energy alert on July 31, which will remain in force throughout August.

The energy crisis has also fuelled a surge in conspiracy theories and fears that Romania could face a nationwide blackout. Energy experts, however, doubt such a scenario.

“People have no reason to fear; they will not be left without electricity. Romania will resort to imports when necessary … though these will be more expensive because all countries in the region need electricity during the same evening peak hours,” energy analyst Corina Murafa said.

Murafa warned that higher electricity costs for consumers could be a likely consequence of the situation, as Romania relies more heavily on imports while domestic nuclear generation remains suspended.

While the shutdown at Cernavoda is not expected to last long, continued heat and low Danube levels could keep pressure on the country’s energy system for some weeks.

World.title: Turkey Targets Major Religious Group With Organised Crime Charges
World.content:
Turkish police detained Alihan Kuris, leader of one of Turkey’s largest religious groups, known as the “Suleymancilar,” and 48 others on Thursday as part of an investigation into an alleged organised crime group.

The Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office said detention warrants had been issued for Kuris and 48 other suspects as part of an investigation into alleged offences.

They include establishing and managing a criminal organisation, membership of a criminal organisation, laundering proceeds of crime, fraud against public institutions and violations of tax law.

“The criminal organisation sought through this method to prevent access to company records and make it more difficult to trace financial transactions,” the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office said in a statement.

It said a report by Turkey’s Financial Crimes Investigation Board, MASAK, found that many companies linked to the suspects had recorded significant increases in financial transactions and purchases and sales since 2020.

Prosecutors alleged that a number of the companies subsequently underwent divisions and transfers, while new companies were established with large amounts of capital, sometimes in different provinces and operating in sectors unrelated to the original companies.

The investigation targets one of Turkey’s largest religious communities.

The so-called Suleymancilar are inspired by Turkish imam and preacher Suleyman Hilmi Tunahan, who was originally from Bulgaria and died in 1959. The group’s main focus is Koranic education and it runs thousands of dormitories, cultural centres and other facilities in Turkey and abroad, particularly in Germany.

The group opened a part of its new headquarters in Cologne in recent weeks with some financial support from the German government.

Turkish Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci said Kuris, Tunahan’s maternal great-grandson. took over the movement in 2016, after which its activities began to be conducted with greater secrecy.

“They are building a large centre in Cologne, Germany. We assess that once this building is completed, all of their activities will be moved there,” Ciftci said, describing Thursday’s operation as one targeting the organisation’s financial network.

The group is also known for its political and business activities. It controls an extensive network of companies and business interests, amounting to a sizeable business empire with activities spanning construction, food production and publishing, among others.

Former group leader Arif Ahmet Denizolgun was Turkey’s transport minister in the 1990s, as a member of the centre-right Motherland Party.

His nephew, Arif Ahmet Denizolgun, was an MP for President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, from 2018 to 2023. Denizolgun is at odds with Kuris’s leadership.

The group has never enjoyed particularly close relations with Erdogan’s AKP, however, as it has traditionally opted to support centrist parties rather than political Islamist parties.

Following the failed coup attempt in 2016 and the subsequent crackdown on the so-called Gulen movement, which the Turkish authorities accused of orchestrating the coup attempt, some Islamist circles urged action against the Suleymancilar.

In Turkey’s 2023 general election and 2024 local elections, the group reportedly supported opposition parties against Erdogan’s ruling alliance.

World.title: ‘Absurd Blockade’: Fresh Parliamentary Deadlock Pushes Kosovo Back Into Crisis Mode
World.content:
This Tuesday, Avni Dehari entered Kosovo’s parliament – but not for the task he is formally entrusted with.

The 79-year-old MP from the ruling Vetevendosje party is parliament’s provisional speaker, as its oldest member, tasked with moderating the inaugural session of the Assembly until MPs vote on a permanent speaker.

Parliament is stuck again in apparent deadlock, with Dehari’s party refusing to submit a name for the speaker, as it first demands an agreement with other parties on the election of a new President of Kosovo.

Parliament’s rules require him to invite the MPs to a session every 48 hours until they elect a speaker.

But the last time Dehari actually presided over a session was last Saturday, August 8, and that session lasted only a few minutes.

World.title: Albania Gambles on Re-Legalising ‘Dangerous’ Online Sports Betting
World.content:
When the Albanian government finalised its ban on gambling in 2019, the official narrative promised to uproot a social scourge that had spread to almost every street corner in Albania. At the time, there was hardly a neighbourhood without two or three betting shops.

Street betting shops and online gambling were banned, while casinos were restricted to certain upscale hotels.

Seven years later, the Albanian government is preparing to legalise online sports betting once again, although it had continued operating informally despite the ban.

Following the adoption of the law by parliament to re-legalise in 2024, the Ministry of Finance told BIRN that all secondary legislation has now been approved and that the regulatory framework is considered complete.

“The system is legally ready, but the licensing process has not yet officially opened,” the ministry said in a written response.

World.title: Political Deadlock in Romania Threatens €770m EU Lifeline
World.content:
An unusual meeting on Tuesday afternoon between Romanian President Nicusor Dan, government representatives and leaders of the main pro-European parties was visibly tense from the outset.

Political leaders were not smiling, not even as a matter of protocol. Their greetings were formal, as was their interaction throughout the meeting. The talks were important because they were expected to adopt a law that would allow Romania to avoid losing approximately 770 million euros in funding from the EU-backed National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR).

European funds are vital to Romania’s strained budget, supporting healthcare, education and infrastructure projects. EU funding is equivalent to around one third of the country’s gross domestic product. Romania must reform its public sector law in order to receive the EU’s funding.

Yet the meeting ended without any concrete result.

World.title: Kosovo Probes Alleged Police Violence Against Serb During Raid
World.content:
North Mitrovica Hospital , Kosovo, where the man received treatment. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s Police Inspectorate said on Wednesday that it was investigating reports published on August 11 claiming officers used excessive force against a Serb man, Nenad Raskovic, during a raid at his home near the northern municipality of Zubin Potok.

Photographs shared on media and social networks show injuries on Raskovic’s back.

The Police Inspectorate, IPK, said it had interviewed Raskovic at North Mitrovica Hospital, where he is receiving treatment.

“The IPK has initiated this preliminary investigation with the aim of verifying the allegations and clarifying all relevant facts and circumstances related to the case,” the Inspectorate, an independent institution overseeing police conduct, said in a statement.

The Inspectorate said it would take all necessary steps, including “cooperating with relevant institutions, obtaining official documents and information, and interviewing people who may have knowledge of the incident”.

The Belgrade-backed Kosovo Serb party, Srpska Lista, said Raskovic said police officers entered his home in Dren village on Tuesday and, after searching the property, began hitting him without explanation.

“After that, Nenad was left tied to a tree. With the help of friends, he was freed and taken to the Family Medicine Centre in Zubin Potok, and then to the Clinical Hospital Centre in Mitrovica,” the party said.

In interviews given to media from hospital, Raskovic alleged that he was beaten by Kosovo police.

The Srpska List party called on Western embassies and organisations, NATO-led peacekeepers in KFOR and the EU rule-of-law mission EULEX to “examine the allegations and take action within their respective mandates to establish the facts and ensure the rights and safety of citizens”.

Petar Petkovic, head of the Serbian government’s office for Kosovo, also posted photos of the alleged injuries inflicted by Kosovo police on Tuesday, saying that “these are photos of [Kosovo Prime Minister Albin] Kurti’s ‘democracy’.

“For weeks, months and years, we have been warning the entire international community about the persecution of Serbs by Kurti’s regime, which has led to this. When those responsible face no sanctions and there is no adequate protection, these are the consequences,” Petkovic wrote.

Kosovo Police confirmed searching Raskovic’s home. Erduan Baliqi, a police spokesperson for the North Region, told BIRN: “Raskovic’s house was among the properties searched during the operation in Dren village… The searches were related to information on weapons.”

Baliqi said the police had “no information about the use of violence”.

Civil society organisations in Serb-majority northern Kosovo have called on the European Union to assess EULEX’s monitoring of the Kosovo Police.

“These allegations require an urgent and independent investigation, as well as an appropriate response from the relevant institutions,” they said in a statement.

The allegations come as attention focuses on war-related crimes in the Zubin Potok area, where excavations have been carried out in several villages in search of mass graves.

So far, remains believed to belong to four people have been exhumed, while three people have been arrested on suspicion of war crimes against civilians.

World.title: New Hungarian President Elected; Vows to Restore the Rule of Law
World.content:
Hungary cannot be built on “vengeance” and building a new future for it “demands both justice and self-restraint”, Hungary’s new president, Andras Baka, said after being elected by the ruling Tisza party’s 140 votes in parliament on Tuesday evening.

The former governing party Fidesz boycotted the vote and called both the process and the new president illegitimate.

The 73-year-old will be sworn in to the largely ceremonial post on August 19 and will remain in office until Hungary’s new constitution is adopted – a process that could take up to five years. The new constitution is expected to pave the way for the direct election of the country’s next president. According to a poll conducted by Median last year, 66 per cent of Hungarians would prefer direct presidential elections, with only Fidesz voters backing the current system by a significant majority of 61 per cent.

Commentators see Baka, a former Supreme Court chief judge and two-term judge serving at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in Strasbourg, as a broadly acceptable candidate for a large majority of Hungarians: an experienced, respected man with solid legal credentials.

Baka was an outspoken critic of the regime of former prime minister Viktor Orban, which removed him from his position as president of the Supreme Court in 2012 after he criticised his judicial reforms, which included plans to transfer cases to more government-friendly judges.

The Orban government passed tailor-made legislation that would have required previous judicial experience in Hungary to become president of the Supreme Court. It was a condition that Baka did not meet, given much of his career had been spent at the ECHR. Baka sued the Orban government and won at the Court of Justice of the European Union’s (ECJ), but was not reinstated to his position.

His election by parliament puts an end to a somewhat embarrassing casting process by new Prime Minister Peter Magyar, whose first choice was Hungary’s renowned chess world champion Judit Polgar, but she politely declined the offer, partly because of controversial remarks made on social media, mostly concerning her silence on political issues.

Baka is clearly a more political choice, especially considering his experience and background. But his election also suggests that Magyar has been willing to choose a figure with a strong independent streak rather than a party loyalist, unlike the previous Fidesz-appointed incumbent, Tamas Sulyok, whose resignation Magyar had made a campaign promise.

“Andras Baka has had an outstanding and highly prestigious career, and he is a very autonomous person. I see his election as president as a possible sign of self-restraint on the part of Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who won a very broad mandate in the April 12 election,” Marta Pardavi, chair of the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, told BIRN.

Baka is distinctly different from influencer-style politicians like Magyar or even Health Minister Zsolt Hegedus, who skyrocketed to fame with his dancing after Tisza’s election victory. Baka is a calm, principled man who believes in core values such as democracy and the rule of law. “His election can send the message that Hungary takes its highest office seriously,” Pardavi added.

Baka himself has made clear that he does not intend to become a pliant partner for the government and will voice criticism when necessary. He has already been one of the leading critics of the Tisza government’s recent constitutional amendment limiting MPs’ mandates to 12 years, arguing that it infringes on passive voting rights – in other words, that it restricts voters’ choice of candidates.

In his speech to parliament on Tuesday, Baka said that the nation had “wasted an entire generation”, and has fallen from being a frontrunner in 1990 to one of the countries lagging behind in the region. He described the country’s situation as critical in areas such as the rule of law, health care, education, child protection, energy and transport.

But he also warned that “an election result in itself cannot restore the rule of law.” The rule of law, he argued, does not only imply that institutions work, but also that people can trust that the rules apply to everyone, without exception.

Baka is also in keeping with Magyar’s conservative background, having served as an MP in Hungary’s first democratically elected parliament after 1990 as part of the Hungarian Democratic Forum (although he never formally joined the party). He used to work with Laszlo Solyom, who later became president and was the last head of state to use the office as a check on the government and openly criticise its policies.

World.title: North Macedonia Parties Share Out Nearly €9 Million from State Budget
World.content:
North Macedonia’s political parties received almost 9 million euros from the state budget this year for their regular operations, with the ruling VMRO DPMNE party taking a record 2.5 million euros and the main opposition Social Democrats, SDSM, seeing its funding fall by around 40 per cent to about 1 million euros.

A BIRN analysis of the 2026 payments, based on data obtained from the Ministry of Justice, shows that the three largest recipients, VMRO DPMNE, the SDSM and the ethnic Albanian Democratic Union for Integration, DUI, together received about 45 per cent of the total funding.

Adding in the smaller Levica [Left] and ZNAM parties, more than half of the money went to just five parties.

The DUI received about 472,000 euros, down from about 840,000 euros last year.

Both falls and rises reflect the parties’ performance in the 2025 local elections and the number of municipal councillors they secured.

North Macedonia’s system ties state funding to electoral performance.

Thirty per cent of the available money is distributed equally among parties and coalitions that meet a 1-per-cent electoral threshold. The other 70 per cent is allocated according to the number of elected MPs and municipal councillors.

This makes local elections particularly important. While parliament has 120 seats, the country’s municipalities have 1,307 elected councillors. In the 2025 local elections, the VMRO DPMNE-led coalition won 548 council seats, compared with 231 for the SDSM-led coalition.

“A councillor and an MP are worth the same, so this explains the competition to get as many councillors as possible,” a source from one of the parties told BIRN under condition of anonymity.

The system acts as an important financial incentive for smaller parties without any MPs, or even any councillors, as they can still qualify for some state funding simply by passing the 1-per-cent threshold in any single municipality during local elections.

In some of the smaller municipalities in local elections, that threshold can be crossed by winning only a few dozen votes.

BIRN previously reported on how seven smaller parties exploited this feature to secure more than 80,000 euros each for the following four years. In some cases, such parties run alone in just one, or in a few, municipalities to reach this threshold, while at national level remaining part of coalitions led by big parties.

Overall, 62 parties qualified for regular state funding in 2026, the data show, although around one-third of them received less than 20,000 euros.

Apart from the almost 9 million euros in annual funding, which consumed 0.15 per cent of the state budget, the state also reimburses party election campaign expenses and provides additional annual funding for the research centres of the four parties with the strongest electoral results.

In 2026, an additional 320,000 euros was allocated for those research centres, shared between VMRO DPMNE, the SDSM, the DUI and Levica.

The funding comes with obligations, such as submitting annual financial statements and reports and declaring any donations to the State Audit Office, which oversees use of the funds.

The law requires the parties to publish these financial reports on their websites by the end of each April. In reality, this requirement is frequently ignored, according to BIRN’s analysis.

The State Audit Office told BIRN that the law does not clearly designate who is responsible for monitoring this obligation. Another issue is that parties are not legally required to have an official website.

The Audit Office said they have begun discussing digitalisation of parties’ financial reporting, including the possibility of creating a single online platform where all the parties would publish their financial reports.

World.title: Croatian Tourism Minister Says Last Minute Bookings are Saving August
World.content:
August the 13th, 2026 – The Croatian tourism minister has stated that last minute bookings are saving August, with more and more people paying closer attention to value for money before making reservations.

Croatian tourism is once again confirming its strength this year, and the results achieved show that we are on the right track, said Tonči Glavina, Minister of Tourism and Sport. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the month of July’s tourism results were better than expected, and indications suggest that the second half of the summer could follow the same pattern.

According to data from the eVisitor system, which records tourist traffic in commercial and non-commercial facilities as well as nautical charters (eCrew system), Croatia recorded 12.4 million arrivals and 59.1 million overnight stays from January to the end of July. Compared with the same period last year, this represents growth of 1 percent in both arrivals and overnight stays.

Of that total, 56.1 million overnight stays were recorded on the Adriatic (up 0.5 percent year-on-year), while the continent, including the city of Zagreb, recorded more than 3 million overnight stays (up 1 percent).

july was fantastic for croatia

eVisitor data also shows that in July this year, Croatia recorded 4.7 million arrivals and 29.6 million overnight stays, which is an increase of 2.5 percent in arrivals and 1 percent in overnight stays compared with July last year. In the seventh month the most guests came from the markets of Germany, Slovenia, Croatia, Poland, the Czech Republic, Austria, Hungary and others. By counties, the most tourists were counted in Istria, Split-Dalmatia County and Kvarner, while the most visited destinations were Rovinj, Vir, Poreč, Medulin and Dubrovnik.

“We are satisfied with the tourism results achieved in the first seven months of this year, and especially with the fact that in July we recorded the best result of the last two years. This confirms that Croatian tourism continues to maintain its competitiveness and resilience and that, despite changes in the market, we are succeeding in maintaining positive trends. We are particularly pleased that good results are also being recorded in financial indicators.

In July the value of fiscalised invoices rose by 18 percent, while the number of issued invoices was 8 percent higher than in the same month last year. Growth is also being recorded in road, air and maritime traffic, and all these results confirm that we have responded well to market circumstances – both through quality promotion of Croatia and through timely adaptation of the offer. I thank the entire tourism sector for the effort invested, and especially accommodation providers who responded to our appeals and, with their promotional offers, additionally contributed to the competitiveness of our offer.

Ahead of us is still a good part of August, after which we will make a complete overview of this main part of the tourist year. Croatian tourism is once again confirming its strength this year, and the results achieved show that we are on the right track and that together we are successfully responding to changes and challenges,” said Tonči Glavina, Minister of Tourism and Sport.

When Croatia’s tourism results are broken down by counties, in the first seven months the most overnight stays were recorded in Istria (16.7 million), Split-Dalmatia County (11.1 million) and Kvarner (9.7 million), while by destinations the leaders were Dubrovnik, Rovinj, Poreč, Split and Umag.

last minute to the rescue

“The course and results of the tourist year so far show that Croatia still has a very strong position on the global tourism market, despite all the demanding circumstances. What we particularly read from this year’s tourist movements is a change in the way guests make decisions about their trips. Last-minute bookings play an important role, and when choosing a destination, the best value for money is increasingly sought, along with safety and easy accessibility. In this context Croatia has a series of advantages – from proximity to our most important source markets and good transport connections to the diversity of the offer that enables different types of holidays.

Given the considerable number of promotional last-minute arrangement prices in August, the tourism sector believes that the August figures will also be good.

The results achieved therefore give us additional wind in our sails for the continuation of the tourist year, all the more so because the Ferragosto period is ahead of us, traditionally very important for travel by Italian guests. In addition to the main summer months, we are also recording excellent advance bookings for the shoulder season, for which promotional activities begin in mid-August, especially on the Polish and UK markets,” said Kristjan Staničić, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board.

Looking at markets, during the first seven months the most overnight stays were recorded by guests from Germany (10.3 million), Croatia (7.6 million), Slovenia (6.7 million), Austria (4.3 million), Poland (3.9 million), the Czech Republic (3 million), the UK (2.2 million), Hungary (2.1 million) and others.

Given the considerable number of promotional last-minute arrangement prices in August, the tourism sector believes that the August figures will also be good, at least at last year’s level.

59.1 million overnight stays were recorded over the first seven months of this year

Interesting trends can also be seen on individual markets. Thus eVisitor figures show that Croatian tourism in July and during the first seven months of 2026 recorded significant growth in tourist traffic from the Czech, Hungarian and Italian markets.

The most pronounced positive shift was recorded on the Czech market. Compared with July last year, the number of arrivals of Czech tourists rose by 12 percent, while the number of their overnight stays was higher by seven percent. In the period from January to the end of July growth of five percent was recorded in both arrivals and overnight stays compared with the same period last year. The Hungarian market is also a reason for satisfaction. During July the number of arrivals of Hungarian tourists increased by eight percent, while the number of overnight stays rose by seven percent.

In the first seven months of the year growth of seven percent was recorded in both arrivals and overnight stays compared with last year. Hungarian guests stayed most on Kvarner, in Istria and Zadar County. The Italian market, which had stagnated in recent years, is also recovering. In the period from January to July the number of arrivals and overnight stays of Italian guests increased by two percent compared with the same period last year, while in July a one-percent growth in arrivals was recorded.

World.title: Croats are Travelling Less and Taking Less Annual Leave This Summer
World.content:
August the 13th, 2026 – Croats appear to be travelling less and taking less annual leave this summer, with the latest research into these habits showing a marked change.

Almost every third person in Croatia is staying at their usual place of residence this summer, primarily due to a lack of financial resources, according to a survey conducted by Alma Career Croatia. Poslovni reports that the results of the latest survey on annual leave, carried out by Alma Career Croatia, an international company best known for the MojPosao/MyJob portal, show that Croatian employees are planning their holidays a little more cautiously this summer.

According to this latest survey, Croatian workers enjoy an average of 25 days of annual leave, and summer is the period when most employees use the largest part of their free days. However, this year’s results show that habits are slowly changing.

shorter summer breaks

Compared with 2025, the number of workers who plan to use fewer days of annual leave during the summer is rising, as is the number of those who aren’t planning on taking any trips at all this year.

The share of employees who plan to use a maximum of seven days of annual leave has increased from 15% in 2025 to 21% in 2026. On the other hand, the share of those planning to rest for 21 days or longer has almost halved (7% last year, 3% this year). The most common choice remains a holiday lasting 8 to 10 days, planned by 37% of respondents. This is followed by those who will rest between 11 and 15 days (29%), while 10% of employees plan annual leave lasting between 15 and 20 days.

The issue with summer that is becoming increasingly problematic is the fact that the weather is becoming so insufferably hot that sitting under the air conditioner is the only choice for a growing number of people. Most can do that at work or at home.

the croatian coast still dominates for most croats, as opposed to heading somewhere abroad

When it comes to destination, Croatia remains the first choice.

More than half of the survey participants (56%) plan to spend their summer holiday within the country, which is only slightly less than last year, when the figure was 58%. There are also somewhat fewer people planning a trip abroad this summer. Their share has fallen from 21% in 2025 to 17% this year.

However, the biggest change is visible among those who do not plan to travel at all. Their share has risen in one year from 27% to 32%, meaning that almost every third respondent will not go on a summer holiday this year. Finances are most often behind such a decision. Among respondents who will not travel, as many as 60% cite lack of financial resources as the main reason, compared with 56% last year.

One to two weeks on the Adriatic; shorter or longer holidays abroad

There are also differences in the length of holidays depending on whether respondents holiday in Croatia or travel abroad. Those who holiday somewhere else within Croatia most often choose a classic break of one to two weeks. As many as 78% of them plan to rest between 8 and 15 days.

People who travel abroad more often choose either very short or significantly longer trips. Thus, 21% of respondents travelling outside Croatia plan a holiday of seven days or less, while among those staying in Croatia the figure is 10%. At the other end of the spectrum, 7% of travellers abroad plan a holiday longer than three weeks, while among those holidaying in Croatia only 2% plan such a break.

World.title: Adidas Strengthens Presence in Croatian Sport as Cibona Signs Partnership
World.content:
August the 13th, 2026 – Adidas is strengthening its present in Croatian sport as the famous Cibona signs a partnership deal with the global sport brand.

As Poslovni reports, one of the most successful Croatian basketball clubs of all and one of the most recognisable global sports brands are joining forces, and Cibona’s players will compete in adidas kit from the new season.

The global sports brand Adidas and Basketball Club Cibona, one of the symbols of Zagreb and Croatian sport, have officially begun a new collaboration. From the 2026/2027 season, Cibona’s senior and junior teams will compete in Adidas sports equipment.

The new partnership connects two brands deeply rooted in sporting history, yet simultaneously oriented towards the future, the development of new generations of athletes and the creation of top conditions for their work and progress. adidas will provide Cibona with modern sports equipment designed to give players maximum comfort, freedom of movement and the best possible performance on the court.

Founded in 1946, Cibona has over eight decades grown into one of the most important institutions of Croatian basketball. The club reached the peak of European glory in the mid-1980s when, led by Dražen Petrović, it won two consecutive European champion titles – in 1985 and 1986. After Croatia’s independence, Cibona won a record 20 national championship titles, and in 2014 it also won the regional ABA League.

“Collaboration with Adidas represents an important step in the development of the club for Cibona and a confirmation of the values that our club has carried for eight decades. We’re connecting with a global brand that understands sport, excellence and the importance of creating new generations of players. We believe this partnership will further strengthen our sporting identity, as well as the bond with the fans who have always been an inseparable part of Cibona. We look forward to everything we’ll achieve together on and off the court,” said Tomislav Šerić, director of Basketball Club Cibona.

The collaboration between Cibona and Adidas is part of the brand’s broader commitment to basketball, sport and athletes at all levels. Basketball is one of Adidas’s global sports categories, alongside football, running and training, while the brand is also active in tennis, golf, motorsport, winter sports, rugby, cricket and numerous other disciplines. For more than 75 years Adidas has been developing products intended for athletes, combining innovation, design and experience gained in professional sport.

“We are extremely pleased that Cibona is becoming part of the adidas sports family. This is a club of exceptional tradition, whose name holds a special place in the history of European basketball and which for generations has been home to top players. We share a belief in the power of sport, the importance of working with young people and a constant drive for progress. We’re extremely proud to support Cibona’s players with equipment that combines sporting innovations, functionality and the recognisable Adidas design, and we look forward to jointly creating a new chapter in the club’s history,” said Petra Franić from Adidas.

The partnership between adidas and Cibona opens a new chapter in the life of a club that placed Zagreb at the centre of the European basketball map. The recognisable three stripes will thus accompany the Wolves from the new season on the path towards new sporting successes.

Players of KK Cibona have for the first time completed a training session in the new training kit from the collection, while the official match kits will be presented later. The kits and selected items from the collection will be available to fans exclusively in the Basketball Club Cibona fan shop.

World.title: Danube Traffic Collapse Could Stretch into September and October
World.content:
August the 13th, 2026 – The current Danube traffic collapse could end up stretching into autumn as contracts worth 800 million euros fail.

Convoys with goods are stuck in front of the Mohovo Channel upstream from Ilok and as many as 60 Danube voyages have been postponed. Marija Brnic reports for Poslovni that over recent days in Vukovar, all eyes have been firmly fixed only on the forecasts of the State Hydrometeorological Institute and the numbers on the local water gauge. Since measurements of the Danube water levels began, it has never been lower, and in recent days it has almost completely halted river traffic in Croatia’s largest river port.

For two weeks already there have been practically no berthings of cargo barges or tourist cruise ships, and the critical point is the Mohovo Channel near Šarengrad, where the depth of the fairway does not meet the minimum conditions for safe and financially viable transport.

The crisis is entering its third week, yet what is worrying is that there are no good news in sight for its end. For August it is certain that regular traffic will not resume, even if heavier rain falls, and concern is also growing about September and even October. The Port of Vukovar has already put forward the first estimates of possible losses.

the port of vukovar is struggling

One topic is how to close natural retention areas by installing weirs, and the other issue that needs to be opened is the cleaning of the Danube along its entire course. With partners, as company director Marijan Kuprešak explained, they had contracted the transhipment of around 200,000 tonnes of various goods over the next three months. At an average transhipment price of 4 euros per tonne, this means the collapse of valuable contracts and a loss of around 800,000 euros in revenue. The scale of the potential damage in such a worst-case scenario is illustrated by the fact that this is somewhat below the level of revenue the company achieved in previous years; last year it stood at 1.2 million euros.

This year was expected at the Port of Vukovar to be a year of recovery from the crisis the company has been going through, largely due to the war in Ukraine and the associated reduction in traffic. At the current depth of the Danube, ships have to sail with reduced capacity, and apart from meaning that more voyages are needed for the same quantity of cargo, there is also the risk of grounding or the cost of ships standing idle, which currently makes this form of goods transport uncompetitive.

Until now it was precisely the lower price that gave river transport an advantage over road or rail. Kuprešak says that truck transport, which users are largely opting for in such situations because of investments in the railway, is several times more expensive than river transport.

Business partners, Kuprešak says, still show understanding, but if the drought continues, because of the dynamics of their own contracts and deliveries they will be forced to divert cargo to trucks and trains, which will of course spill over further onto their costs and the final prices of products. According to available information, cruise ships are also not docking in Vukovar and around 60 contracted voyages have been cancelled, mostly from Germany, for which the paid money has been refunded. The companies have suffered a loss of business of around one million euros per voyage.

Companies can as a rule recover any losses only through insurance companies, and even if a state of natural disaster were declared, previous practice shows that the state does not cover such damage outside the agricultural sector. However, Kuprešak says that at the level of shipowners, ports and landing stages of the countries all directly affected by the Danube water-level crisis, discussions are beginning about a possible initiative to seek assistance through horizontal support from the European Commission.

Non-repayable subsidies at that level would help, he says, to cover the losses that everyone will be hit by this year, but as climate change increasingly affects the European area and impacts rivers, an equally important issue that the state and the EU need to address is securing the navigability of the Danube. And that, Kuprešak says, is becoming increasingly threatened.

“One topic is how to close natural retention areas by installing weirs, and the other issue that needs to be opened is the cleaning of the Danube along its entire course,” Kuprešak stresses.

1 million euros in losses have been suffered by the companies that organise voyages on the Danube.

issues impacting croatia from germany to romania

In some countries, they have already carried out blasting and dredging to ensure passage at bottlenecks, but because of the extreme drought and record-low water levels, which appear to be becoming an increasingly pronounced problem in these areas, the issue will have to be approached more systematically and cover the entire course of the Danube, from Germany to Romania.

Blasting and the removal of underwater rock masses as well as deepening the riverbed is a permanent solution also for the Mohovo Channel, because it is the most sensitive point in the Croatian section of the Danube. For many Croatian companies the functioning of the Danube and the Port of Vukovar is an important business link, and among the users are numerous agro-combinates, producers of artificial fertilisers, cement and bulk cargo for the construction industry.

Until now the Danube was considered a navigable waterway 365 days a year, and a problem would at most appear because of ice in the winter months, but now the risk is becoming the summer period and drought. Shipowners, ports and landing stages therefore also see the historic drought affecting the Danube and river transport as an opportunity to sound the alarm in Brussels for the launch of a comprehensive, strategic regulation of the Danube and the permanent securing of its navigability.
