World.title: Pauline Hanna inquest: Unused Polkinghorne documentary footage shown at Coroner's Court
World.content:
Footage from the cutting room floor of a documentary about Philip Polkinghorne's criminal trial has been played at the inquest into Pauline Hanna's death.

Polkinghorne was found not guilty of murdering Hanna, his wife, in 2024.

Now, a coronial inquest is attempting to determine how she died and the circumstances surrounding her death.

Excerpts of interviews with Polkinghorne, filmed in 2022 inside the Remuera home where Hanna was found dead the year before, were included in a Blonde Razor Productions series. It aired in 2025.

At the time of the interviews Polkinghorne was charged with murder. He has since been acquitted.

In unused footage shown at the Coroner's Court in Auckland on Thursday, Polkinghorne told the documentary interviewer he did not use any electronic devices after watching TV with Hanna and going to sleep in separate bedrooms - the last time he says he saw his wife alive.

"She went to bed, and then I went to bed thereafter. I'd finished with a laptop and went to sleep. I didn't use any electronic devices that night to my recollection, didn't take my laptop to bed or anything like that."

Giving evidence at the inquest on Tuesday, Polkinghorne discussed evidence showing he was on his phone until about 2am the morning Hanna's body was found.

Polkinghorne at the inquest on Tuesday. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

He said he often stayed up late watching YouTube and it was a "bad habit" of his.

Polkinghorne also denied deleting WhatsApp messages between him and sex worker Madison Ashton.

"I discovered when I was in the police station, the day Pauline died, that my phone [messages] had been deleted. Who deleted it, how it was deleted, I don't know."

On Tuesday, Polkinghorne admitted to deleting the messages, saying they were embarrassing and unrelated to his wife's death.

Police counsel Alysha McClintock watched intently, having earlier accused Polkinghorne of changing his evidence several times since he was first interviewed by police, the details of which can't be reported on.

In another clip, Polkinghorne told the interviewer about his police interview the day Hanna was found, and what led him to walk out.

"I did not have a support person, I was freezing, I did not have access to a lawyer; I didn't know I needed one. I didn't have any access to anything, I wasn't given my rights.

"I was interrogated and videoed for five or six hours that day."

He got a call midway through from his friend, defence lawyer Tony Bouchier.

"He told me to walk out of the police station. I said 'no, I'm trying to help them Tony, I'm trying to help them discover what went wrong'."

He said police then accused him of lying about something which cannot be reported because of suppressions made by the Coroner.

"I thought this is enough and I just walked out."

World.title: Gardner breaks silence on affair with teammate, retains vice-captaincy
World.content:
Australia vice-captain Ash Gardner has apologised for the pain caused by her marriage breakdown and thanked Cricket Australia for backing her leadership.

Gardner's affair with Australian teammate Georgia Voll while married to ex-wife Monica Wright created headlines.

Wright publicly questioned the lack of action by CA in the wake of the affair, calling attention to "a clear power imbalance" when a senior member of staff has an affair with a junior.

Wright said Gardner should not be allowed to stay as vice-captain and questioned why CA had said nothing on the matter.

Gardner's marriage breakdown came as the result of an affair with teammate Georgia Voll (pictured). (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg, speaking on SEN on Thursday, said "additional policies" would be put in place in situations where perceived or real conflicts of interest existed, when relationships between players had been disclosed.

He confirmed CA had been made aware of the relationship between Gardner and Voll before it appeared in the press, but also backed Gardner to stay in her position.

"Ash is a highly regarded leader in our system. The CA board make leadership decisions and have oversight over all leadership decisions," Greenberg said.

"Ash is our vice-captain for a reason, because she's highly regarded, but what we will do is in situations where there are personal relationships is make sure there are additional guardrails, so the perception of conflict or conflict itself — talking about things like selection — are handled appropriately and respectfully."

Todd Greenberg (pictured) says Gardner remains a highly-valued leader within the Australian team. (AAP: James Ross)

"We've got policies in place but we will put additional ones in place given Ash is now vice-captain. If there are relationships that have been disclosed and they have been, then we will make sure that conflict — perceived or real — around selections are removed, so Ash is not involved in those things."

Greenberg said the relationship between Gardner and Voll was "new news" in the media.

"But for those that were in the team and leading the team, we've been well across this for a period of time," he said.

Gardner addressed her affair and the position of the hierarchy in a post on Instagram.

"While my separation from my wife is a personal matter, I understand my current relationship status needed to be addressed by Cricket Australia given my position as vice-captain," Gardner wrote.

"I am grateful that the CA Board has chosen to support my continued leadership. I look forward to playing a strong role as a leader and providing the best possible support for my teammates in the season to come.

"I am grateful for the time Monica and I shared and sorry for the pain this has caused. I wish her nothing but happiness and success in the future.

"I won't be making any further public comment on this matter at this time and ask that the privacy of those involved is respected."

Greenberg made the point "respect" for all concerned was paramount.

"It is a very personal matter for the player, and I think there's a level of respect that needs to go with that," he said.

"Cricket's got very strong respect-at-work policies, so we've got a policy that's been developed over time that can deal with these sorts of things."

AAP

World.title: Quick hits: A 'peanut' jibe, a Starc record and a brain explosion
World.content:
Steve Smith called a Bangladesh bowler a "peanut" for making an appeal, but he could probably have labelled a couple of his batting colleagues as such on a dire batting display for Australia.

Meanwhile, Mitch Starc collected another accolade with yet another top order wicket for the Aussies

As it happened: Bangladesh minnows humble Australia's giants on day one in Darwin

Here are the quick hits from day one of the first Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

1. Weatherald falls in front of hometown crowd

Weatherald was unable to impress in front of his home crowd. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/CA)

Local boy Jake Weatherald began the first Test under significant pressure, having clung onto his opening spot after struggling through his debut series against England.

And there was significant support for the Northern Territorian in Darwin, with the crowd rising and falling as he attempted to get his innings going.

But once again, Weatherald was unable to find his feet at Test level, eventually reaching and swiping and nicking off for an unconvincing 23 off 37 deliveries.

It was Weatherald's 10th sub-50 score from his 11 Test innings, and one that only raised more questions about his viability as a Test match opener

Weatherald, the first Australian men's Test cricketer born and raised in the Northern Territory and now the first Territorian to play Test cricket in Darwin, with three more opportunities to secure a spot on the plane to South Africa in October.

2. Green's pre-lunch brain explosion

Bangladesh was overjoyed to claim Green's wicket with the final ball before lunch. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

With Australia teetering at 3-61, the under-pressure Cam Green decided to take the game on.

Perhaps the Australian most in need of a score, the all-rounder began his innings with a pair of well-timed drives, before hooking Taskin Ahmed for a maximum over backward square leg.

However, Green's counterattack was short lived, with the big man playing one shot too many in the shadows of the first break.

With what turned out to be the final ball of the morning session, Green all but gave his wicket away, meekly chipping one to a grateful Mushfiqur Rahim on the on-side.

Australia headed to lunch at 4-74, Bangladesh couldn't believe their luck, and Green, having come out with such purpose, trudged off for a run-a-ball 13.

3. Smith's triple reprieve

So often the man for a crisis, Steve Smith is no stranger to standing tall as wickets tumble around him.

But Australia's idiosyncratic world beater was anything but convincing as he somehow managed to prod his way to lunch after coming to the crease at 2-52.

Smith should have been out on 2, with his thick edge falling through the fingers of a stooping second slip.

A matter of balls later, Smith was once again nicking towards the cordon — but this time, the ball flew through a gap between second slip and gully, with Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto having only just removed a man from behind the wicket.

And it appeared that Smith's luck was well and truly in when he survived a line-ball DRS review.

With Smith swinging hard outside off, Bangladesh went up for caught behind with some confidence. Umpire Kumar Dharmasena was unmoved, and Shanto wasted no time in sending the decision upstairs.

The technology, however, showed no conclusive evidence of an edge, with the ball passing perilously close to Smith's blade but failing to make its mark on ultra edge.

Bangladesh couldn't believe it as Smith was handed his third reprieve of the morning.

4. Smith talks Bangladesh out of a review, lands "peanut" jibe

Smith talked Bangladesh out of a review before late in the second session. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Having burnt two reviews in the first session, Bangladesh had just one DRS Hail Mary to play with for the bulk of the Australian innings.

Late in the second session, seamer Ebadot Hussein was tempted to break the glass for one that he never should have been.

His LBW shout against Smith was clearly far too high, but that didn't stop the Bangladeshi brains trust gathering for a serious discussion in the middle.

Smith couldn't believe it.

"Knee roll you reckon? It was up here you peanut!" Smith could be heard saying through the stump mic, gesturing to his hip area.

"What game are you watching?"

Smith's derision was enough to talk Bangladesh out of the review, but his honesty didn't end up counting for much — the Australian vice-captain eventually top-edging a short ball to be caught for 71.

5. Starc makes history

Australia's Mitchell Starc added another record to his list. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/CA)

The records keep coming for Australia's top-order destroyer, Mitchell Starc.

Fresh from being named his country's Test player of the year last Friday, the 36-year-old carved out another piece of history, becoming the most lethal left arm bowler in the history of the format.

Starc procured a leading edge from opener Shadman Islam to claim the 434th wicket of his Test career, with Nathan Lyon making amends for an earlier dropped chance.

Starc's milestone scalp took him past former Sri Lanka spinner Rangana Herath.

However, that was the only breakthrough of the day in what was a humbling start to the season for Australia.

World.title: Pallister downs McIntosh to claim 200m gold medal at Pan Pacs
World.content:
Australia's freestyle star Lani Pallister has collected gold and silver medals in her arduous opening to the Pan Pacific championships in the United States.

Pallister triumphed in the women's 200m freestyle and then set a personal best when finishing behind American legend Katie Ledecky in the 1500m freestyle in Irvine, California on Wednesday (Thursday AEST).

Dolphins teammates Sam Short (men's 800m freestyle), Brittany Castelluzzo (women's 200m butterfly) and Ben Armbruster (men's 50m butterfly) also triumphed on the opening night of the Pan Pacs.

The Dolphins won four of 11 gold medals on offer, with Pallister's remarkable year continuing.

Sam Short claimed gold in the men's 800m freestyle. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

Just weeks after winning four Commonwealth Games gold medals in Glasgow, Pallister pipped Canadian ace Summer McIntosh in the 200m final.

The Australian clocked one minute 53.67 seconds — just 0.02s outside her personal best in the event — with McIntosh second in 1:53.86.

About two hours later, Pallister then returned to the pool for the gruelling 1500m freestyle and set a her best time over the distance.

In what was essentially a match race against peerless American great Ledecky, who hasn't lost in the event in 16 years, Pallister put in a gallant effort.

Lani Pallister (left) and Moesha Johnson (right) were beaten out by Katie Ledecky (centre) in the 1500m freestyle. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

The 26-year-old shadowed Ledecky, the winner of nine Olympic and 23 world championship gold medals, for the initial 500 metres.

The American great then produced her renowned burst to create a handy advantage en route to touching in 15:36.09.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Pallister's 15:38.62 eclipsed her previous best of 15:39.14 from June last year.

In the men's 800m freestyle, Short went close to a personal best as he edged American rival Bobby Finke.

Short clocked 7:37.02, just 0.71s shy of his best time in the event, with Finke finishing some five-and-a-half seconds behind in second.

Earlier, Armbruster claimed Australia's first gold medal of the pool meet, winning the men's 50m butterfly in 22.75 seconds, 0.02s outside the Australian record jointly held by Kyle Chalmers and Matt Targett.

And Castelluzzo took out the women's 200m 'fly in 2:06.24 from her Dolphins teammate Liz Dekkers (2:06.56).

AAP

World.title: 'I'll remember the people': Sidebottom among retiring AFL premiership duo
World.content:
Collingwood great Steele Sidebottom has officially told Magpies teammates he will be retiring at season's end.

The dual Magpies premiership hero's announcement on Thursday comes just hours after Richmond midfielder Dion Prestia also called it quits.

Debuting in 2009, Sidebottom has played 373 AFL games — the second most in Collingwood's storied history, only behind Scott Pendlebury.

A member of the Magpies' 2010 premiership side as a 19-year-old, Sidebottom then kicked a famous goal late in the 2023 grand final to help seal the club's next flag 13 years later.

Sidebottom (left) and Scott Pendlebury (right) have played the most matches together as teammates in VFL/AFL history. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

With Collingwood guaranteed to be in the wildcard round of the finals, at least, Sidebottom will be hoping for a fairytale farewell.

The versatile midfielder won Collingwood's Copeland Trophy in 2017 and 2018, also earning All-Australian honours once.

"As a young kid from 'Tally' [Tallygaroopna], I could never imagine I'd finish my AFL career with over 370 games, two premierships and 18 years of memories," Sidebottom said.

"When I look back on my time at Collingwood, I'll remember the people.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"So many teammates, coaches, staff and volunteers have invested their time and energy into helping me along the way."

Sidebottom might not be the only senior Collingwood player to retire this year, with Pendlebury also weighing up his future after breaking the VFL/AFL games record in May.

The Magpies have the oldest list in the AFL and are attempting to stay in premiership contention with a group in transition.

At Richmond, Prestia has joined premiership teammate Nathan Broad in ending his career.

After starting his career with Gold Coast, Prestia enjoyed instant success after making the switch to the Tigers in 2017.

Prestia won three premierships in his first four seasons with Richmond after joining at the end of 2016. (Getty Images: Mackenzie Sweetnam)

The midfielder played in three premierships (2017, 2019, 2020) in his first four seasons at Richmond.

Despite being riddled by injury in 2020 and restricted to just five games during the pandemic season, Prestia returned to play an important role in all four of the Tigers' finals.

"I felt like a Richmond man from the very beginning," Prestia said.

"My decision to come to Richmond was not to prove what I could do, but to be a part of a club that I saw potential for greatness, and didn't we prove that right?"

Prestia and Broad will be given a farewell in front of the Richmond army this Saturday when the Tigers host St Kilda at the MCG.

AAP

World.title: Solomon rubbishes rumours of rifts with Essendon coaching candidates
World.content:
Interim Essendon coach Dean Solomon has described a rumoured falling-out with Mark McVeigh as like an "episode of Home and Away".

After Solomon chose not to put his hand up to be the Bombers' full-time coach, Essendon are closing in on announcing a leader as soon as next week.

McVeigh has been tipped to win the job, even ahead of Essendon icon James Hird.

It has led to suggestions of a rift among the trio, something Solomon has strenuously denied.

Solomon (centre) says there is no ill-feeling towards either Hird (left) or McVeigh (right) after pulling out of the Essendon coaching race. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

"We don't know where they've come from — they're rumours," Solomon said.

"[McVeigh's has been] one of my best mates since the age of 15.

"I've known Hirdy since the age of 17.

"The talks with me potentially not being here next year, whether that stimulated a bit of that conversation, we're unsure.

"But I feel like it's a bit of an episode of [long-running Australian TV soapie] Home and Away.

McVeigh, currently an assistant with Sydney, has been touted as the favourte to win the Essendon job. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

"There's nothing there. We all want to see this club heading in the right direction."

Solomon, McVeigh and Hird all played together at the Bombers, with Solomon and Hird playing in Essendon's most recent premiership side in 2000. McVeigh played with the pair in a losing grand final in 2001.

The trio also worked together briefly at GWS when McVeigh was the Giants' interim coach in 2022.

Solomon initially declared he would stay on at the Bombers next year, even if he wasn't senior coach.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

But his family remains living in northern NSW, complicating matters for him.

"Part of the process of thinking about going in the process for the senior coaching role was sitting down with my family and talking about that," Solomon said.

"My wife and kids live in northern NSW.

"I've had 10 to 11 months away from them at the moment.

"Is that sustainable long-term? It's probably not."

Solomon stressed the next coach didn't need to be an Essendon person, referencing the legendary Kevin Sheedy, who grew up supporting the Bombers but whose playing career was at Richmond.

"He just needs to be the right person," Solomon said.

"A lot of people surrounding our football club are really frustrated.

"We want to be great, and we want to be great really quickly.

"This is a big job and it's an exciting challenge."

AAP

World.title: Hulking prop set to be 1,000th Wallaby as Kiss reshuffles deck
World.content:
The 1,000th Wallaby is poised to be capped in Townsville after hulking prop Massimo De Lutiis was named on the bench to face Japan.

Les Kiss, in his second game in charge, has also recalled fly half Carter Gordon at Declan Meredith's expense.

With Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii injured, he has given Isaac Henry a starting debut at outside centre a week after he earned his first minutes in a tight Osaka defeat of Eddie Jones's side.

Lukhan Salakaia-Loto's Test return has also been secured, the Queensland Reds firebrand set to partner Lachlan Shaw — in his starting debut — in the second row, with Jeremy Williams on the bench and Josh Canham rested.

The Kiss era has begun, and new coach Les is seeking the 'Wallaby way' The new Wallabies era under Les Kiss began with a win in tough conditions against an improving nation, but coach Les Kiss wants more than just wins to be the legacy of his tenure.

Kiss has also shaken up the back row, with Charlie Cale and Carlo Tizzano to partner skipper Harry Wilson, leaving Fraser McReight on the bench and Rob Valetini out of the 23.

Brandon Paenga-Amosa will get his chance under Kiss as replacement hooker while Filipo Daugunu has also been included on the bench as backline cover.

Angus Bell and Taniela Tupou also return to the starting side after stirring second-half cameos in Osaka, while the back three are unchanged and Tate McDermott and Ben Donaldson again provide play-making options on the bench.

It continues the theme of Kiss's tenure, with the new coach keen to assess his options before a long run of Tests ahead of next year's Rugby World Cup in Australia.

"The coaches have looked to find some balance in the selection after what was a physically taxing Test week in the heat in Japan," Kiss said.

"The whole group has worked hard this week and we know where we need to improve.

"This Saturday in Townsville gives us an opportunity to grow and strengthen our game on home soil in front of our supporters."

Gordon impressed at fly half against Ireland, before missing the next two Tests with a calf injury.

Meredith started in the past three Tests alongside Brumbies clubmate Ryan Lonergan, who has been retained the starting scrum half role.

WALLABIES (1-15): Angus Bell, Josh Nasser, Taniela Tupou, Lachlan Shaw, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Charlie Cale, Carlo Tizzano, Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Carter Gordon, Harry Potter, Hunter Paisami, Isaac Henry, Max Jorgensen, Tom Wright.

BENCH (16-23): Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Aidan Ross, Massimo De Lutiis, Jeremy Williams, Fraser McReight, Tate McDermott, Ben Donaldson, Filipo Daugunu

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of the second Test between the Wallabies and Japan on Saturday afternoon from 2pm (AEST).

AAP

World.title: Cunningham's trans stance opens WNBA up to its latest hijacking atempt
World.content:
Pre-game press conferences are usually a bit of a nothingburger in the WNBA.

Coaches will answer questions about their starting line-ups, address recent trends and it is all very smooth and easy.

However, when Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White arrived at the podium prior to her team's clash against the New York Liberty this week, the mood was different.

White didn't let the journalists ask questions first, as is usually the case in these settings. Her press conference began and ended with a passionate two-minute address.

"The hate, the fear-mongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win. It won't win. We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided," White said in part.

"Every day, these women put their ass on the line … I stand by them. I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell."

White's statement comes after another week where WNBA headlines have had very little to do with the on-court product.

It is sadly old news for a league that is undoubtedly growing but continues to be hijacked by different agendas, whether they be political, racial or financial.

WNBA player claims 'white privilege' saw her ejected after foul Chicago's DiJonai Carrington was ejected for a foul on Indiana Fever's Sophie Cunningham, but stormed off only to post "white privilege" on social media minutes later.

Racial tensions in the WNBA were heightened earlier this week when Chicago Sky defender DiJonai Carrington tweeted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" and tagged the Fever account after being ejected from a game against the Fever due to a hard foul on Fever guard Sophie Cunningham.

Cunningham believed the foul was "absolutely" intentional, adding that Carrington probably had some "pent-up stuff".

White, Cunningham's coach on the Fever, did not think Carrington intended to hurt Cunningham, and was criticised by some for not supporting her players. It was a criticism that left the Fever coach seething.

Cunningham is the WNBA's latest main character, and it is hardly her first time in the limelight.

Sophie Cunningham (right) first went viral after becoming Caitlin Clark's unofficial bodyguard on the court for the Fever. (Getty Images: Jess Rapfogel)

The 29-year-old isn't one of the WNBA's best players, but she is one of its most marketable.

A combination of a suite of endorsement deals, a Sports Illustrated Swimsuit cover, a guest UFC referee spot and an unofficial role as star teammate Caitlin Clark's bodyguard has all combined to net her 3.8 million Instagram followers.

For comparison, the WNBA's consensus best player and four-time league MVP A'ja Wilson has just 1.5 million followers.

Cunningham was the subject of an ESPN feature last month where she spoke out against the participation of transgender women in women's sports, saying "young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men".

Sophie Cunningham has no problems being the villain on her Fever team. (Melissa Tamez/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

When pressed about her comments a few days later, Cunningham did not back down, saying her stance is simply "common sense".

"I think I'll always believe in that," she said.

"I think it's really important to protect children, and that's little girls who are also involved in that category. I stand on what I said."

Cunningham has always presented her views on transgender athletes under the guise of protecting the sanctity of women's sport, and while she may be well-intentioned, the views are problematic in a league that prides itself on diversity and being a safe space for the trans community and other minorities.

Cheryl Reeve has shown her support to the transgender community in the wake of Sophie Cunningham's comments. (Jerry Holt/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images)

Her comments were met with a wave of support for the transgender community from within the WNBA.

Cheryl Reeve, the head coach and president of the Minnesota Lynx, wore a T-shirt reading "Trans Kids Belong" when her team faced Cunningham's Fever.

"I come from a space of inclusion," she said.

"The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports."

The WNBA's Player's Association also denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" in a statement.

While Cunningham cares about the league and its future, her views opened the door to people outside the WNBA to gatecrash and use it as a vehicle to push their agendas,an all too familiar a tale for the league.

Unsurprisingly, US President Donald Trump and his vice-president JD Vance wasted little time jumping on the Cunningham train, with Vance labelling her "inspiring".

Riley Gaines, a vocal campaigner against the participation of transgender women in women's sports, also took a sudden interest in Cunningham and the WNBA.

Two former NBA players, Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White, have taken the jig a step further by declaring their intentions to enter the 2027 WNBA draft, more as an attack on the league's current eligibility guidelines and gender inclusivity as a whole rather than a genuine attempt to commence women's basketball careers.

It is a shameless publicity stunt that will ultimately fail. Sadly, it is coming at the cost of both the transgender community and women's sport as a whole.

White has done multiple interviews in a long-haired wig since declaring his draft eligibility and has claimed he is in his "feminine era".

Like Gaines, neither Kanter nor White have previously displayed much public interest in the WNBA.

Perhaps realising the firestorm her comments caused, Cunningham took aim at media covering the WNBA, accusing reporters of covering "everything except basketball" in the days following her ESPN interview.

The irony of it is that Cunningham's comments regarding transgender women in the WNBA came despite there being no transgender players in the league currently, or none about to enter the draft.

She was the one who drove the conversation away from the league's on-court product.

There should be headlines about the 2027 draft class. USC's Juju Watkins is one of the most exciting draft prospects in WNBA history. Her teammate Jazzy Davidson is another star in the making and could also declare.

Instead, we're all here talking about Kanter, a player who spent 11 seasons in the NBA, and White, a former first-round NBA draft pick, threatening to finagle their way into the league while pretending to care about the women's game.

Republican party's bid to claim Clark

Caitlin Clark's arrival in the WNBA has seen the league's popularity skyrocket over the past two seasons. (Getty Images: Michael Hickey)

Clark's arrival in the WNBA as the top pick in 2024 supercharged the interest in the league.

While her sensational long-range shooting and playmaking have endeared her to basketball fans, a different set of traits — being a catholic white woman from Iowa — made her the top target of the Republican Party.

Being the Republican representative of the WNBA is not a role Clark has ever asked for.

That hasn't stopped the Republican Party from attempting to use Clark as a weapon to wield in order to try and stoke race wars within the league, given the majority of its players are of colour.

Last month, eleven Republican politicians wrote to the WNBA asking the league to protect Clark from fouls that they deemed to be "attacks" on her because she is white.

The politicians claimed they were worried that "attacks against Clark may be racially motivated".

The Fever said they were unaware of the Republican letter and added that neither "our organisation nor Caitlin has had any interaction with anyone in this congressional group".

Ironically, while the Republicans complained over so-called attacks on Clark, it was a black player who fouled her, Alyssa Thomas, who was subjected to racist attacks on social media. Thomas was suspended for one game for her collision with Clark.

As Cunningham's teammate, Clark has also been involuntarily dragged into the transgender debate and has said it wasn't a topic of discussion within the Fever locker room.

Clark was asked for her thoughts on the matter in a post-game press conference and said: "It's for leagues and governing bodies to work with their athletes to find solutions".

Conservatives are unimpressed that, unlike Cunningham, Clark has not publicly denounced the participation of transgender athletes in women's sport.

A bizarre sex toy invasion

The WNBA has also been used for financial gain, infamously for the betting company Polymarket.

Last season, multiple games were forced into stoppages after green coloured sex toys were thrown onto the court.

The toys were aimed at the court and towards the players, and one accidentally hit a man watching a game in the stands.

Eventually, members of a meme-coin group, Green Dildo Coin, took responsibility for the bizarre acts, claiming they were simply promotional stunts to promote the launch of their meme-coin.

Polymarket is a company that allows you to bet on pretty much anything, and as it turned out, people were betting on what games sex toys would be thrown on and what colour the toys would be, and then winning the money themselves by throwing the toys into the court.

One of the toys thrown came close to hitting Cunningham, and she denounced the actions on her podcast.

"Everyone's trying to make sure the W is not a joke and it's taken seriously, and then that happens," she said.

Reeve, as she did on the transgender topic, spoke out again, calling the sex toy saga the league's latest "distraction".

"The sexualisation of women. This is the latest version of that," she said.

"It's not funny and it should not be the butt of jokes on radio shows, or in print or any comments."

Loading...

The WNBA is now in its 30th season and continues to go from strength to strength, whether its detractors like it or not.

A host of brilliant young players, headlined by Clark, are bending the realms of what was previously thought possible in the women's game.

Sport and politics are always more intertwined than people think, or like to admit, and unfortunately sport will always be wielded as a political tool by bad-faith operators for as long as it exists.

That is not a good enough excuse for the WNBA to be treated the way it so regularly is.

Cunningham may be passionate about defending women's sport, but has to know that she opened the door for the latest attack on her own league.

World.title: Sexual favours scandal rocks South Korea football association
World.content:
The Korean Football Association (KFA), the governing body of soccer in South Korea, has issued a public apology for "various controversies", including an allegation that payments were made for sexual favours for foreign referees.

South Korean broadcaster JTBC reported last Thursday, local time, that the KFA had provided such services to foreign referees on multiple occasions in 2011 and 2012, including when the referees were in the country for qualifying matches for the 2014 World Cup and the 2012 London Olympics.

In its news report, JTBC cited a 2016 sports ministry investigation that found the KFA had provided inappropriate entertainment to foreign referees on seven occasions between March 2011 and March 2012, including trips to massage parlours where the fees included the costs of sexual services.

South Korea qualified for the 2012 Olympic Games and the 2014 World Cup.

On social media, the KFA issued a public apology for several controversies, including the team's poor results at this year's World Cup and "media reports regarding events from over a decade ago that even many of our own staff members were unaware of".

"However, we wish to clearly state that such inappropriate conduct or misuse of corporate cards is absolutely not occurring at the association at present," the KFA said, as reported by BBC.

"Our association, which ought to bring joy and exhilaration to football fans through the fierce pursuit of goals and the fair sportsmanship that emerges in the process, has recently lost sight of its fundamental purpose and finds itself in a truly dire situation."

The allegations add to scrutiny of the association over a separate issue involving the appointment of former national team coach Hong Myung-bo.

Hong Myung-bo resigned after the 2026 FIFA World Cup. (Getty Images: Chung Sung-Jun)

Hong and KFA president Chung Mong-gyu both resigned following the World Cup.

Seoul police raided the KFA's offices on Thursday as part of an investigation related to Hong's appointment, police told Reuters.

Hong returned as national team coach in 2024 after a previous spell in charge from 2013 to 2014. His appointment drew scrutiny after the KFA abandoned a months-long search involving foreign candidates and selected Hong following a brief meeting.

The controversy resurfaced after South Korea's disappointing World Cup campaign ended in a group-stage exit.

Reuters/ABC

Tech.title: It looks like Apple’s iPhone 18 really will skip the fall launch this year
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to an Economic Daily News report spotted by MacRumors, executives for Apple supplier Pegatron confirmed during an earnings call that the iPhone 18 Pro series phones will launch this fall, but the base iPhone 18 won’t arrive until the first quarter of next year. The more affordable iPhone 18e and a new iPhone Air are also rumored to launch around the same time, in line with rumors that have been circulating for more than a year.

Analyst Ming-Chi Kuo and The Information both reported last year that Apple was planning to only launch its premium iPhones in fall 2026, and earlier this year another Apple supplier said one of its customers was postponing a phone launch to early 2027.

Along with the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple’s rumored “Ultra” foldable is reportedly launching this fall. The EDN report cites Pegatron execs saying that memory and chip shortages are causing the peak shipping seasons to shift, as its customers like Apple figure out how to spread out the parts they have and increasingly prioritize higher-priced models that have larger margins.

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel 11 phone preorders come with up to $350 in gift cards
Tech.content:
Brad Bourque is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Looking to get your hands on the latest Pixel devices? After weeks of leaks and rumors, Google has officially announced its next generation of Pixel phones and watches.

The base Pixel 11 starts at $899, the Pro and Pro XL are $1,099 and $1,299 respectively, and the Pro Fold starts at $1,899. The watch comes in two sizes, with the smaller 41mm model starting at $399, and the larger 45mm model starting at $429. The phones are available for preorder now, and will ship on August 20th, 2026.

If you’re looking to preorder an unlocked phone on its own, your main options are Best Buy, Amazon, and directly from the Google Store. All three are running a similar introductory deal, where you’ll receive a gift card for a future purchase at that retailer, with the value depending on which model you buy. The Pixel 11 includes a $100 gift card, the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL include a $200 gift card, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold includes a $350 gift card. Only Google lists an end date for the promotion, which is August 27th, 2026.

If you’d also like a Pixel Watch 5, Google and Amazon will give you additional credit towards that purchase instead of the gift card. The Pixel 11 and 41mm watch bundle is $1,168.99, effectively a $130 discount if you bought the two devices separately, but only in obsidian. The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL with a 41mm watch as a bundle is discounted by $250. The Amazon bundles include only the Wi-Fi versions of the Pixel Watch 5 and only in limited color combinations. The Google store will let you apply the credit to other in-stock variants. If you buy a Pixel 11 Pro Fold, you can opt for a 41mm Wi-Fi watch for free, with Amazon offering obsidian only and Google letting you choose your colors.

Each phone is powered by the new Tensor G6 processor, which Google says is capable of 25 percent faster web browsing and 15 percent improvement to app loading speeds over the Tensor G5. The camera and video features are a focus of the new Pixel 11 series phones. The new Magic Capture feature lets you forget about snapping a great shot, and instead stitches together a series of clips and photos from a longer video. All four phones also featuring upgraded batteries and fast charging, with wireless charging support for Qi2.2 up to 25W.

If you’re deciding which Pixel is right for you, make sure to check out our initial hands-on impressions for the new Pixel 11 series phones and the Pixel Watch 5.

Where to preorder the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL

The Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099 for the base model with 256GB of storage, and goes up to $1,219 for the 512GB model, or $1,449 for the 1TB model. The larger Pixel 11 Pro XL starts at $1,299 for the 256GB configuration, with the 512GB costing $1,419 and the 1TB model priced at $1,649. For both phones, the 256GB version has 12GB of memory, while the larger capacity models have 16GB of memory.

Apart from the screen size, resolution, and battery capacity, the two phones are otherwise identical to each other. They feature updated cameras, including a 50MP wide angle, 48MP telephoto with up to 5x optical zoom, a 48MP ultrawide sensor, and a 42MP selfie camera with a 103 degree field of view. The phones are available in four colors: canyon, fog, olive, and obsidian.

Where to preorder the Pixel 11

The Pixel 11 starts at $899 for the model with 256GB of storage, and the price rising to $1,019 for the 512GB model, both of which have 12GB of memory. The 6.3-inch display has a 1080 x 2424 resolution and 60-120Hz refresh rate, with HDR support up to 2000 nits, or 3000 nit brightness with HDR off. For cameras, the Pixel 11 sports a 48MP sensor wide camera, a 13MP ultrawide, a 10.8 MP telephoto with 5x optical zoom, and a 10.5MP selfie camera with a 95 degree field of view. The phone is available in four colors: frost, pistachio, hibiscus, and obsidian.

Where to preorder the Pixel 11 Pro Fold

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold starts at $1,899 for the base model with 256GB and 16GB of RAM, with a 512GB model for $2,019, and a 1TB option for $2,249 available as well. It’s available in two colors: olive and obsidian.

The only foldable phone in Google’s Pixel lineup, the 11 Pro Fold features a 6.5-inch external display, and a 8-inch internal display when opened. Both screens feature refresh rates up to 120Hz, and HDR support. The internal and front selfie cameras are 10MP sensors, and the main camera block features a 10.5MP ultrawide, 10.8MP telephoto with up to 5X optical zoom, and a new 48MP wide camera with upgraded light sensitivity.

Where to preorder the Pixel Watch 5

The updated Pixel Watch 5 comes in two sizes, with the 41mm model starting at $399, and the larger 45mm model starting at $429. In addition to faster processing and more memory, there are a variety of new features for exercising, like a workout builder, and a more accurate GPS in crowded areas. The watch adds a variety of new long-term health features under the umbrella of “Health Guardian” which can detect some medical emergencies, watch blood pressure trends, and keep track of insulin resistance.

Carrier offers and promotions

AT&T is offering a variety of discounts if you want to upgrade to the new phones or the Pixel Watch 5. Most notably, you can get a Pixel 11 Pro for free via 36 months of credits if you trade in a Pixel phone of any year or condition, although you’ll need to keep the service active for the duration and have a service of at least $80 a month. The same deal is available for a Pixel 11 Pro XL with qualified trade-ins. If you’re starting a new line and buying a device that’s $500 or more with an installment plan, you can also claim 50 percent off a Pixel Watch 5.

Tech.title: Twitch streamers can now opt out from training Amazon’s AI
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Twitch users can now opt out of allowing their content to be used to train Amazon’s generative AI models. Opting out means that “your streams, VODs, clips, stream chats, and pictures and text on your channel” won’t be used in “future training” of an Amazon AI model “whose purpose is to generate or synthesize text, audio, images, or video,” according to a Twitch support page.

Other “AI-supported” features like captions and safety tools will still function if you opt-out of generative AI training. However, if you participate in a chat on another person’s stream, “their opt-out preferences govern if that chat can be used for training,” Twitch says.

The “Training for Generative AI” toggle is present for me in Twitch’s settings under the Security and Privacy tab. It was toggled on when I found it, and I’ve asked Amazon if that’s the default.

Here’s the full text of Amazon’s description for the toggle:

Allow your channel content to train generative AI content models at Amazon. Turning this off does not opt you out of Twitch and Amazon using your channel content for other purposes described in the Twitch Privacy Notice, including using AI-supported Twitch features that benefit the community by facilitating streamer growth and monetization (such as real-time sponsorship campaign assistance), viewer discovery (such as recommendations), and community safety (such as AutoMod). Tech.title: How Google’s new Pixel 11 phones compare to last year’s models
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google just added four new phones to the Pixel family: the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. They’re slightly more expensive than their predecessors, but they come with some notable upgrades, including improved cameras and a new Tensor G6 chip that should deliver faster performance. The phones also have new photography tools, like Magic Capture, along with improvements to Gemini Intelligence, expanded Live Translate capabilities, and the ability to use Circle to Search directly through the camera.

To make deciding whether you’ll upgrade or hold onto your last-gen phone a little simpler, we’re focusing on comparing the specs of the 6.3-inch Pixel 11 and Pixel 10 models, as well as the 6.8-inch Pro XL models. If you’re curious about how the Pixel 11 Pro Fold compares to its predecessor (and to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 series foldables), we’ve got a spec comparison right here.

Before we get to the specs, here’s a breakdown of what’s new.

They’re more expensive, but you get more storage

The most obvious difference is that, like almost everything these days, they’re more expensive than before. The Pixel 11 starts at $899, $100 more than its predecessor, but Google has doubled the base storage to 256GB with 12GB of RAM. The Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099 — $100 more than the Pixel 10 Pro’s launch price — with the same 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM, and is available with up to 1TB of storage and 16GB of RAM. Meanwhile, Google’s larger 6.8-inch Pixel 11 Pro XL starts at $1,299 and offers the same storage and RAM configurations as the Pro.

Tensor G6 allows for even more AI features

Both the Pixel 11 and Pro phones run on Google’s new Tensor G6 chip, which the company claims should improve performance by up to 25 percent compared to its predecessor. The new chip also powers a host of AI upgrades, including improvements to Gemini Intelligence, which Google says can now pull more context from supported apps to proactively surface useful information. There are also new voice-to-text tools that remove filler words and clean up formatting, while writing assistance can use what’s on your screen to help draft, rewrite, and refine messages. Live Translate is also available on videos, podcasts, and voice messages, and Circle to Search now works directly through the camera, letting you identify objects, translate text, or search your surroundings without snapping a photo first.

The cameras get some notable upgrades inside and out

There are a number of camera improvements, too, along with new photography and video features. On the hardware side, the Pixel 11 has a slimmer camera bar that sits flush when paired with one of Google’s phone cases. It can also zoom in farther than its predecessor, reaching up to 30x for photos, while the Pixel 11 Pro series gets an updated 1/1.3-inch 50-megapixel sensor for its main camera and a redesigned telephoto sensor that Google says captures 32 percent more light. The Pro can also zoom up to 120x and features a 42-megapixel selfie camera. The Pro should be quicker at shooting in the dark, too, with Google claiming its Instant Night Sight can capture photos up to 4.5 times faster.

Google has made several software improvements as well. The new Magic Capture mode in the camera app automatically captures photos and videos to make them ready to share with a tap. Camera Looks let you create custom styles for photos, while the Pixel 11 Pro series can record stabilized video at up to 8K using Pro Stable Video with Video Boost. A new Creator Suite also features tools for trimming and rearranging clips, using a teleprompter while recording, and improving speech clarity, and it automatically saves clips to a designated project album.

How the Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 compare

Those are some of the biggest changes, but they’re far from the only differences between the two lineups. For example, both the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro offer an Extreme Charging Mode that prioritizes charging over other tasks for a faster boost when you’re short on time. The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL also gets HiLight, colored LEDs around the camera flash that can alert you to things, like calls when your phone is face down or when Gemini is activated.

Tech.title: Some Claude users are mad that Anthropic’s new watermarks will catch them using it at their jobs, classes
Tech.content:
Anthropic recently made the decision to watermark Claude’s outputs — inserting invisible code into the chatbot’s editorial text that marks it as AI-generated.

Anthropic rolled out this new policy to satisfy the EU AI Act’s Transparency Code, which now requires tech companies to label content that has been AI-generated or edited in a manner identifiable to computer systems. Yet while European regulators may be happy, some AI users are decidedly not.

One need look no further than Reddit to find evidence of brewing discontent, though other posters on the site are not in agreement. One of the more histrionic posts I came across was from a user named visionode, whose account is notably only three weeks old. According to visionode, the new watermarking system is a draconian conspiracy designed to victimize innocent chatbot users worldwide.

Visionode’s basic argument appears to be that, while savvy Claude users may be able hide evidence of their AI usage by paraphrasing or otherwise cleaning their outputs through other AI services, the average user of Claude will be caught.

“Who will get caught? You. The student who used Claude to reorganize a paragraph. The journalist who asked the AI to summarize a two-hundred-page transcript. The writer who had creative block and asked for synonyms. Those guys come out of the process with a digital tattoo on their forehead.”

Far be it from me to undermine visionode’s outrage, but those are not the best examples. A journalist asking AI to summarize a two-hundred-page transcript is not going to be bothered by a watermark attached to that summary, unless they are copying and pasting the summary verbatim into their article — which is plainly unethical and shouldn’t be happening.

It is equally unethical for a student who copies and pastes Claude’s output into an essay after asking it to “reorganize a paragraph.”

Other Redditors were also not particularly supportive of the poster’s outrage.

“Get a load of this guy,” one poster merely commented.

Another asked the OP to take “a deep breath.”

Visionode wasn’t the only one complaining. Another unhappy camper called the watermarks “unethical” and “disgusting” and argued that by using Claude, they had done the lion’s share of the work. In their view, the chatbot was merely a “tool” that had facilitated their arduous labor.

“I gave the instructions, context, decisions, and countless refinements, claude was the tool. If Claude starts watermarking the code or anything else it generates, what exactly is it claiming credit for?” the poster asked.

Again, other users dogpiled onto the critic.

“It’s not claiming credit though,” one user shot back. “It’s about being able to detect AI generated outputs because of the risks AI generated outputs can cause in various situations.”

“Bro couldn’t even complain about Claude without using Claude to write it,” another quipped.

Some critics have steered clear of the victimhood narrative and made slightly more nuanced arguments against Anthropic’s new policy.

For instance, one poster complained of a general hypocrisy in watermarking an editorial product that was, itself, generated by hoovering up other people’s work. “I think it’s a very sinister direction to take,” said the user. “I don’t use Claude to write anything but having an AI that watermarks your work is terrifyingly ironic given how many of the frontier models came by their training data.”

In general, however, users have tended to support the watermarking system as a sensible way to track material that was generated by algorithm. “There is literally no good argument for why this isn’t a good idea,” a user on another thread said. “The only reason you wouldn’t want this is to lie to people.”

Tech.title: AI nuclear power firm Fermi finally has a new CEO
Tech.content:
In Brief

Fermi, the AI nuclear power firm, has named a new CEO more than three months after firing co-founder Toby Neugebauer from the top executive post.

Fermi said Wednesday it has hired Lee McIntire, an independent member of the company’s board who has held chief executive positions at CH2M Hill and TerraPower, the nuclear power startup founded by Bill Gates.

Fermi America, which was co-founded by former U.S. Energy Secretary Rick Perry, is developing an AI campus in Amarillo, Texas, called Project Matador that will eventually use nuclear reactors to power data centers.

The announcement, along with Monday’s news that it had signed TensorWave as its first binding customer lease for its Project Matador campus, provided a welcome boost to Fermi’s stock. (The stock is up nearly 23% since Monday.) The young company took a hit in April when Neugebauer and CFO Miles Everson were pushed out of the company. Tech.title: Northrop’s robot space mechanic is a new way to keep satellites at work longer
Tech.content:
High above the Earth, a new generation of robots designed to keep satellites working longer is replacing its predecessor — quite literally.

This week, a spacecraft built and operated by Northrop Grumman called a Mission Extension Vehicle (MEV) unplugged from a communications satellite operated by the Australian firm Optus. For more than a year, the MEV spacecraft has been stuck to the back of the Optus satellite, keeping it in the right place in space so it can continue its mission.

Now, the satellite life-extension spacecraft is leaving to make room for its replacement. In July, four new Northrop spacecraft launched into orbit on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. One is called the Mission Robotic Vehicle (MRV), a powerful satellite equipped with two advanced robotic arms that was developed by DARPA, the U.S. military research organization. The other three are called Mission Extension Pods, or MEPs, smaller, simpler satellites that are essentially modular propulsion systems.

Those four spacecraft are currently headed for targets around 27,000 miles above the Earth. In 2027, the MRV will use its robotic arms to attach one of the MEP pods to the Optus satellite, which should keep it in orbit for years to come.

The satellites that provide communications or scan the planet with various sensors only last for so long. They typically fail when they run out of fuel to stay in the right place, not because their computers and transceivers stop working. The Optus satellite was launched in 2009, and designed for a 15-year lifespan. If all goes well, the satellite could fly — and generate revenue — for another six years.

Now, cheaper launch costs and lower-cost space components are making spacecraft repair missions a reality.

The goal is “a paradigm shift where we can see space as sustainable, with a more resilient architecture and infrastructure base where we can do things like spacecraft repairs, life extension, or even upgrades and maintenance of satellites,” according to Northrop’s director of logistics and servicing, Cassie Wong.

There are two MEVs in orbit right now, launched in 2019 and 2020, which have provided 10 years of life extension to three customers, including two different Intelsat spacecraft and the Optus satellite. MEV-1 will wait in a parking orbit for another customer, while MEV-2 is currently attached to its Intelsat customer until 2030.

The Mission Robotic Vehicle, or MRV, represents an evolution of the business model. Satellite operators buy and own the MEPs, which are permanently attached to their spacecraft. That frees up the MRV to service more vehicles, creating a cheaper offering.

The offering requires some serious technology chops. The vehicles need to autonomously approach one another and dock safely, not a simple task when both are moving at velocities of thousands of miles an hour. The MEVs use a docking probe to plug in and hang onto satellite thruster nozzles. Meanwhile, the MRVs will need to carefully attach the MEPs using their robotic arms.

Unlike most satellites, the MRV is designed to be refueled in orbit — in part, a proof of concept for the kind of capabilities other satellites will need if this kind of in-orbit servicing becomes a norm. Right now, the extra cost and weight of such adaptations keeps spacecraft operators from investing in them.

Indeed, the current trend in satellites is flying lots of cheap, effectively replaceable spacecraft in low orbits, as Starlink and Amazon LEO do. On the other hand, spacecraft keep getting bigger, and there are plenty of expensive, large satellites in orbit that could benefit from life extension. Wong hopes that the MRV will take on other missions in the future, adding new components to satellites as well as adjusting their orbits.

That’s likely to include defense customers, given the number of expensive satellites it owns in high orbits, and DARPA’s involvement in developing the MRV’s arms. Indeed, the U.S. Space Force has previously characterized a Chinese servicing spacecraft with robotic arms as a weapon, since it could theoretically grapple and degrade a rival satellite. Northrop says that its vehicles are focused on servicing missions.

The vehicle could also be used in LEO, Wong says, to extend the life with valuable assets there. The startup Katalyst Space is attempting a similar mission to extend the life of a NASA space telescope after malfunctions left its vehicle tumbling last month. The company has a fix in place and hopes to complete the mission.

Tech.title: Amazon will train on Twitch streamers’ content by default, unless they opt out
Tech.content:
The streaming platform Twitch will now use creators’ content to help train generative AI models for its parent company, Amazon. This move has inspired swift and concentrated backlash from the Twitch community, especially because creators are opted in to having their content used for this AI training by default.

For Amazon, these stream recordings are incredibly valuable, offering thousands of hours of audio and video content to help train AI models. But Twitch users worry that since creators have to manually opt out, they might be surrendering their content to train Amazon’s AI content models without even knowing it. This is especially concerning on a platform like Twitch, where creators are often recording livestreams of themselves and their voices for many hours per week.

Image Credits:Twitch /

In a stream on the official Twitch channel, Twitch Head of Community Mary Kish and Chief Product Officer Mike Minton addressed a live audience of nearly 3,000 aggrieved users, many of whom were posting anti-AI sentiments in the chat.

“Why is it not opt-in? That’s what everybody is spamming in chat. I get it. ‘Let me opt in versus making me opt out,’” Minton said. “Well, there’s an honest answer… If this was opt-in, nobody would opt in. That’s honestly the answer.”

Twitch knows that its community of streamers is largely opposed to the use of generative AI, since the most prevalent generative AI products are trained on books, images, videos, and other materials scraped from the internet without consent.

Even Twitch’s approach to breaking this news shows that the company is braced for backlash. Instead of telling the community that Amazon would begin training on Twitch users’ content, Twitch framed this change as “[adding] a setting that lets you opt out of having your channel content used to train generative AI content models across Amazon.”

In some cases, this created confusion among streamers about whether their content had already been fed to Amazon without their knowledge. When one user asked if their videos had already been used for training, Minton responded, “I don’t actually know the answer to that question because I don’t know what Amazon […] has done in terms of model training and what they’ve used and not used.”

Kish noted that Twitch is not unique in its use of user content for AI training. Meta, for example, uses public content from its platforms to train its own AI models, meaning that if your Facebook and Instagram accounts are public, then your data has probably already been used for Meta’s AI training. (If you live in the U.K., you can opt out of Meta’s training — if not, the only way to “opt out” is to use private settings, which isn’t feasible for creators who monetize their accounts.)

Kish said that even including an opt-out option on Twitch is “a reflection of reacting to this community’s voice that you are not wanting to train Gen AI models, and we want to give you that option.”

To opt out of AI training on Twitch, users can navigate to their channel settings (not the creator dashboard), select the security and privacy tab, scroll down to the option “training for generative AI,” and toggle it off.

Tech.title: Grubhub’s $24M FTC settlement is finally reaching diners and drivers
Tech.content:
Well over half a million Grubhub drivers and customers are set to receive a share of $23.8 million following allegations that the food delivery company misled workers about their potential earnings and engaged in other deceptive practices.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) announced on Wednesday that it’s distributing the money to 640,038 consumers, with most recipients receiving a check in the mail. Some will receive their payments through PayPal.

The payouts stem from a lawsuit the FTC and Illinois attorney general filed against Grubhub in December 2024. The complaint accused the company of a range of unlawful practices, including making misleading claims about how much drivers could earn, restricting customers’ access to their accounts and money, and listing restaurants on its platform without their permission.

Another allegation involved Grubhub’s restaurant listings. According to the complaint, the company had as many as 325,000 restaurants on its platform that were not affiliated with Grubhub. The FTC alleged that Grubhub used those listings to make its platform appear larger.

The complaint also alleged that Grubhub sometimes refused to remove restaurants after they asked to be taken off the platform. Instead, the company allegedly tried to convince some of those businesses to enter into paid partnerships.

The settlement required Grubhub to change how it operates in several areas. For instance, the company must be more accurate when advertising potential driver earnings, give customers a way to challenge account restrictions that leave them unable to access their accounts or funds, and obtain a restaurant’s consent before listing it on the platform.

Today’s announcement puts renewed attention on Grubhub’s treatment of its drivers and diners and the company’s broader business practices. Notably, it comes just one month after a federal judge granted final approval of another settlement worth nearly $25 million and involving approximately 60,000 Grubhub delivery drivers in California.

Grubhub also isn’t the only delivery company to face scrutiny. In the past, DoorDash has faced criticism and legal challenges over driver compensation, while Uber Eats has dealt with allegations involving customer charges and its relationships with restaurants.

This could account for much of its growing popularity among enterprises that have adopted it. The company says its customers include Mercedes-Benz, NASA, and Goldman Sachs.

Tech.title: As AI safety concerns mount, three pioneers make the case for staying open
Tech.content:
As projects like Pacing the Frontier look to major labs as a way to keep AI research safe, open source models have become a sore spot for the industry. With free distribution and little control over how they’re used, open-weight models aren’t easily controlled, leading some labs to treat them as downright scary.

But at the Ai4 conference in Las Vegas last week, three of the world’s most respected AI researchers — Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, World Labs CEO and co-founder Fei-Fei Li, and Coursera co-founder Andrew Ng — spoke out on the issue. And while they disagreed on particular tactics, all three made a powerful case for keeping AI open.

For the three speakers, the core concern was allowing a handful of major AI companies to control the pace of progress. When a few companies control access to a technology, as Apple and Google do with mobile operating systems, innovation can slow and the companies that control the platforms can influence what gets built on them.

Andrew Ng said that he worried about a similar dynamic emerging in AI. “I don’t want there to be gatekeepers,” Ng said. “That limits how all of us can access AI.”

Companies have an incentive to protect their competitive advantages, including by influencing the rules that govern the industry. That could create a dynamic where only the largest, best-capitalized firms have the resources to build the most advanced AI systems.

Ng’s solution was to maintain multiple providers, with models and companies competing rather than allowing a handful of players to dominate the field. “If I were to try to give one prescription, it would be to promote openness,” Ng said, “because AI is amazing technology and I want it to be in everyone’s hands.”

But not everyone agreed that open-weight models would help preserve that state of play. Hinton, in particular, drew a distinction between open source software, which makes the underlying code available for inspection and modification, and open-weight models, which release the parameters of a trained AI model to the public.

“Open source is great. You show people the code, and lots of people look at the lines of code and say, ‘Oh, there’s a bug.’ Open weights means you train a big model and then you give people the weights. That’s very different,” Hinton said. “I was against open [weights] because it makes it so easy for people to take these big foundation models, which are very expensive to train, and for much less money train them to do bad things like cyber attacks.”

But whatever his reservations, Hinton acknowledged that open-weight models are already a permanent fixture of AI. “I think that battle’s been lost. We now have open-weight models, so the barrier to lots of people getting these big models, which was the cost of training foundation models, that barrier has disappeared. It’s too late.”

Yet accepting reality didn’t mean ignoring the risks. Hinton’s position was clear: AI would continue to advance, and he thought that was largely a good thing. He said it would boost productivity and improve education and healthcare. “Worrying about the possible bad effects of AI and the things that intelligent beings might do when they’re smarter than us. I don’t think that’s unfair. I think it is unfair to label anybody who thinks like that as a fear-monger,” Hinton added.

Ng took a different view. The question, he argued, wasn’t whether open models were risky, but who controlled access and who would win the market. Whoever built the cheaper model would have the advantage. If China’s open-weight models gained widespread adoption across Asia, Africa, and/or the developing world, he warned, they could influence how billions of people encountered ideas about democracy, freedom, and human rights.

“One thing I hope we do is encourage American competitiveness and open source AI. It turns out that AI is a tremendous source of soft power. You can see the way China’s model has tremendous accomplishment with Africa, for example,” Ng said. “But my worry is because of all the lobbying in the U.S. and the fear-mongering, building open source AI in America is struggling to compete with open-weight models coming out of China, and my worry is that if China figures out a fundamentally more cost-efficient way to build AI, then things that are more cost-efficient have a fundamental business adoption advantage.”

Li pushed back on that framing. “It’s very dangerous to make this a dichotomy between complete openness all the way to complete closedness,” she said. “In complex software systems as well as scientific systems it’s much more nuanced.”

Li used nuclear physics as an example: Scientific papers are published openly, but uranium is regulated, while laboratory work falls somewhere in between. The lesson, she explained, was that openness doesn’t have to be an all-or-nothing choice. Different layers of the ecosystem can operate at different levels of openness.

She also highlighted collaborations between public and private institutions, such as the Human Genome Project. The resulting knowledge became a platform that others could build on, she said, allowing pharmaceutical companies to profit, scientists to advance their work and society to benefit.

“So I think we have to use [AI] as that kind of infrastructure,” Li said. “We need some levels of openness, both in scientific discovery, in education, in global partnership, as well as lucrative business models for entrepreneurs. But we also will accept closed-source systems. This debate, especially at the sweeping level of ‘we can only tolerate one,’ is a false debate. We need to get to a level of nuance.”

But everyone agreed that some level of regulation would be necessary to keep AI on the right track. “What we want to do is develop AI in a direction that helps people, and regulation will help us do that,” Hinton said. “You can’t leave it to people like Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg to decide how AI should be done.”

Tech.title: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings raises $2B to bring AI to the enterprise
Tech.content:
Thrive Holdings has raised $2 billion in new funding at a $12 billion valuation from investors like SoftBank, D1 Capital Partners, and Altimeter Capital.

Thrive Holdings is akin to a private equity firm for AI, buying traditional businesses like accounting firms and implementing AI into their workflows. So far, Thrive has focused on accounting and information technology, but part of Wednesday’s raise will go toward expanding a new vertical in physical assets. Key to that strategy is Thrive’s close relationship with OpenAI.

The New York Times was first to report the news.

The firm is a spinout of Thrive Capital, one of OpenAI’s major investors. In December 2025, OpenAI took an ownership stake in Thrive Holdings. Part of the deal involved OpenAI sending employees to work with Thrive’s companies to accelerate AI adoption.

That hands-on model of AI implementation has become a business in its own right, and may help explain investor enthusiasm behind Thrive’s latest fundraise. OpenAI and Anthropic have both partnered with large private equity firms to launch The Deployment Company and Ode with Anthropic, respectively — billion-dollar ventures that are building teams of elite engineers who embed themselves into enterprises and implement AI solutions into workflows.

The raise comes off the back of proven success for Thrive’s companies, which has surpassed 70 businesses on Thrive Holdings’ platforms. The company has focused on two pillars to date: Current, its accounting arm with more than 50 firms and more than 2,000 professionals, and Shield, its information technology arm with around 20 companies on the platform.

Current’s self-improving tax agents, dubbed TaxAI, processed more than 7,000 tax returns at 98% accuracy, lowering tax prep times at participating firms by over 30%, according to Thrive. Meanwhile, Shield’s AI products have sped up help desk resolution times by 36x, and the platform has doubled the number of custom AI agents deployed in the last month.

Part of Wednesday’s fundraise will help Thrive launch a third platform focused on regulatory services for the built environment, described by a spokesperson as: “the work required to get physical assets approved, built, certified, and kept in operation.”

“The U.S. needs to build and modernize more critical infrastructure, but projects are often constrained by local, technical, and regulatory complexity,” Anuj Mehndiratta, a founding member of Thrive Holdings, told TechCrunch. “This applies across data centers, manufacturing, healthcare, power, water, transportation, and other physical infrastructure.”

That sort of complexity is where Thrive, well, thrives — large, fragmented, mission-critical, and operationally complex. While Mehndiratta says AI won’t replace field work, local judgement, or professional sign-off, it can help ease manual workflows like research, reporting, permit preparation, inspection documentation, and compliance tracking.

“We think AI partnered with a lot of the experts and practitioners at these businesses can really help compress [regulatory bottlenecks], keep the safety standards high, but also be able to do it with less of a burden to the actual building of that and help it do it more efficiently, lower cost and do it faster,” Kareem Zaki, a founding member of Thrive Holdings, said in a statement emailed to TechCrunch.
